MY3a-1.claim: In January 2024 police in Cox's Bazar said that Rohingya who flee the Ukhiya camps and try to go to Malaysia or another country by sea would from then on be charged under the Overseas Employment and Migrants Act and sent to jail.
MY3a-1.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
MY3a-1.why_new: Cross-country Malaysia sea-route 'The law' covers Malaysia and Thailand law and Bangladesh practice, not this 2024 police policy of charging the passengers themselves.

MY3a-2.claim: On 5 January 2024 Cox's Bazar assistant judge Maitree Bhattacharya saw three Rohingya girls (two aged 12, one 14) from Balukhali camp being put on a wooden boat for Malaysia at Lombarighat on the Teknaf Marine Drive; police with her rescued them and arrested a trafficker, and in what was reported as the first Overseas Employment and Migrants Act case against Rohingya fleeing the camps the girls were sent to jail with the trafficker, bailed on 9 January and were to be returned to the camp, from where they must attend court.
MY3a-2.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
MY3a-2.why_new: New case; the cross-country Cases list starts its 2024 entries in October.

MY3a-3.claim: Police and Rohingya leaders said in January 2024 that in the previous five years law enforcers had rescued at least 5,000 Rohingya being trafficked to Malaysia by trawler from the Teknaf, Ukhiya, Cox's Bazar Sadar and Maheshkhali coasts, and that none of those rescued had been charged or jailed.
MY3a-3.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
MY3a-3.why_new: Cross-country gives 1,134 rescued in 2016-2023 [MA0058]; this source gives at least 5,000 Rohingya in about 2019-2023, a much larger figure (conflict).

MY3a-4.claim: On 16 January 2024 Malaysia's human resources minister, Steven Sim, and home minister, Saifuddin Ismail, spoke about Malaysia's review of its bilateral foreign-worker agreements with 15 countries including Bangladesh, saying labour was unevenly distributed across the economy, and the home minister said recruitment fees, other costs, contract clauses and health would be reviewed.
MY3a-4.why_new: The guide's 2024 closure account starts with the March 2024 deadlines; this January 2024 review announcement is missing. The guide counts 14 source countries elsewhere; Malaysia's ministers and its High Commissioner say 15.

MY3a-5.claim: In January 2024 Malaysia's human resources minister said the authorities had finished investigating five companies accused of promising hundreds of workers jobs and not giving them, that employers who hired such workers must pay their wages whether or not there is work, and that companies and people who break the law will not be allowed to hire migrant workers.
MY3a-5.why_new: Adds Malaysia's stated rule that wages are owed even with no work, relevant to ghost-job cases.

MY3a-6.claim: Malaysia's human resources minister said in January 2024 that 751 Bangladeshi migrant workers had filed cases with Malaysia's Labour Department claiming unpaid wages of about Tk 5.11 crore (at RM1 = Tk 23.26).
MY3a-6.why_new: A count of Bangladeshi wage claims at the Labour Department, not in the guide.

MY3a-7.claim: Prothom Alo reported in January 2024 that more than 70% of foreign workers in Malaysia came from Bangladesh, Indonesia and Nepal, and the remaining 30% from India, Vietnam, Pakistan and Thailand.
MY3a-7.why_new: Share of the foreign workforce by source country, not in Size.

MY3a-8.claim: Malaysia's home minister said in January 2024 that the government would also allow workers to be transferred between sectors in line with quotas.
MY3a-8.target_section: If you want to change employer
MY3a-8.why_new: Bears on the guide's Need to know on whether cross-sector moves are possible [J0063, F0077].

MY3a-9.claim: By UNHCR figures cited by researchers of North South University's Centre for Migration Studies in January 2024, 8,312 Rohingya refugees tried to reach Malaysia by sea in 2018-22, and 589 of them died at sea.
MY3a-9.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
MY3a-9.why_new: New UNHCR attempt and death count for 2018-22.

MY3a-10.claim: Centre for Migration Studies researchers wrote in January 2024 that traffickers first take Bangladeshis and Rohingya to Teknaf, then by boat to the Myanmar-Bangladesh sea border and on in small boats to Myanmar's Samila coast, where migrants pay traffickers in advance for the leg to Malaysia or Australia, in some cases more than was agreed in Teknaf; returnees put the cost of reaching Malaysia this way at Tk 4 to 5 lakh.
MY3a-10.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
MY3a-10.why_new: The Samila stop and the total Tk 4-5 lakh are new; cross-country gives only Tk 20,000-50,000 paid before boarding.

MY3a-11.claim: Centre for Migration Studies researchers wrote in January 2024 that Rohingya men already in Malaysia persuade parents in the camps to marry them their young daughters without dowry on the promise the wife can then go safely to Malaysia, and use Facebook, Imo and WhatsApp to draw young women; some who set out die at sea, some are sold as slaves in Myanmar, and some who reach Malaysia are sold there and cut off from their families.
MY3a-11.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
MY3a-11.why_new: Adds the no-dowry mechanism and the outcomes; cross-country mentions only a promise of marriage.

MY3a-12.claim: The same researchers wrote that traffickers use the family and friends of Rohingya already in Malaysia to persuade others in the camps to go, with promises of help after arrival.
MY3a-12.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
MY3a-12.why_new: Recruitment through relatives in Malaysia is not in the cross-country section.

MY3a-13.claim: RMMRU (Refugee and Migratory Movements Research Unit) reported in January 2024 that Malaysia was the second-largest destination for Bangladeshi workers in 2023, after Saudi Arabia, in a year when more than 13 lakh workers left Bangladesh, the most ever.
MY3a-13.why_new: Malaysia's rank among destinations in 2023 is not in Size.

MY3a-14.claim: In February 2024 at least 63 young men from Kazipur and Motmura unions in Gangni upazila, Meherpur, who went to Malaysia in November 2023, said they had been held for three months in a three-storey building in Kuala Lumpur with their passports taken, no work, visas mostly expired, not allowed out and fed only potatoes, dal and rice twice a day.
MY3a-14.why_new: New case of confinement and no work on arrival.

MY3a-15.claim: The Meherpur men said three cousins, Suruj Ali and Awal of Sahebnagar and Abdullah of Mohammadpur, took Tk 4 to 5 lakh from each of them, promising construction work at Tk 45,000 to 50,000 a month within 40 days of arrival; they alleged that 54 of them were taken on 6 November 2023 to an agency office on Road 4, Banani, Dhaka, kept there some days, flown out on 11 November, and had their passports taken by agency people after landing in Malaysia.
MY3a-15.why_new: Shows the village broker chain (relatives, a Dhaka travel agency) and the promised wage.

MY3a-16.claim: One of the three, Abdullah, told Prothom Alo he was a computer operator at the Dhaka travel agency involved, said everyone was expected to have work by 28 February and those who did not would be sent home, and did not answer whether money would be refunded; a Kazipur union member said more than a hundred people from the area went through a Dhaka travel agency and none got work.
MY3a-16.why_new: Travel agency (not a licensed recruiting agency) as the sender; adds to the tourist-visa route evidence.

MY3a-17.claim: The wife of one of the Meherpur men said he went after selling one decimal of their homestead land and borrowing Tk 3 lakh at high interest.
MY3a-17.why_new: Another borrowing example (homestead land sold plus high-interest loan).

MY3a-18.claim: Meherpur's Deputy Commissioner said in February 2024 that the district law-and-order committee had advised the families to file cases, but none was willing to.
MY3a-18.target_section: If an agency or broker takes your money
MY3a-18.why_new: Evidence of families' reluctance to file cases.

MY3a-19.claim: Migration experts told Prothom Alo in February 2024 that migrants already abroad collect job demand from their employers and send it to acquaintances and relatives at home, and that about 90% of demand letters reach Bangladesh this way.
MY3a-19.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: What is a demand letter?
MY3a-19.why_new: How demand letters reach Bangladesh; not specific to Malaysia, where demand goes through FWCMS.

MY3a-20.claim: By BMET data reported in February 2024, 97% of workers Bangladesh sent abroad in 2019-2023 went to just 10 countries, and Malaysia was one of eight countries that took more than 10,000 a year on average.
MY3a-20.why_new: Malaysia's place among the few large corridors (corridor comparison).

MY3a-21.claim: In its statement of 20 March 2024, Bangladesh Civil Society for Migrants (BCSM) said some syndicate agencies had sent workers to Malaysian firms that had no capacity to employ them, and in some cases to companies that did not exist under that name, after taking lakhs of taka from each worker.
MY3a-21.why_new: The guide cites BCSM's statement only for its demand for punishment [MA0017]; the ghost-employer allegation is new.

MY3a-22.claim: A Prothom Alo editorial of 24 March 2024 said Malaysia decided to stop new recruitment as pressure on its government from international human rights organisations grew.
MY3a-22.why_new: Adds the stated reason for the 2024 freeze. The editorial dates the 2022 reopening to August 2022; the guide says July 2022 [MA0021] (conflict).

MY3a-23.claim: Malaysia's tourism minister told its parliament that 3,604 Bangladeshis held MM2H passes on 31 January 2024, the fifth-largest group after China, Australia, South Korea and Japan, out of 56,066 active pass holders including dependants; Bangladeshis had once been third.
MY3a-23.why_new: Bangladeshi MM2H numbers are not in the guide.

MY3a-24.claim: Prothom Alo reported in March 2024 that under the December 2023 restructuring, MM2H applicants had to be 30 or older and hold a fixed deposit of RM5 million (Platinum), RM2 million (Gold) or RM500,000 (Silver), and spend 60 days a year in Malaysia.
MY3a-24.why_new: CONFLICT with the guide (official sources): age 25+ [Z0041], deposits USD 150,000/500,000/1,000,000 [E0106], 90 days a year for under-50s [E0103]. Likely the 2024 article reflects the December 2023 rules since revised; keep the guide's version unless re-verified.

MY3a-25.claim: Prothom Alo reported in March 2024 that Bangladesh Bank had permitted only a small number of institutions to invest abroad, and that there were allegations that money laundered out of Bangladesh was being invested in Malaysian 'second homes'.
MY3a-25.why_new: Supports the guide's point that money for MM2H can't legally leave Bangladesh [N0051].

MY3a-30.claim: A statement by several UN experts on 19 April 2024 said Bangladeshi migrant workers were being cheated in Malaysia and alleged that government officials of both countries were involved with the ring; Bangladesh's expatriates' welfare secretary, Md Ruhul Amin, said on 21 April the Ministry was reviewing it.
MY3a-30.why_new: The guide cites UN experts only on BOESL fees [YB0015]; the allegation of official involvement is new.

MY3a-31.claim: BOESL said on 16 May 2024 that it had been given the chance to send 10,000 workers to Malaysia at zero migration cost, had received demand for 1,695, and had sent 1,308 since October 2022 (331 in 2022, 839 in 2023 and 138 in 2024), with 73 more due to fly the next day.
MY3a-31.why_new: CONFLICT: adds a fourth count to the guide's Need to know (1,381 [A0059], ~1,500 [MB0059], 1,467 cleared [MA0063]); with the 73 the total would be 1,381, matching A0059. Also gives demand of 1,695 vs 'more than 10,000' [MA0063].

MY3a-32.claim: The 73 BOESL workers flying on 17 May 2024 at the employer's cost were to earn RM1,500 a month (Tk 37,500) with housing provided by the company; BOESL said it holds job fairs around the country, selects marginal and farm workers, and trains them on the work, Malaysian language and culture, and sending money home legally.
MY3a-32.why_new: Wage, housing and selection method for the 2022-24 BOESL route.

MY3a-33.claim: BOESL's managing director, Mallik Anwar Hossain, said in May 2024 that under the agreement, if a worker works properly for three years another member of his family can go to the same company at no cost.
MY3a-33.why_new: A BOESL benefit not in the guide.

MY3a-34.claim: The Wage Earners' Welfare Board's director general said in May 2024 that a Tk 1,000 insurance premium is paid in the name of zero-cost BOESL workers too, giving them five years' insurance cover and the Board's other help.
MY3a-34.target_section: Step 6: Orientation, BMET clearance and the flight
MY3a-34.why_new: Confirms zero-cost workers are insured; relevant to the 'zero cost' Need to know.

MY3a-35.claim: The managing director of Probashi Kallyan Bank, Mojibur Rahman, said in May 2024 that people going to Malaysia through recruiting agencies were spending Tk 4 to 5 lakh.
MY3a-35.why_new: Another 2024 cost figure, from a state bank head.

MY3a-36.claim: In May 2024, with the 31 May deadline approaching, the Dhaka-Kuala Lumpur fare, normally Tk 20,000 to 25,000 at most, rose to Tk 80,000 to 1 lakh by mid-month, and all seats from 27 to 31 May showed sold out on Biman's website.
MY3a-36.why_new: Airfare surge before the 2024 deadline is not in the guide; it explains why some cleared workers could not fly [MA0111].

MY3a-37.claim: Ethar Fariel Hamid, managing director of Fariel Tours and Travels, complained to the Prime Minister's Office on 26 May 2024 that Biman's special-flight tickets for Malaysia were not shown on the GDS (global distribution system) and Biman officials were profiting corruptly, and told Prothom Alo that tickets were opened on the GDS only for a bribe of Tk 20,000 to 25,000 each, pushing the price to Tk 1.05 to 1.10 lakh; Biman sources said special-flight fares started at Tk 68,000 and its acting marketing director said 99% were sold through the GDS.
MY3a-37.why_new: Bribery allegation over special-flight tickets; new.

MY3a-38.claim: Prothom Alo reported in May 2024 that in normal times the cheapest Dhaka-Kuala Lumpur ticket cost Tk 24,000 to 25,000, against Tk 14,000 to 15,000 from Kolkata, and the flight from Dhaka takes 3 hours 55 minutes.
MY3a-38.target_section: Step 6: Orientation, BMET clearance and the flight
MY3a-38.why_new: Normal fare level, useful against the Tk 45,000 airfare in BOESL's 2025 costing [YI0025].

MY3a-39.claim: The civil aviation minister, Muhammad Faruk Khan, said on 30 May 2024 that Biman was running three or four flights a day to Malaysia, that agencies had known a month ahead that 31 May was the last date but made no arrangements, and that on 29 May permission was given for a charter flight on an Air Cambodia aircraft requested by some people from Malaysia.
MY3a-39.why_new: Government's account of the last-week flight crunch; new.

MY3a-40.claim: On 31 May 2024 thousands of people crowded Dhaka airport, many without tickets, hoping to reach Malaysia before the deadline; Habibur Rahman of Natore, who had paid Tk 6.5 lakh raised by mortgaging land and a bank loan, had waited three days at the airport while the firm stopped answering his calls, and Rubel Mia of Narsingdi had paid Tk 6 lakh to a firm named Ahad Enterprise to go as a construction worker.
MY3a-40.placement: What happened to the stranded workers of 2024
MY3a-40.why_new: Airport scenes and named cases of the last day; new.

MY3a-41.claim: At least 10 other Malaysia-bound passengers at Dhaka airport on 31 May 2024 told Prothom Alo they had paid Tk 5 to 7 lakh each to the firms sending them.
MY3a-41.why_new: Upper end (Tk 7 lakh) above the guide's 2022-24 range of Tk 3.5-6 lakh.

MY3a-42.claim: The state minister for expatriates' welfare, Shafiqur Rahman Chowdhury, said on 1 June 2024 that Malaysia had given quota for more than about 5 lakh workers, that BAIRA could not give the Ministry a list of who had visas and when they would fly, which caused the flight problems, and that the Ministry had arranged about 22 special flights.
MY3a-42.why_new: Quota size for the 2022-24 round; the next day he gave 23 special flights (article d42dfb7f, 2 June 2024).

MY3a-43.claim: At a Ministry press conference on 2 June 2024, 101 agencies were said to have got approval for 5,26,676 workers in the 2022-24 round; not all got final approval from Malaysia, BMET cleared 4,93,642, of whom 4,76,672 went and 16,970 could not go in time.
MY3a-43.why_new: Official totals for the 2022-24 round; the guide's Size says 'about 4.5 lakh went' [A0001], other figures 5.5 lakh [MA0070].

MY3a-44.claim: On 2 June 2024 the Ministry formed a six-member committee headed by Additional Secretary (Employment) Nur Md Mahbubul Haque to investigate the 2022-24 corruption, report within 7 working days and work to get affected workers compensated; anyone could complain to it, including workers charged more than the Tk 78,990 cap.
MY3a-44.placement: What happened to the stranded workers of 2024
MY3a-44.why_new: The 2024 investigation committee is not in the guide.

MY3a-45.claim: The expatriates' welfare secretary, Md Ruhul Amin, said on 2 June 2024 that recruiting agencies would refund those who got clearance but could not go, that BAIRA had taken responsibility for this, and that agencies that did not refund would face legal action.
MY3a-45.placement: What happened to the stranded workers of 2024
MY3a-45.why_new: The promise behind the refunds; the guide says many got none [YI0011].

MY3a-46.claim: The secretary said on 2 June 2024 that employers come to the Malaysian airport to collect workers, that in the previous few months no employer had failed to do so, and that work was being arranged for the five thousand who had earlier found none.
MY3a-46.why_new: Ministry's claim, to set beside workers' accounts of no work on arrival.

MY3a-47.claim: The secretary said the Ministry had not allowed workers to be sent in the names of companies Malaysia had blacklisted.
MY3a-47.placement: What happened to the stranded workers of 2024
MY3a-47.why_new: Links to BAIRA's claim that 47 companies were blacklisted at the end (article d4c9264f).

MY3a-48.claim: Tanvir Mia (22) of Debgram, Akhaura, Brahmanbaria, for whom Tk 6.5 lakh had been paid a year earlier, according to his uncle, to broker Alamgir Hossain of Nayadil village and his brother in Malaysia for a supermarket job, had a flight date of 19 January cancelled and another flight cancelled at the end of May 2024; on Friday 31 May he fell from the train taking him home from Dhaka into the Meghna at Bhairab and went missing, and rescuers believed he had drowned.
MY3a-48.placement: What happened to the stranded workers of 2024

MY3a-49.claim: Tanvir's family said they trusted the broker because he had sent 30 people to Malaysia three days earlier, and his father sold 130 decimals of land for the trip and his own business.
MY3a-49.why_new: Shows how a broker's recent departures build trust, and a local broker with a brother in Malaysia.

MY3a-50.claim: After Tanvir's death in June 2024 his father said the brokers through whom he had tried to send his son had not contacted the family and had fled their homes.
MY3a-50.why_new: What happens with the broker after a failed departure.

MY3a-51.claim: People in the sector told Prothom Alo in June 2024 that Bestinet's contract with the Malaysian government ended on 31 May 2024, that Malaysia stopped taking workers so as not to renew it with this controversial company, but that the contract might now be extended by three years.
MY3a-51.why_new: Bestinet's contract term is not in the guide; conflicts in part with the Auditor-General finding that it had no formal contract [D0024].

MY3a-52.claim: Prothom Alo reported in June 2024 that against the Tk 78,990 cap workers had paid Tk 5.5 lakh on average in the 2022-24 round.
MY3a-52.why_new: Minor variant of the guide's Tk 5.44 lakh average [A0001]; low priority.

MY3a-53.claim: At a 4 June 2024 press briefing held on behalf of the panel of 101 agencies, it was said that 2 to 3% of cleared workers usually fail to go, that this time Malaysia blacklisted 47 companies near the end over various complaints so workers with visas under them could not go, and that few were stopped by air tickets.
MY3a-53.placement: What happened to the stranded workers of 2024
MY3a-53.why_new: The 47 blacklisted employers are a new cause of the 2024 stranding.

MY3a-54.claim: At the same briefing Ruhul Amin Swapan said the real number of workers who could not go was 5,000 to 6,000, that if diplomatic efforts to send them failed their migration costs would be returned, and that those affected could apply to get money back from the original agency; BAIRA's secretary general, Ali Haider Chowdhury, said the number was not certain and BAIRA would help the Ministry's committee list them.
MY3a-54.placement: What happened to the stranded workers of 2024
MY3a-54.why_new: CONFLICT: adds 5,000-6,000 to the guide's Need to know on the stranded count (16,970 / 17,777 / 31,304 / 40,000 / 11,000).

MY3a-55.claim: At the 4 June 2024 briefing BAIRA's secretary general, Ali Haider Chowdhury, said the last-minute rush would not have happened had Malaysia stopped visas from 15 May, and Ruhul Amin said Malaysia issued visas to the end, some on 30 May.
MY3a-55.placement: What happened to the stranded workers of 2024
MY3a-55.why_new: Late visa issue as a cause of stranding.

MY3a-56.claim: At the 4 June 2024 briefing MP Nizam Uddin Hazari said there is no such word as syndicate, that Malaysia selected the agencies and his was chosen 'coincidentally', and that he was not involved in sending workers or visa trading and only did processing; former BAIRA president and MP Benzir Ahmed said he had not gone to lobby Malaysia; BAIRA president Mohammad Abul Bashar said the two governments' agreement let Malaysia choose the agencies and the MPs had a right to do business.
MY3a-56.why_new: Replies of named agency owners; the guide gives Snigdha's executive director's reply [MA0029] but not Hazari's or Benzir's own.

MY3a-57.claim: The written statement at the 4 June 2024 briefing of the 101-agency panel said the 101 agencies included the government agency BOESL and Md Noor Ali's agency, Unit Eastern Private Limited, and accused a group led by Noor Ali of a media smear campaign ahead of the BAIRA election despite doing business in Malaysia under various names.
MY3a-57.why_new: The guide counts 100 agencies; BAIRA and the Ministry say 101 including BOESL.

MY3a-58.claim: Malaysia's High Commissioner in Dhaka, Haznah Md Hashim, said on 5 June 2024 that Malaysia was not extending the deadline for taking workers because the same deadline applied to all 15 source countries, and on BAIRA's allegation that e-visas had been issued on 2 June said Malaysia could not accept any allegation without proof.
MY3a-58.why_new: Malaysia's refusal of the extension is not in the guide.

MY3a-59.claim: The state minister said on 5 June 2024 that those holding a BMET card or e-visa who could not go would be arranged compensation.
MY3a-59.placement: What happened to the stranded workers of 2024
MY3a-59.why_new: Government's compensation promise; set against 'many got no refund' [YI0011].

MY3a-60.claim: On 9 June 2024, after the time for complaints to the committee had ended, the state minister said action would follow its investigation, that its report would recommend penalties, and that steps would be taken for those harmed.
MY3a-60.placement: What happened to the stranded workers of 2024
MY3a-60.why_new: Shows the complaint window was short; outcome of the committee unknown (possible Need to know).

MY3b-1.claim: In a Prothom Alo column of 10 June 2024, three North South University researchers wrote that some palm oil producers in Malaysia often refrain from recruiting Bangladeshi workers.
MY3b-1.why_new: The guide does not mention plantation employers avoiding Bangladeshi workers.

MY3b-2.claim: The same column of 10 June 2024 said Malaysia's step of taking no new Bangladeshi workers, announced in March 2024, was meant to curb recruitment irregularities and frame proper policy, and was mainly part of re-evaluating its labour policy and filling the quota for foreign workers set in the 12th Malaysia Plan.
MY3b-2.why_new: The guide gives the 2024 closure dates but not Malaysia's policy reasons (labour-policy review, 12th Malaysia Plan foreign-worker quota) as these researchers put them.

MY3b-3.claim: By 11 June 2024, 3,000 complaints from workers who could not go to Malaysia had reached the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare, the state minister, Shafiqur Rahman Chowdhury, said; a Ministry official told Prothom Alo that some applications carried several workers' names, so the number of workers complaining was higher and no final count had been made.
MY3b-3.why_new: The guide does not record the complaints stranded workers filed with the Ministry in June 2024.

MY3b-4.claim: The Ministry's probe committee on the Malaysia labour-market irregularities and the stranded workers, headed by additional secretary (employment wing) Noor Md Mahbubul Haque, was told to report within seven working days, was given five more working days on 11 June 2024, and was collecting information from the immigration department, 101 recruiting agencies and BAIRA, Prothom Alo reported.
MY3b-4.why_new: The guide's chronology has no entry for the Ministry's June 2024 probe committee.

MY3b-5.claim: On 11 June 2024 the state minister, Shafiqur Rahman Chowdhury, said no syndicate would be accepted, the government wanted every agency to be able to work, and legal action would be taken against agencies whose workers got no work after reaching Malaysia.
MY3b-5.why_new: Adds the June 2024 government position on agencies whose workers found no job; the guide's May 2024 entry has only that complaints were being looked into.

MY3b-6.claim: Md Rajib of Shibchar, Madaripur, went to Malaysia about three months before 17 June 2024 after spending Tk 4 lakh 90 thousand, had still found no job, was staying with an uncle in Kuala Lumpur for food and lodging, and had sent no money home, Prothom Alo reported.
MY3b-6.why_new: A named June 2024 case of a worker with no job after paying Tk 4.9 lakh; the guide's 2024 no-work examples are counts and one Facebook post.

MY3b-7.claim: Migrants told Prothom Alo in June 2024 that a large share of workers in Malaysia get no holiday even on Eid day and go to work instead of to Eid prayers; Md Raihan Kashem, in Malaysia six to seven years and working at a supershop in Malacca, said he gets no leave on Eid and has never in any year been given time to pray.
MY3b-7.placement: other: what happens in practice on Eid
MY3b-7.why_new: The guide gives the legal holiday entitlement (11 paid public holidays) but no account of practice on Eid.

MY3b-8.claim: On Eid day 2024 a migrant named Iftekhar Ahmed wrote in the Facebook group "Malaysia Kajer Khobor" that he was going to duty from 10 am to 10 pm and had been refused a single day off, and another migrant, Md Ashraful Ahmed, replied that he worked from 6 am to 8 pm.
MY3b-8.placement: other: what happens in practice on Eid
MY3b-8.why_new: Worker-reported 12- and 14-hour Eid shifts, against the guide's 12-hour legal limit and holiday pay rules.

MY3b-9.claim: Bangladeshi migrants in Malaysia use a Facebook group named "Malaysia Kajer Khobor" (মালয়েশিয়া কাজের খবর, Malaysia work news) and a Facebook page named "Malaysiaprobashi Bangladeshi", one of whose admins is Rakib Rana, Prothom Alo reported in June 2024.
MY3b-9.why_new: The guide names the 'Malaysia Probashi Bangladeshi' group only as a source; 'Malaysia Kajer Khobor' is not in it.

MY3b-10.claim: The state minister for expatriates' welfare, Shafiqur Rahman Chowdhury, told Parliament on 24 June 2024 that a six-member inquiry committee had been formed, that workers who held the required papers but could not go to Malaysia had been asked to complain to it, that more than 3,000 complaints had been received, and that steps would be taken so affected workers got compensation.
MY3b-10.why_new: The guide does not say stranded workers were told to complain to the inquiry committee or that compensation was promised in Parliament.

MY3b-11.claim: When a mentally ill worker or one with no address is found at Dhaka's Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, the Probashi Kallyan (expatriate welfare) desk or the Airport Armed Police phone Al-Amin (Nayan), manager of BRAC's Migration Welfare Centre, who by the US State Department's account at its June 2024 TIP Hero award had helped at least 34,000 returnees and trafficking victims.
MY3b-11.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Where victims and families get help
MY3b-11.why_new: Cross-country item 12 lists BRAC's airport help but not how the airport desk and Armed Police route vulnerable returnees to it.

MY3b-12.claim: Al-Amin, who received the US State Department's TIP Hero award on 24 June 2024, said he was himself trafficked when he went to work in Malaysia; Prothom Alo reported that this was in 2007, that he came home the same year, that he started work in BRAC's migration programme in 2017, and that he is president of Anirban Survivor Voice, the largest network of trafficking survivors in Bangladesh.
MY3b-12.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Where victims and families get help
MY3b-12.placement: other: who runs BRAC's airport help
MY3b-12.why_new: Background on the person behind BRAC's Migration Welfare Centre and Anirban Survivor Voice, both named elsewhere in the cross-country guide.

MY3b-13.claim: Supreme Court lawyer Tanvir Ahmed filed a writ in the High Court attaching two 2 June 2024 press reports (one headed that 30,000 young men's dreams were broken and Tk 20,000 crore looted, the other, in an English daily, that more than 3,000 workers got no ticket), questioning the authorities' inaction and seeking a three-member inquiry committee led by an additional secretary; on 30 June 2024 the bench of Justices Mustafa Zaman Islam and S M Masud Hossain Dolon orally asked the state to find out and report what a committee it had heard was formed had investigated and what action had been taken, giving it one week.
MY3b-13.why_new: The guide's High Court mentions are about the 2026 licence cancellations; the 2024 stranded-worker writ is not there.

MY3b-14.claim: At a meeting on 2 July 2024 the Ministry told Parliament's standing committee on expatriates' welfare that its inquiry committee had submitted its report on 24 June but the report was not complete, and that it had received about 3,000 complaints from workers who could not go; the standing committee, chaired by Imran Ahmad, asked the Ministry to establish exactly how many could not go, since the media reported 17,000.
MY3b-14.why_new: Adds that in July 2024 the government itself had no exact count of stranded workers; relevant to the guide's Need to know on the count.

MY3b-15.claim: On 4 July 2024 the state minister, Shafiqur Rahman Chowdhury, said that at a meeting the day before BAIRA had agreed that agencies would refund workers who could not go to Malaysia, paying back as much as each worker could prove he had deposited, by 18 July, and that agencies that did not would face legal action.
MY3b-15.why_new: The guide says only that many stranded workers got no refund and some a small one; the official refund order and its proof-of-payment condition are missing.

MY3b-16.claim: At a Ministry press conference on 4 July 2024 it was stated that 5 lakh 32 thousand workers had been approved to go to Malaysia, 4 lakh 76 thousand had actually gone, and 17,000 with clearance could not go.
MY3b-16.why_new: Conflict: the guide says about 4.5 lakh went in 2022-24 [A0001]; the Ministry's figure is 4.76 lakh, with 5.32 lakh approved.

MY3b-17.claim: The Ministry said on 4 July 2024 that it had formed the inquiry committee on 2 June, the committee had reported on 24 June, and 2,055 workers had complained to it with their papers.
MY3b-17.why_new: Gives the count of stranded workers who complained with papers (2,055), against the 3,000 complaint figure used in June.

MY3b-18.claim: On 4 July 2024 the state minister said more or less all of the 100 approved agencies were responsible, and that stranded workers would be put on a priority list to go first when the market reopened after a joint technical committee meeting due at the end of July; Prothom Alo reported that the papers of the workers who could not go were held, more or less, by all 100 agencies.
MY3b-18.why_new: The priority-list promise of 2024 is not in the guide, which records only the later BOESL route for 7,873.

MY3b-19.claim: By Bangladesh Bank data, remittance from Malaysia grew 35% in the 2023-24 fiscal year, which people in the sector attributed to the rise in workers going there in recent years; by BMET data, 2023, with more than three and a half lakh workers, was the highest year for departures to Malaysia between 2004 and 2023.
MY3b-19.why_new: The guide has no remittance figure for Malaysia; the 3.5 lakh for 2023 is already there [MA0013], the 35% growth and 20-year peak are not.

MY3b-20.claim: In the High Court writ over the stranded workers, the deputy attorney general, Tushar Kanti Roy, told the court on 15 July 2024 that the inquiry committee's report had come, and later told Prothom Alo the six-member committee's report had been submitted; the court set the next day for its order.
MY3b-20.why_new: Step in the 2024 High Court case, not in the guide.

MY3b-21.claim: On 16 July 2024 the High Court bench of Justices Mustafa Zaman Islam and S M Masud Hossain Dolon, on the writ filed on 3 June by lawyer Tanvir Ahmed, ordered the authorities to file an update every three months on the steps taken over the mismanagement that left workers with final clearance unable to go to Malaysia, and issued a rule asking why their inaction should not be declared illegal and why the money those workers deposited should not be ordered returned with profit and compensation paid.
MY3b-21.why_new: The High Court rule on refunds with profit and compensation for stranded workers is not in the guide.

MY3b-22.claim: On 25 July 2024 the state minister, Shafiqur Rahman Chowdhury, said BAIRA had told him 70% of the workers who could not go to Malaysia had got their money back, but the number could not yet be given: each worker was to confirm in writing once paid, BAIRA was to submit the list to the Ministry, and agencies that could not refund in full would face legal action.
MY3b-22.why_new: Conflict: the guide says many got no refund [YI0011]; BAIRA claimed 70% by July 2024, and the adviser later confirmed only 25% (see MY3b draft from 7680462f).

MY3b-23.claim: The state minister said on 25 July 2024 that a letter had been sent to the Malaysian government about the workers who could not go, and that whether the market would reopen would be known at the two countries' joint technical committee meeting the following month.
MY3b-23.why_new: Adds the July 2024 letter to Malaysia about stranded workers.

MY3b-24.claim: Prothom Alo reported in July 2024, in an article based on a press release, that there were about 1.4 million Bangladeshi expatriates in Malaysia, besides about 5,000 Bangladeshi students.
MY3b-24.why_new: Conflict in scale: the guide gives about 8 lakh work-pass holders [U0057]; this is a total-expatriate estimate (14 lakh) plus a student count the guide lacks.

MY3b-25.claim: Prothom Alo reported in July 2024 that in Bankra, on the Kopotakkho river at the border of Monirampur and Jhikargachha upazilas in Jashore, some local men tried to go to Japan illegally through brokers but were taken through Thailand and the jungle into Malaysia, came home after three years and then began sending people to Malaysia themselves; the bazar committee's general secretary said at least 10 of the area's multi-storey buildings are known as 'Malaysia buildings'.
MY3b-25.why_new: Shows how returnees from Malaysia became the village recruiters; the guide notes brokers are often returnees but has no origin story.

MY3b-26.claim: On 18 August 2024 Prothom Alo reported that the ACC had begun an inquiry, by a three-member team led by deputy director Mohammad Nurul Huda, into four former MPs who traded through the Malaysia syndicate, Nizam Uddin Hazari, Lt Gen (retd) Masud Uddin Chowdhury, Benzir Ahmed and A H M Mustafa Kamal, all of whom had been in hiding since the government fell on 5 August, Mustafa Kamal reportedly in Singapore.
MY3b-26.why_new: The guide dates the ACC's start only loosely ('2024-25'); this gives the August 2024 start and the four named ex-MPs.

MY3b-27.claim: The ACC's summary of the allegations, reported in August 2024, said high-ranking officials of both the Bangladeshi and Malaysian governments were involved with the syndicate, and did not separately name Ruhul Amin (Swapan), known as its ringleader.
MY3b-27.why_new: The ACC's own allegation of official involvement on both sides is not in the guide.

MY3b-28.claim: On 21 August 2024 the High Court bench of Justices Naima Haider and Sashanka Shekhar Sarkar ordered the ACC and Bangladesh Bank's Financial Intelligence Unit (BFIU) to investigate the allegations of irregularity, corruption and money laundering in sending workers to Malaysia and report within 90 days, on a writ filed on 15 July by S M Rafiq, proprietor of the recruiting agency United Export Limited.
MY3b-28.why_new: The court order behind the ACC/BFIU investigation is not in the guide.

MY3b-29.claim: The same High Court rule of 21 August 2024 asked why a full policy should not be ordered to ensure workers pay only the government-fixed Tk 78,990 for Malaysia, and why the agencies through whose negligence and irregularity more than 17,000 workers could not go in time should not be ordered to compensate them.
MY3b-29.why_new: Second pending High Court rule on compensation for stranded workers; not in the guide.

MY3b-30.claim: Recruiting agency owners told Prothom Alo in September 2024 that every worker going to Malaysia had to be registered in Migram, the software formally called FWCMS, whose registration fee was RM100 (about Tk 2,700), but about Tk 1,07,000 was taken per worker instead, of which the local collecting firm kept Tk 7,000 and sent the remaining Tk 1 lakh to Bestinet in Malaysia, the transactions being illegal.
MY3b-30.target_section: The processing agency: the toll gate
MY3b-30.why_new: Explains what the Tk 1,07,510 in the CID case [MA0117] was: the guide has the figure but not the RM100-fee mechanism.

MY3b-31.claim: Prothom Alo reported in September 2024 that only syndicate members' names were in Migram and that members paid the RM100 fee per worker through an e-wallet; two recruiting agency owners said Bestinet allowed the RM100 fee to be paid from the e-wallet only after Tk 1,07,000 had been deposited for that worker.
MY3b-31.target_section: The processing agency: the toll gate
MY3b-31.why_new: The e-wallet gate is not in the guide.

MY3b-32.claim: The money had to be deposited at the Madani Avenue, Dhaka, office of Catharsis International, the agency of Ruhul Amin (Swapan), whose staff took in crores of taka in cash every day, two syndicate members told Prothom Alo; S M Rafiq, managing director of United Export Limited, a syndicate member, said every syndicate agency had to deliver Tk 1,07,000 a worker to the Catharsis office.
MY3b-32.target_section: The processing agency: the toll gate
MY3b-32.why_new: Where and how the toll was paid; not in the guide.

MY3b-33.claim: Fakhrul Islam, managing director of the agency Human Resource Development Centre and BAIRA's joint secretary general, said in September 2024 that the agency he sent workers through took a syndicate fee of Tk 1,52,000 a worker just for arranging the BMET clearance, which in fact costs Tk 6,000, and that the airfare and all the worker's other costs had to be paid separately.
MY3b-33.target_section: The processing agency: the toll gate
MY3b-33.why_new: The guide has Fakhrul's Tk 1,52,000 figure [MA0060] but not that it bought only the clearance (real cost Tk 6,000) with airfare on top.

MY3b-34.claim: Records of Bangladesh's RJSC (the Registrar of Joint Stock Companies and Firms) show Bestinet registered in Bangladesh on 24 March 2014 as Bestinet Bangladesh Limited, with Aminul Islam bin Amin Nur as chairman and Mohammad Ruhul Amin as managing director; Prothom Alo also reported that Amin held 10,000 of its 12,000 shares and Ruhul Amin 2,000, that on 28 March 2019 Amin's shares were transferred to Ruhul Amin and his brother Saiful Islam became a director, and that in 2022 the company was renamed Catharsis Solutions Limited.
MY3b-34.why_new: Documentary business link between Amin and Swapan; the guide reports only allegations that they worked together.

MY3b-35.claim: Ruhul Amin told Prothom Alo that Bestinet Bangladesh had no connection with Malaysia's Bestinet and that Aminul Islam gave up his share because he got no business in Bangladesh; on 20 June 2024 he called the allegations of taking and laundering money false and said both governments gave all approvals and agencies with good contacts in Malaysia got approval after heavy lobbying.
MY3b-35.why_new: Swapan's own response; the guide says both deny wrongdoing [YA0045] but has not his words or his account of how agencies were approved.

MY3b-36.claim: On 2 January 2023 ("last year" in a September 2024 report), acting on a BAIRA letter, the Ministry wrote to the High Commission in Kuala Lumpur that most agencies selected through FWCMS lacked the facilities and capacity to recruit and send workers, that automatic selection let them charge high migration costs, and that although 12 visa centres were approved, only FWCMS's Dhaka office, MEFC (Malaysia Employment Facilitation Centre), issued workers' e-visas; it asked for visas to be issued from several centres.
MY3b-36.why_new: The guide has no record of the Ministry's own 2023 letters or of MEFC's monopoly on e-visas. Note: 'last year' in a Sept 2024 article reads as 2023, though the surrounding text could mean 2024; a reviewer should confirm.

MY3b-37.claim: MEFC's office is in Catharsis Tower in Banani, Dhaka; Malaysia-bound workers' passports were submitted there for the visa and agencies collected them there, sources told Prothom Alo in September 2024.
MY3b-37.why_new: Where the passport actually went for the e-visa in 2022-24; not in the guide.

MY3b-38.claim: On 9 May 2023 the Ministry wrote to the High Commission in Kuala Lumpur asking it to take up with Malaysia complaints from several agencies that Bestinet was not allocating e-wallet top-ups, a problem several Malaysian employers had also reported to Malaysia's home ministry.
MY3b-38.why_new: Shows the Ministry knew of the Bestinet gate in 2023; the guide says the Ministry never acted [MA0046].

MY3b-39.claim: Prothom Alo reported in September 2024 the allegation that about Tk 5,000 crore was laundered to Malaysia as syndicate fee at Tk 1 lakh a worker and another Tk 3,750 crore through the visa trade, at least Tk 8,750 crore in all, a large share of the USD 1.12 billion (about Tk 11,000 crore) Bangladesh Bank recorded as remittance from Malaysia in the 2023-24 fiscal year.
MY3b-39.target_section: Where a Tk 5.5 lakh deal goes
MY3b-39.why_new: A laundering estimate the guide lacks (it has the Tk 24,000 crore business and Tk 6,500 crore fee figures).

MY3b-40.claim: Clearances for 4 lakh 92 thousand 416 workers were taken in the names of the 100 syndicate agencies in a little over a year and a half, and at least half of those job letters are alleged to have been bought, at an average of RM6,000 (Tk 1.5 lakh) a worker, Prothom Alo reported in September 2024.
MY3b-40.target_section: The demand letter: the first price
MY3b-40.why_new: Gives a clearance total (4,92,416) and an RM price per bought visa for 2022-24; the guide has Tk 1.6 to 2 lakh to middlemen [A0002]. Conflict on totals with Size (4.5 to 4.76 lakh went).

MY3b-41.claim: In a letter of 22 August 2024 to the Chief Adviser, BAIRA member Mostafa Mahmud alleged that Aminul Islam bin Amin Nur and Ruhul Amin had also built a Malaysia syndicate in 2017 and that over the two rounds the ring looted Tk 17,544 crore.
MY3b-41.why_new: New total and date; the guide has Mostafa Mahmud only on the 2017 complaints [MA0065].

MY3b-42.claim: S M Rafiq, managing director of United Export Limited, itself a syndicate member, wrote to the Prime Minister's Office on 28 May 2024 that the main figures in sending money from Bangladesh to Malaysia were Ruhul Amin (Swapan) and his Malaysian partner Aminul Islam bin Amin Nur.
MY3b-42.why_new: An allegation from inside the syndicate; the guide lists United Export only among the 49 cancelled licences.

MY3b-43.claim: Iftekharuzzaman, executive director of Transparency International Bangladesh (TIB), said in September 2024 that workers from neighbouring countries go to Malaysia at the employer's cost while Bangladesh's rules are different, and that a ring in Malaysia acts as the representative of the Bangladeshi ring.
MY3b-43.why_new: TIB's view is not in the guide.

MY3b-44.claim: As of September 2024, 3,604 Bangladeshis had settled in Malaysia under its "Second Home" programme, Prothom Alo reported.
MY3b-44.why_new: The MM2H section has no count of Bangladeshi participants.

MY3b-45.claim: On 24 September 2024 the expatriates' welfare adviser, Asif Nazrul, said it had been confirmed that 25% of the 17,000 workers who could not go to Malaysia had got their money back, and that refunds to all of them would be ensured.
MY3b-45.why_new: Conflict: BAIRA claimed 70% refunded by July 2024 (a7e606e6); the government confirmed 25% in September 2024. The guide says only that many got no refund.

MY3b-46.claim: The expatriates' welfare adviser, Asif Nazrul, announced on 24 September 2024 that migrants could now repay their Probashi Kallyan Bank loan instalments by sending remittance directly to the bank, which had not been possible before, and that 12 commercial banks had agreed to lend to migrants once Bangladesh Bank gave a credit guarantee.
MY3b-46.why_new: Cross-country Loans gives PKB terms but not repayment by remittance; whether the 12-bank scheme started is unknown (2024 announcement).

MY3b-47.claim: At the expatriates' welfare adviser's press conference on 24 September 2024, the Ministry stated that sending a worker abroad needed approvals from three bodies and that its own recruitment permission would no longer be required, that brokers would be registered, and that recruiting agencies would be given category certificates based on experience.
MY3b-47.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: BMET clearance and the smart card
MY3b-47.why_new: Conflict: the cross-country guide says that on 4 November 2026 the Ministry told BMET to give no clearance for 12 countries without the Ministry's recruitment permission [F0187]; this 2024 announcement dropped that permission generally.

MY3b-48.claim: The adviser said on 24 September 2024 that VIP service for migrants at the airport would start within a month, first for those arriving from the Middle East, with every VIP facility except the lounge and a special immigration desk.
MY3b-48.why_new: A 2024 announcement; whether it was delivered is unknown, so it may belong only as a Need to know.

MY3b-49.claim: BAIRA members said at a press conference on 3 October 2024 that because of corruption and irregularity 50,000 workers could not go to Malaysia, 17,000 of whom had completed every step, and that 95% of recruiting agencies were discriminated against by the syndicate.
MY3b-49.why_new: Conflict: adds a 50,000 count to the guide's list of stranded-worker figures (16,970, 17,777, 31,304, about 40,000, about 11,000).

MY3b-50.claim: At the 3 October 2024 press conference, BAIRA's joint secretary general, Fakhrul Islam, read a statement naming former BAIRA secretary general Ruhul Amin (Swapan) as the syndicate's main ringleader, built with former MPs and ministers including Benzir Ahmed, Nizam Hazari, Lt Gen (retd) Masud Uddin Chowdhury and Awami League leader Mohiuddin Mohi, and saying no action had been taken against them.
MY3b-50.why_new: Adds a dated BAIRA allegation; the guide's Objections list starts in May 2025.

MY3b-51.claim: BAIRA's eight demands of 3 October 2024 included ending Malaysia's power to select Bangladeshi recruiting agencies, letting the employer choose the agency, a central online system from the Ministry so all agencies could send workers at low or no cost, and sending the workers stranded by the syndicate again at low cost and free of the syndicate.
MY3b-51.why_new: Earlier BAIRA demands than the May 2025 memorandum the guide records.

MY3b-52.claim: At a joint press conference in Dhaka with the Chief Adviser, Muhammad Yunus, on 4 October 2024, Malaysia's Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said his government would give immediate attention to 18,000 Bangladeshi workers going to Malaysia in a first phase, subject to all conditions being met, and that workers must not be treated as modern slaves.
MY3b-52.why_new: The 18,000 pledge is not in the guide; it later sent 7,873 through BOESL.

MY3b-53.claim: About eight lakh Bangladeshis were working in Malaysia in October 2024, about four and a half lakh of whom had migrated between August 2022 and May 2024, Prothom Alo reported.
MY3b-53.why_new: Matches the guide's 8 lakh (end-2025) and 4.5 lakh; adds an October 2024 date point. Low priority.

MY3b-54.claim: On 4 October 2024 President Mohammed Shahabuddin, meeting Malaysia's Prime Minister, called Malaysia the second-largest destination for Bangladesh's workers and asked Malaysia's cooperation in sending more.
MY3b-54.why_new: The guide does not rank Malaysia among Bangladesh's destinations.

MY3b-55.claim: The expatriates' welfare adviser, Asif Nazrul, said on 5 October 2024 that the 18,000 workers Anwar Ibrahim promised to take were not new workers but those who had completed every step and could not go, that a promise does not mean certainty, and that Bangladesh would formally request through its embassy that the promise be carried out.
MY3b-55.why_new: Identifies the 18,000 as stranded workers; not in the guide.

MY3b-56.claim: Asif Nazrul said on 5 October 2024 that Bangladesh had made three proposals to Anwar Ibrahim: reopen the closed market, open recruitment to all agencies instead of a few, and consider raising Bangladeshi workers' wages.
MY3b-56.why_new: The guide's Status starts in June 2026; this is Bangladesh's 2024 position. Low priority.

MY3b-57.claim: On 5 October 2024 Bangladesh's Wage Earners' Welfare Board and PERKESO, the social security organisation under Malaysia's labour ministry, signed a cooperation memorandum on the health, occupational safety and welfare of Bangladeshi workers in Malaysia, under which every Bangladeshi worker there is to be registered with PERKESO.
MY3b-57.target_section: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job
MY3b-57.why_new: The WEWB-PERKESO memorandum is not in the guide.
MY3b-57.h2: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job

MY3b-58.claim: As stated at the signing on 5 October 2024, 12 lakh 15 thousand 536 Bangladeshi workers had registered with PERKESO, 7 lakh 11 thousand 655 of them active; by August 2024, 11,439 had received temporary disablement benefit totalling about RM15 million (Tk 37 crore), 364 permanent disablement benefit totalling RM1.27 million, and 175 funeral benefit totalling RM870,000.
MY3b-58.target_section: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job
MY3b-58.why_new: Evidence that PERKESO claims do pay Bangladeshis, with counts; the guide gives the schemes but no payout numbers.
MY3b-58.h2: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job

MY3b-59.claim: The adviser said on 5 October 2024 that an assistant would accompany outgoing workers at every stage at the airport and that a special lounge for migrants was being set up, with the space chosen, and might open within about a month.
MY3b-59.why_new: A 2024 announcement; whether the lounge and assistants exist in 2026 needs checking.

MY3b-60.claim: Mohammad Jamal of Cox's Bazar, persuaded by a broker named Ayub to go to Malaysia on a Tk 4 lakh deal, was taken with nine others in July 2023 by small boat from Gorjonia in Ramu upazila to a small fishing trawler carrying 73 people, five of them girls under 18; after three days the trawler's hull split at the Myanmar border, the passengers surrendered to Myanmar's navy, and he spent 11 months 19 days in a Myanmar jail before coming home with government help, Prothom Alo reported in October 2024.
MY3b-60.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
MY3b-60.why_new: A named 2023 case with the broker, price, departure point and outcome; not in the cross-country Cases.

MY3b-61.claim: Jamal said Bangladeshi prisoners in the Myanmar jail did all the work, from growing vegetables to cooking, and were fed rice-water at about 7 am, some rice with dried chillies at 11 am and rice once more at 4 pm; the government brought 173 Bangladeshis home from Myanmar's prisons in April 2024.
MY3b-61.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
MY3b-61.why_new: Detention in Myanmar after a failed boat journey; the cross-country section has Myanmar prison cases but not these conditions or the April 2024 return of 173. Note: the article places Jamal among the 173 returned in April but quotes him as returning in July.

MY3b-62.claim: Kamal (a pseudonym) of Teknaf made a Tk 1 lakh deal with a man named Abu to go to Malaysia, to be repaid after he found a good job; brokers pressed for Tk 3 lakh ransom, Malaysian police chased the boat into Indonesian waters, the Bangladeshis on board sank the trawler after two of them died in a quarrel with Rohingya passengers, the Indonesian navy rescued them, and after 11 months' detention there the Bangladesh government brought them home, at a total cost to him of Tk 2 lakh 30 thousand, he told Prothom Alo in October 2024.
MY3b-62.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
MY3b-62.why_new: Shows the pay-after-arrival deal and ransom at sea; the cross-country Cases lack an Indonesia ending.

MY3b-63.claim: Kamal said that during three months at sea passengers got plain rice, chilli and a glass of water once a day, those who died of hunger were thrown into the sea, anyone who asked for food or water was beaten, and the brokers collected money from families while torturing passengers.
MY3b-63.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
MY3b-63.why_new: Adds a survivor's account; the section has the Coast Guard's general description.

MY3b-64.claim: Manik Molla of Teknaf said in October 2024 that he had been looking for seven and a half years for his youngest brother Shakil, who left by sea for Malaysia at 17; about two years earlier a broker told him Shakil was in a Malaysian prison, took money from the family, and then disappeared.
MY3b-64.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
MY3b-64.why_new: A second scam on families of the missing (a broker claiming news of the missing person); not in the section.

MY3b-65.claim: Local brokers mainly target teenagers and young men, promising a job paying a lakh of taka with little outlay; people aged 18 to 35 with money are offered onward travel through Malaysia and Indonesia to Australia, the United States or New Zealand, and women are promised good jobs in hotels, motels, parlours or shopping malls, Prothom Alo reported in October 2024.
MY3b-65.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
MY3b-65.why_new: Adds the lures used on Bangladeshis (the section's lures are mostly about Rohingya).

MY3b-66.claim: By UNHCR's figures, 8,312 Rohingya refugees tried to reach Malaysia by sea from 2018 to 2022, and 589 of them died at sea.
MY3b-66.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
MY3b-66.why_new: A 2018-22 death count the section lacks.

MY3b-67.claim: Sohel, son of the widow Hasina Akter of Karachi Para village in Teknaf, boarded a boat for Malaysia and was not heard from again; the government told her he was held in a Malaysian prison, and she said the government would bring him back once all papers were submitted, Prothom Alo reported in October 2024.
MY3b-67.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
MY3b-67.why_new: Shows families must submit papers for the government to bring back a detained person; the how is missing (Need to know).

MY3b-68.claim: Three North South University researchers wrote in Prothom Alo on 9 October 2024 that the Bangladesh government had tried business-to-business (B2B), government-to-government (G2G) and G-plus-B2B models to solve the Malaysia problem and none had yet proved effective, and that because of powerful syndicates, brokers and middlemen Bangladeshi workers were forced to bear high costs.
MY3b-68.why_new: The guide names G2G Plus for 2016-18 only; this names all three models. Opinion; low priority.

MY3c-1.claim: An explosion at a chemical factory in Malaysia at about 11:30 am on the Thursday before 14 October 2024 burned three Bangladeshi workers from the same Ramzanbeg area of Munshiganj municipality over most of their bodies; Jabbar Ali (42) died on the Friday, Abu Taher (32) at dawn on the Saturday and his nephew Abdus Salam (24) at about 5 pm on the Sunday while under treatment, Prothom Alo reported on 14 October 2024.
MY3c-1.why_new: The guide has the death procedure but no case of a workplace explosion; a dated case of three deaths in one factory blast.
MY3c-1.h2: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job

MY3c-2.claim: Jabbar Ali's nephew Khairul Islam said the three workers burned in the October 2024 Malaysian chemical-factory blast lay on the road for an hour and a half afterwards, and that some of them might have survived if treatment had started in time.
MY3c-2.why_new: Family's account of delayed emergency care after a workplace accident; not in the guide.
MY3c-2.h2: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job

MY3c-3.claim: On 14 October 2024 the Munshiganj Deputy Commissioner, Fatema Tul Jannat, said the district was in contact with the Bangladesh High Commission in Malaysia on how to bring home quickly the bodies of the three workers killed in the factory blast, while the families demanded that the government bring the bodies quickly.
MY3c-3.why_new: Shows the district administration's role in repatriation of bodies; the guide's procedure runs through the Welfare Board and does not mention the DC's office.
MY3c-3.h2: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job

MY3c-4.claim: Taslima Begum, mother of Abdus Salam, said she borrowed Tk 3.5 lakh at interest from various people to send him to Malaysia about a year and a half before October 2024 through her brother Abu Taher; Salam could not work for his first six months, sent some money within a year, and she had repaid Tk 1.5 lakh including interest and still owed lenders Tk 2 lakh.
MY3c-4.why_new: A concrete 2023 cost (Tk 3.5 lakh, below the guide's Tk 4.5-6 lakh range), the six months without work, and the debt left when a worker dies; the guide has survey percentages but few individual cases.

MY3c-5.claim: Abu Taher had worked in Malaysia for 10 years at the same company and, because the company was good, took his nephew Abdus Salam there about a year and a half before October 2024, relatives said.
MY3c-5.placement: Through a relative in Malaysia: case
MY3c-5.why_new: A case of the relative route into the relative's own company; the guide describes the route but gives no case.

MY3c-6.claim: Late on Tuesday night 15 October 2024 Teknaf police raided a house in Dakshin Lambari, Teknaf Sadar union, Cox's Bazar, and rescued 20 people gathered to be trafficked to Malaysia by sea, 12 Rohingya including women and children and 8 Bangladeshis, and detained three brokers, Luna Begum and Md Riduan of Dakshin Lambari and Md Abdullah of Kachubunia, Sabrang union, the Teknaf Model police station OC Muhammad Gias Uddin said.
MY3c-6.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
MY3c-6.why_new: The cross-country Cases list has 12 and 14 Oct 2024 and 14 Dec 2024 but not this 15 Oct raid, which included 8 Bangladeshis.

MY3c-7.claim: The eight Bangladeshis rescued in Teknaf on 15 October 2024 came from Patenga in Chattogram, Whykong in Teknaf, Ghonarpara in Cox's Bazar municipality, Munshir Deil in Maheshkhali, Kauarkop in Ramu and PM Khali in Cox's Bazar Sadar, and the OC said an organised ring had gathered them for Malaysia in exchange for large sums of money.
MY3c-7.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
MY3c-7.why_new: Shows the sea route also recruits Bangladeshis from Chattogram and Cox's Bazar coastal upazilas, not only camp Rohingya; the cross-country section frames it mainly as Rohingya.

MY3c-8.claim: When police and the Coast Guard detained 26 Rohingya at Inani beach, Ukhiya, on the morning of 14 October 2024 as they were being taken to Malaysia, another 80 to 90 Rohingya escaped, Prothom Alo reported.
MY3c-8.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
MY3c-8.why_new: The 14 Oct Inani case is already in the cross-country Cases list; this adds only that 80 to 90 more escaped.

MY3c-9.claim: Dhaka Metropolitan Detective Branch police arrested the former expatriates' welfare minister Imran Ahmad in Banani, Dhaka, on the night of Sunday 20 October 2024, and on 21 October Magistrate Mehera Mahbub of the Dhaka Chief Metropolitan Magistrate's court allowed three days' remand in the Paltan police station case under the human trafficking law, against the 10 days police sought.
MY3c-9.why_new: The guide does not name Imran Ahmad, the minister during the 2022-24 round, or his arrest.

MY3c-10.claim: The Paltan police station trafficking case was filed on 3 September 2024 against 103 people, among them former minister Imran Ahmad, former secretary Ahmed Munirus Saleheen, former MP and M International managing director Lt Gen (retd) Masud Uddin Chowdhury, and former MP Benzir Ahmed of Ahmed International; the complainant is Altab Khan, owner of Afia Overseas.
MY3c-10.placement: Timeline item: correct date of the Paltan case
MY3c-10.why_new: CONFLICT: the guide dates Altab Khan's Paltan case '3 September 2025' (twice, incl. the March 2026 Masud Uddin Chowdhury item); this article of 21 October 2024 says 'গত ৩ সেপ্টেম্বর', i.e. 3 September 2024. Also adds the named accused (Imran Ahmad, Ahmed Munirus Saleheen). Note the article prints 'M International' where the guide has Five M International.

MY3c-11.claim: According to the police remand petition in the Paltan case, when Malaysia's labour market opened on 1 October 2022 Altab Khan obtained demand letters from Malaysian companies through his own licence, but when he went to the expatriates' welfare ministry, Imran Ahmad and the ministry's secretary told him the workers had to be sent through the 100 licences of their syndicate, and Tk 1.5 lakh per worker was then demanded for visa processing.
MY3c-11.target_section: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut
MY3c-11.placement: other: How the 2022-24 syndicate was formed (allegation in the Paltan case)
MY3c-11.why_new: Adds the allegation that the minister and secretary themselves routed demand letters to the 100 syndicate licences. Minor difference: the petition says the market opened 1 October 2022; the guide says Malaysia reopened in July 2022 (the MoU/opening vs first departures). Target is the H4 'Who controls it' or 'The processing agency: the toll gate'.

MY3c-12.claim: The Paltan police remand petition, by investigating officer Sub-Inspector Nazmul Hasan, says the complainant was threatened after pointing out that the government-to-government arrangement allowed Tk 78,990 per worker, and that Tk 24,000 crore was laundered through the Malaysia trafficking syndicate.
MY3c-12.why_new: The guide has the Tk 24,000 crore figure from sector people and RMMRU; this is the police's own petition stating it.

MY3c-13.claim: The police remand petition alleges that Imran Ahmad, the principal accused, helped the trafficking ring by having his wife's elder brother's son open an app named 'Ami Probashi', and that his ring created discrimination among businesses although there are more than two thousand recruiting agents.
MY3c-13.placement: other: allegation against the then minister
MY3c-13.why_new: The guide does not mention the allegation linking the Ami Probashi app to the minister's family; relevant because Ami Probashi is a platform migrants use.

MY3c-14.claim: In a notice reported by Prothom Alo on 4 November 2024, the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment announced recruitment of Bangladeshi workers for a plantation sector in Malaysia, with 31 January 2025 as the last date for those workers to enter Malaysia.
MY3c-14.placement: What happened to the stranded workers of 2024 / Status history: plantation window
MY3c-14.why_new: CONFLICT/gap: the guide says the corridor has been shut to new workers since 31 May 2024 with no exception before the 2025 stranded-worker scheme; this records a Ministry-announced plantation-sector window in Nov 2024 to Jan 2025.

MY3c-15.claim: The November 2024 plantation notice required the medical test, the visa, BMET clearance, pre-departure orientation and the air ticket all to be completed by 15 January 2025, and said no money beyond the government-fixed migration fee of Tk 78,990 was to be paid to a recruiting agent or anyone else.
MY3c-15.why_new: Shows the Tk 78,990 cap still applied in the Nov 2024 window; the guide's cap section refers only to the July 2022 order.

MY3c-16.claim: The November 2024 notice told plantation workers to learn the job terms, pay and benefits from the recruiting agent, to deal money with no one but an approved recruiting agent, to make every payment against a written receipt or document or through a bank account, and to verify the agent on the Ministry's website or through the call centre 16135.
MY3c-16.why_new: Mostly consistent with Step 1 'Before paying'; adds that the Ministry's own notice told workers to verify the agent via its website or 16135. Low priority if Step 1 already covers it.

MY3c-17.claim: On 4 October 2024 Malaysia's prime minister gave an assurance that Malaysia would take 18,000 workers, according to Prothom Alo's timeline of the interim government's first 100 days.
MY3c-17.placement: What happened to the stranded workers of 2024
MY3c-17.why_new: The guide's stranded-worker timeline starts the remedy only in 2025; this dates the first Malaysian commitment (4 Oct 2024, Anwar Ibrahim's Dhaka visit).

MY3c-18.claim: The Chief Adviser opened a lounge for migrants at the airport on 11 November 2024, according to Prothom Alo's timeline of the interim government's first 100 days.
MY3c-18.why_new: Dates the opening of the airport migrants' lounge the guide lists (it does not say this is the same 'Probashi Lounge'); low priority, arguably cross-country.

MY3c-19.claim: Law Adviser Asif Nazrul said on 20 November 2024 that he hoped delivery of renewed passports to migrant workers in Malaysia and other countries would start from 10 December, that officials had told him foil paper for printing passports was being brought in, and that passport problems affected not only Malaysia but many Middle Eastern countries.
MY3c-19.target_section: How long you can stay and renewing
MY3c-19.why_new: The guide gives the passport fee in Kuala Lumpur but nothing on the late-2024 printing backlog that held up renewals (which renewals of the PLKS depend on).

MY3c-20.claim: Asif Nazrul said in November 2024 that there was no crisis in issuing e-passports but that migrant workers want MRP (machine-readable) passports rather than e-passports, that the MRP is outdated, and that the national aim is to move from MRP to e-passports.
MY3c-20.target_section: How long you can stay and renewing
MY3c-20.why_new: The guide mentions only the e-passport; adds that workers abroad preferred MRP renewals in 2024. Arguably CROSS-COUNTRY: The passport office.

MY3c-21.claim: A Malaysia-based Bangladeshi expatriate with 21 years of life abroad wrote in Prothom Alo on 24 November 2024 that about 15 lakh expatriates live in Malaysia.
MY3c-21.why_new: CONFLICT: the guide says about 8 lakh held work passes at end-2025; this is a writer's unsourced estimate of all Bangladeshis living there (would include the undocumented). Use only as a Need to know if at all.

MY3c-22.claim: The same writer said in November 2024 that migrants coming for services at the office in charge of e-passports in Malaysia were perhaps being lightly struck by security guards of the private company handling passports while many crowded and pushed, and guessed, without knowing for sure, that the pushing may have been the reason.
MY3c-22.target_section: How long you can stay and renewing
MY3c-22.why_new: Ground-level detail on the passport office in Malaysia (the guide names the ESKL charge but not conditions there).

MY3c-23.claim: The writer said that because Bangladesh missions expect migrants to know all the rules and have no time to explain them, many migrants hire brokers and pay extra to avoid harassment over passports, travel passes and document attestation.
MY3c-23.target_section: How long you can stay and renewing
MY3c-23.why_new: Shows brokers operate around High Commission services in Malaysia; the guide does not mention this.

MY3c-24.claim: Former ambassador M Humayun Kabir, president of the Bangladesh Enterprise Institute, said in an interview published on 1 December 2024 that Bangladesh's labour market in Malaysia had closed and had reopened on the Chief Adviser's initiative.
MY3c-24.placement: What happened to the stranded workers of 2024
MY3c-24.why_new: CONFLICT: the guide (and other Dec 2024-Jan 2025 articles in this batch) say the market stayed closed; this is a commentator's claim, likely referring to the 18,000-worker assurance. Include only if useful as an example of mistaken 'Malaysia has opened' claims (see CROSS-COUNTRY myth 'Malaysia has opened again').

MY3c-25.claim: Malaysia's Immigration Department said that in a coordinated operation at three places in Cheras, Kuala Lumpur, on the night of Wednesday 11 December 2024 it rescued 11 Bangladeshis aged 30 to 38 from a trafficking ring believed to be led by three Bangladeshis, and arrested three main suspects aged 35 to 38 and a 32-year-old Bangladeshi woman with one of them.
MY3c-25.why_new: A case of Bangladeshis trafficked and exploited by Bangladeshi-led rings inside Malaysia; the guide's Cheras mention is a July 2026 smuggling transit house, a different case.

MY3c-26.claim: In the 11 December 2024 Cheras operation, Malaysia's Immigration Department said in a statement that it seized 17 Bangladeshi passports, 20 mobile phones, RM800 and USD 800 in cash and two cars, that the victims had been trafficked and exploited by the syndicate for financial gain, and the rescued were in its care while the investigation continued; Director General Datuk Zakaria Shaban confirmed the rescue of the 11.
MY3c-26.why_new: Shows what happens to rescued trafficking victims (held in Immigration's care); the guide has nothing on this.

MY3c-27.claim: Expatriates' Welfare Secretary Md Ruhul Amin told Prothom Alo in December 2024 that the two countries would meet soon to reopen Malaysia's labour market, closed since June 2024, and that Brunei had been opened and workers were going to Russia.
MY3c-27.placement: What happened to the stranded workers of 2024
MY3c-27.why_new: Dated official statement in the gap between the closure and the 2025 joint technical group; minor.

MY3c-28.claim: By BMET data reported on 18 December 2024, more than 11 lakh workers went abroad in 2022, 13 lakh in 2023 and 9 lakh in the first 11 months of 2024; overseas employment fell further after Malaysia closed in June 2024 and rose again on Saudi Arabia, which took 60% of the year's workers and more than 80% in October and November.
MY3c-28.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Which countries can I go to for work right now?
MY3c-28.why_new: Corridor context (Malaysia's closure and Saudi dependence) for the cross-country doc; historical, may be superseded.

MY3c-29.claim: At about 4 am on Sunday 29 December 2024 police raided Abdul Amin's house on a hilltop in Moddhom Kachchhapia, Baharchhara union, Teknaf, Cox's Bazar, rescued 66 people gathered to be trafficked to Malaysia by sea (18 men, 11 women and 37 children; 5 Bangladeshis and 61 Rohingya from the camps), detained five members of the ring and recovered four rifle bullets, a ramdao and a kirich (machete and blade).
MY3c-29.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
MY3c-29.why_new: Not in the cross-country Cases list.

MY3c-30.claim: Police said the Baharchhara house was the ring's den: people were gathered there through brokers with promises of a better life, jobs and, for unmarried women, marriage; those brought from the Rohingya camps were first charged Tk 20,000 each, and the ring intended to hold them and extort more money by force on the pretext of getting them to Malaysia.
MY3c-30.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
MY3c-30.why_new: Confirms the Tk 20,000 first payment (cross-country has Tk 20,000-30,000) and adds that the first payment is followed by forced extortion while held.

MY3c-31.claim: By BMET data reported by Prothom Alo on 3 January 2025, more than 3.5 lakh workers went to Malaysia in 2023, but after the market closed in June 2024 fewer than one lakh went in all of 2024, a fall of more than two lakh.
MY3c-31.why_new: The guide gives 2022 and 2023 departures but no 2024 figure.

MY3c-32.claim: In 2024, 90% of the 10 lakh Bangladeshi workers who went abroad went to five countries, Saudi Arabia, Malaysia, Qatar, Singapore and the UAE, and as of January 2025 the Malaysian and UAE markets were closed and recruitment to Oman stopped, leaving Saudi Arabia the only large market open, BMET data and Prothom Alo reported.
MY3c-32.why_new: Corridor comparison (audit item 4: Bangladesh numbers vs other corridors); could also go CROSS-COUNTRY.

MY3c-33.claim: A Prothom Alo editorial of 6 January 2025 said Malaysia's market closed for all source countries because of allegations of a ring (syndicate) being formed, that not even everyone registered to go could go, and that Bangladesh raised the problem with Malaysia's prime minister on his short visit to Dhaka after the interim government took office, with no progress known since.
MY3c-33.why_new: Largely in the guide (closure for all countries, blamed on the Bangladeshi syndicate); adds only that as of 6 Jan 2025 no progress was known after the Anwar visit. Low priority.

MY3c-34.claim: Chief Adviser Muhammad Yunus asked Malaysia's High Commissioner in Dhaka, Mohd Shuhada Othman, at a meeting reported by Prothom Alo on 13 January 2025, to give Bangladeshi workers multiple-entry visas so that they could go home easily when needed.
MY3c-34.target_section: Going home on leave and coming back
MY3c-34.why_new: POSSIBLE CONFLICT: the guide says the yearly PLKS renewal already includes a multiple-entry visa for Bangladeshi workers; the Chief Adviser's January 2025 request implies workers lacked one then. Worth a Need to know.

MY3c-35.claim: At the same January 2025 meeting Yunus asked Malaysia to let in the 18,000 Bangladeshi workers who could not join work by the May 2024 deadline, and High Commissioner Mohd Shuhada Othman said a joint technical committee of Malaysian and Bangladeshi officials had been formed on the matter, had met in Kuala Lumpur on 31 December 2024 and was to meet again the next day.
MY3c-35.placement: What happened to the stranded workers of 2024
MY3c-35.why_new: The guide lacks the joint technical committee and its meetings (31 Dec 2024, 14 Jan 2025).

MY3c-36.claim: At midnight on Monday 20 January 2025 Navy and police rescued 19 people, two Bangladeshis and 17 Rohingya from Ukhiya-Teknaf camps, gathered in huts at the house of Zafar Alam in the hilly Madhyam Kachchhapia area of Baharchhara union, Teknaf, to be trafficked to Malaysia by sea; Zafar Alam (30) was caught after a chase, the others fled, and a case was being prepared, the Teknaf OC said.
MY3c-36.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
MY3c-36.why_new: Not in the cross-country Cases list.

MY3c-37.claim: On 22 January 2025, about a hundred workers who had been unable to go to Malaysia, some wearing burial shrouds, blocked one side of the SAARC Fountain intersection at Karwan Bazar, Dhaka, from 9 am, chanting against the syndicate and demanding to go to Malaysia and to meet the Chief Adviser, then moved to the front of the expatriates' welfare ministry after police cleared them.
MY3c-37.placement: What happened to the stranded workers of 2024
MY3c-37.why_new: The guide's stranded-worker list has no account of the workers' protests.

MY3c-38.claim: Expatriates' Welfare Secretary Md Ruhul Amin said on 22 January 2025 that the technical committees of the Bangladesh High Commission in Malaysia and of Malaysia's Home Ministry had met twice, that Malaysia had agreed in principle, that another meeting was due in February, that he hoped the matter would be final by April, and that 18,000 workers would go in phases.
MY3c-38.placement: What happened to the stranded workers of 2024
MY3c-38.why_new: Fills the 2025 gap in the guide's stranded-worker timeline.

MY3c-39.claim: The secretary said on 22 January 2025 that the workers' list had been sent to Malaysia, the method was not yet fixed and would be discussed at Malaysian minister level, sending would start within 15 days of Malaysia's decision, and efforts were being made so that the workers would not face a new burden of costs to go.
MY3c-39.placement: What happened to the stranded workers of 2024
MY3c-39.why_new: Set against the guide's fact that BOESL later charged them another Tk 1,62,500 each: the Ministry had said in Jan 2025 it was trying to avoid new costs.

MY3c-40.claim: The secretary said that, as of two days before 22 January 2025, recruiting agencies had refunded the money of 81% of the workers who could not go to Malaysia and submitted lists with the workers' signatures to the Ministry, that the deadline for the rest was Thursday 23 January, and that action would be taken against agencies that did not refund.
MY3c-40.placement: What happened to the stranded workers of 2024
MY3c-40.why_new: CONFLICT: the guide says 'Many got no refund and some a small one [YI0011]'; the Ministry claimed 81% had been refunded by Jan 2025 (amount refunded per worker not stated). Reviewer should reconcile.

MY3c-41.claim: Prothom Alo reported on 22 January 2025 that 16,970 workers who had completed every step and held final clearance could not reach Malaysia by the 31 May 2024 deadline, that the protesting workers put the number at 18,000, and that the government had promised to recover their money from the recruiting agencies.
MY3c-41.placement: What happened to the stranded workers of 2024
MY3c-41.why_new: Adds the 18,000 figure (workers' own count, also used by both governments) to the guide's Need-to-know list of stranded counts.
