MY3c-42.claim: On the afternoon of Saturday 25 January 2025 the Bangladesh Navy raided a traffickers' den in the Kachchhopia hills, Baharchhara union, Teknaf, rescued 17 men, women and children held hostage for trafficking to Malaysia by sea, 3 of them Bangladeshis and the rest Rohingya from Ukhiya and Teknaf camps, and arrested a trafficker named Ali Abdullah, Lieutenant Commander Afzal Hossain of the Navy's Teknaf contingent said.
MY3c-42.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
MY3c-42.why_new: Not in the cross-country Cases list.

MY3c-43.claim: Baharchhara union parishad chairman Amjad Hossain said in January 2025 that trafficking syndicates bring Rohingya from the Ukhiya-Teknaf camps to several points on the Baharchhara coast, lure them with promises of Malaysia, hold them in the hills and demand ransom, and that police, RAB and Navy operations had rescued about 150 such victims in January 2025 alone.
MY3c-43.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
MY3c-43.why_new: Adds a January 2025 count of rescues; the cross-country numbers run to January 2025 (600 caught in the year) but not this monthly figure.

MY3c-44.claim: Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mohammad Rafiqul Alam said on 27 January 2025 that the Bangladesh High Commissioner met Malaysia's Home Minister Saifuddin Nasution Ismail on 5 December 2024 about the roughly 18,000 workers who missed the 31 May 2024 deadline, and the Home Minister proposed a Joint Technical Group of Malaysian Immigration and High Commission representatives to take them in phases.
MY3c-44.placement: What happened to the stranded workers of 2024
MY3c-44.why_new: The guide has no account of how the stranded-worker scheme was set up.

MY3c-45.claim: The spokesperson said the Joint Technical Group met on 31 December 2024 and 14 January 2025, and that Bangladesh, after checking its list of more than 17,000 workers with Malaysian stakeholders, informed them of an initial list of 7,964 workers identified as eligible to enter Malaysia in the first phase; the group would decide by what process they would go.
MY3c-45.placement: What happened to the stranded workers of 2024
MY3c-45.why_new: Differs from the guide's 7,873 later cleared through BOESL: 7,964 was the initial first-phase eligible list in Jan 2025. Both may stand with dates.

MY3c-46.claim: The 2024 annual report of the digital migration platform Ami Probashi, reported on 5 February 2025, says Malaysia remained the second largest destination for Bangladeshi workers in 2024 but departures there fell sharply to 93,000, and names Malaysia's new labour policy as the main reason.
MY3c-46.why_new: Gives a 2024 Malaysia figure (93,000), consistent with BMET's 'fewer than one lakh'; the guide has no 2024 figure. Note the Paltan case alleges the Ami Probashi app was set up by the then minister's relative.

MY3c-47.claim: By the Ami Probashi 2024 annual report, 10,09,146 Bangladeshi workers went abroad in 2024, 27% fewer than the 13,90,811 of 2023, with 62% going to Saudi Arabia; enrolment in technical training centre courses fell to 1,12,166 from 2,36,270, and women's share of BMET registrations rose from 2.78% to 4.79%.
MY3c-47.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Which countries can I go to for work right now?

MY3c-48.claim: On 5 February 2025 a section of BAIRA (the recruiting agency owners' association) held a human chain in front of the expatriates' welfare ministry, where its leaders said the Amin-Swapan ring was manoeuvring to form a syndicate again around the reopening of the Malaysian market; several BAIRA leaders then gave the ministry secretary a memorandum, signed by 12 members including Riazul Islam, Noman Chowdhury, Khandaker Abu Ashfaq and Md Fakhrul Islam, alleging that the syndicate of Malaysian national Amin Noor and his Bangladeshi partner Ruhul Amin alias Swapan had extorted Tk 1,07,000 from each worker sent to Malaysia and demanding strict legal action against the two.
MY3c-48.why_new: The guide's objections list starts on 5 May 2025; this earlier memorandum gives the Tk 1,07,000 per-worker figure BAIRA attributes to Amin and Swapan (the guide's toll range Tk 1.07-1.52 lakh cites other sources).

MY3c-49.claim: BAIRA members' memorandum of 5 February 2025 said that every year a syndicate hoards air tickets and sells each at double the price or more, ruining poor outgoing workers, and asked for action against it and for a labour fair for migrant workers.
MY3c-49.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Who pays for the air ticket?
MY3c-49.why_new: Cross-country ticket-hoarding allegation; the Saudi attestation point in the same memorandum belongs to the Saudi guide.

MY3c-50.claim: Kuddus Bepari (33) of Majumdarkandi, Rajoir, Madaripur, who had worked in Malaysia for 7 years and came home in August 2024 to see his newborn child, was frustrated because the Malaysian labour market was not going well, and the local broker Monir Sheikh, learning of it, lured him into a Tk 16 lakh 'body contract' to reach Italy through Libya, according to police, family and local sources.
MY3c-50.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Recruited while abroad or just back
MY3c-50.why_new: The cross-country 'In Malaysia' bullet has only a general BRAC statement; this is a named case of a Malaysia worker on home leave recruited onto the Libya route.
MY3c-50.h2: Dalal scams: the usual tricks and how to spot them

MY3c-51.claim: Kuddus Bepari, sent from Dhaka to Egypt in early November 2024 and on to Libya, and his brother-in-law Sujon Howlader (39), who also paid broker Monir Tk 16 lakh, were put on an engine boat from the Benghazi coast on 24 January 2025 after about two months in a detention house; the boat sank within hours, Sujon's death was confirmed by his wife Munni Begum and Kuddus was missing, believed dead by his family.
MY3c-51.why_new: Adds two named victims to the cross-country January 2025 sinking (which has two other Rajoir men).

MY3c-52.claim: To pay broker Monir Sheikh, Kuddus Bepari wrote two bighas of land worth Tk 40 lakh to the broker's wife, Hamida Begum; Monir ran a tailoring shop at Rajoir bazar until about two years earlier, married his three daughters to men living in Libya whom locals say are linked to traffickers and mafias there, has bought land worth at least Tk 5 crore in his wife's name in seven months, and, locals say, makes each contract for Tk 16 lakh.
MY3c-52.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: The contract price and the final price
MY3c-52.why_new: Shows payment in land rather than cash and the broker-to-Libya family chain; not in cross-country.

MY3c-53.claim: A broker of another Madaripur ring, speaking anonymously in February 2025, said local brokers only collect people and money for Bangladeshi brokers living in Libya, taking Tk 12 lakh to send a person to Libya and Tk 4 lakh more for the 'game' (the sea crossing), and that most local brokers in Madaripur now work for Miraj Howlader of Mridhakandi, Shikarmangal union, Kalkini, whom he called a big mafia figure in Libya.
MY3c-53.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: The contract price and the final price
MY3c-53.why_new: Gives the split of the Tk 16 lakh price (12 + 4); not in cross-country.

MY3c-54.claim: Madaripur's Additional Superintendent of Police (Administration and Finance), Bhaskar Saha, said in February 2025 that by family accounts three people from Rajoir upazila had died and seven were missing, presumed dead, after the recent sinking, that no family had yet come to file a case, and that police were hunting several named brokers.
MY3c-54.why_new: The cross-country 'February 2025, Rajoir' item lacks the 3 dead / 7 missing count and that no case had been filed.

MY3c-55.claim: A February 2025 piece in Prothom Alo's expatriate section said Bangladeshi workers are seen at every tourist spot in Cameron Highlands, Pahang, and that Bangladeshis exclusively dominate the vegetable farms there.
MY3c-55.why_new: Ground detail on where Bangladeshis work (agriculture in Cameron Highlands); low priority, a reader's piece.

MY3c-56.claim: On 11 March 2025 BAIRA members met the expatriates' welfare adviser, Asif Nazrul, and asked that no ring be allowed to form again in the Malaysian market, saying that under the previous government MPs and ministers had formed a ring and plundered it; BAIRA leader Khandaker Abu Ashfaq said they had made that request.
MY3c-56.why_new: Adds a dated BAIRA approach to the adviser between the Feb and May 2025 memoranda; minor.

MY3c-57.claim: Malaysia's Border Control and Protection Agency (AKPS) detained 15 Bangladeshis at Kuala Lumpur International Airport on Monday 17 March 2025 who wore cricket uniforms and showed an organiser's letter for a 21 to 23 March tournament; AKPS found the letter fake, no such event, and the named 'sponsor' knew nothing of it, and said it believed they were part of a syndicate entering for another purpose and would act under immigration law.
MY3c-57.target_section: Irregular routes, and where an irregular stay ends
MY3c-57.why_new: The Business visit Scams section mentions fake sports-competition invitations generally [P0040]; this is a dated case with the outcome (detention at KLIA, action under immigration law). Could equally go to Business visit > Scams.

MY3c-58.claim: Before Malaysia's market closed in June 2024 the price of a ticket to Malaysia rose above Tk 1 lakh, Prothom Alo reported on 9 April 2025.
MY3c-58.placement: What happened to the stranded workers of 2024
MY3c-58.why_new: The guide says some stranded workers could not get air tickets; this gives the price reached. Could also go to Step 6 item 4 (the ticket).

MY3c-59.claim: In February 2025 the civil aviation and tourism ministry issued 10 directives against abnormal ticket prices, requiring tickets to be sold at the Civil Aviation Authority's approved price list and discounted tickets to be given to migrant workers, and Biman's managing director, Md Safiqur Rahman, said in April 2025 that Biman was giving workers discounted tickets.
MY3c-59.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Who pays for the air ticket?
MY3c-59.why_new: Cross-country: a worker-ticket discount rule the cross-country FAQ on air tickets doesn't mention.

MY3c-60.claim: Ticket agencies said in April 2025 that under the previous government a ring formed around ticket sales in which Biman held back cheap tickets and released dear ones and the ring resold cheap tickets at high prices, and aviation expert Kazi Wahidul Alam said a Tk 1 lakh ticket abroad carries Tk 40,000 in government taxes.
MY3c-60.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Who pays for the air ticket?
MY3c-60.why_new: Cross-country context on why worker fares are high; low priority.

SA3a-1.claim: Bangladesh's ambassador in Riyadh, Mohammad Javed Patwary, said at the embassy's National Expatriates' Day event (reported in an embassy press release, January 2024) that, on the embassy's initiative, contracts had been signed with two Saudi law firms to recover the unpaid wages and dues of Bangladeshis who died in Saudi Arabia, and that 'last December' Tk 33 crore owed to the families of 65 dead Bangladeshis was recovered and sent home.
SA3a-1.placement: Compensation and unpaid wages from Saudi Arabia
SA3a-1.why_new: The guide says the embassy pursues compensation in Saudi courts with the heirs' power of attorney [E0032] but not that it uses two contracted Saudi law firms, nor any recovery figure.
SA3a-1.h2: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job

SA3a-2.claim: According to the Bangladesh embassy in Riyadh (January 2024), BMET and Takamol for Business Services signed the agreement to run the Skills Verification Programme (SVP) on 27 September 2022, under which workers in 29 occupations could pass the test in Bangladesh and get the Saudi skill certificate.
SA3a-2.why_new: Gives the start date of SVP in Bangladesh. Conflict: the guide says 108 listed trades by late 2026 [SM0037]; this 2022-2024 figure is 29 occupations, so the list has grown.

SA3a-3.claim: According to the Bangladesh embassy in Riyadh, Bangladeshi migrants sent USD 21.61 billion home in fiscal year 2022-23, of which USD 3.07 billion, 16% of the total, came from Saudi Arabia.
SA3a-3.why_new: The guide gives no remittance figure from Saudi Arabia.

SA3a-4.claim: The Bangladesh embassy in Riyadh said in January 2024 that Saudi Arabia's selection to host World Expo 2030 and the 2034 FIFA World Cup had opened wide job opportunities for skilled workers in construction, cleaning, maintenance, and tourism and hospitality.
SA3a-4.target_section: Is it open now, and who can go?
SA3a-4.why_new: The guide has no growth-opportunity line for the corridor (an aim the audit asks for).

SA3a-5.claim: According to the Bangladesh embassy in Riyadh (January 2024), workers in Saudi Arabia who could not finish their studies can sit SSC, HSC and degree examinations through the Open University, on the embassy's initiative.

SA3a-6.claim: On 15 January 2024 Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Human Resources and Social Development lowered the maximum that may be paid to a recruitment service provider for hiring a domestic worker, setting SR 11,750 for a worker from Bangladesh, against SR 14,700 for the Philippines, SR 13,800 for Sri Lanka, SR 9,000 for Kenya, SR 8,300 for Uganda and SR 5,900 for Ethiopia, and said the caps may not be exceeded.
SA3a-6.target_section: Women domestic workers: the money should run the other way
SA3a-6.why_new: The guide has the SR 11,750 figure dated July 2026 [SM0035] but not when it was set (15 January 2024, as a reduction) or the comparison with other sending countries.

SA3a-7.claim: Under the new migrant-worker insurance contract made on 12 March 2023, as Prothom Alo reported in January 2024, a worker gets no insurance benefit for suicide or self-harm within six months of cover starting, death or illness from HIV/AIDS or similar disease, death in dangerous sports or adventure activities, death from alcohol or drug addiction, death in war, riot or an attack by criminals, or execution under a court sentence.
SA3a-7.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: What does the migrant insurance cover?
SA3a-7.why_new: The cross-country insurance section lists what it pays but no exclusions; the Saudi guide says only that suicide claims are often rejected [E0097]. Relevant to Saudi executions (What can get you jailed or deported).

SA3a-8.claim: Under the March 2023 insurance contract, a worker who dies naturally or in an accident during the cover period, or within 90 days after it ends, is paid the full Tk 10 lakh, and when a worker dies abroad the money goes to the worker's bank account after the body comes home without any application, according to the Welfare Board and Jiban Bima Corporation (January 2024).
SA3a-8.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: What does the migrant insurance cover?
SA3a-8.why_new: The 90-day grace after expiry is not in either guide; the Saudi guide says no application is needed if the body comes home [E0013] but not that the money goes to the worker's own bank account.

SA3a-9.claim: By Jiban Bima Corporation's count, 32,24,343 workers went abroad from the start of the compulsory migrant insurance in late 2019 to the end of 2023, and only 1,397 workers or families claimed on it; in fiscal 2022-23 the Welfare Board paid Tk 31 crore 72 lakh 10 thousand in death insurance to the families of 860 workers.
SA3a-9.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: What does the migrant insurance cover?
SA3a-9.why_new: Claim and payout figures are not in either guide.

SA3a-10.claim: Prothom Alo reported in January 2024 that disability and early-return benefits must be claimed, that the government agencies hold no information on workers who come back disabled or within six months, and that people involved said there is no special effort to tell workers about the insurance before they leave.
SA3a-10.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: What does the migrant insurance cover?
SA3a-10.why_new: Explains why the Tk 50,000 job-loss and disability benefits are rarely claimed; not in either guide.

SA3a-11.claim: Shariful Islam of Tangail went to Saudi Arabia in October 2023 at a cost of Tk 5 lakh, worked 22 days, was detained by police and sent home on an outpass in December; he told Prothom Alo he did not know why he was sent back or whether he had paid for insurance, and that he had applied nowhere since returning and nobody had told him to.
SA3a-11.why_new: A Saudi case of a worker sent home within six months who never claimed the Tk 50,000 job-loss benefit; the guide has the benefit [E0011] but no case.
SA3a-11.h2: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job

SA3a-12.claim: Amirun Begum of Narsingdi went to Saudi Arabia in November 2022 and, by the Saudi death certificate, died by suicide on 4 September 2023; her body came home two months later, and when her father asked at Probashi Kallyan Bhaban in Dhaka on 14 January 2024 about the Tk 3 lakh, a staff member there looked at the certificate and said that because she had killed herself she would not get the insurance money.
SA3a-12.why_new: A Saudi case behind the guide's line that suicide claims are often rejected [E0097].
SA3a-12.h2: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job

SA3a-13.claim: OKUP chairperson Shakirul Islam told Prothom Alo in January 2024 that once a destination country sends a death certificate saying 'suicide', the worker's family can do nothing more about it, and that demands have been raised to bring suicide and AIDS deaths under insurance cover and for health insurance for workers.
SA3a-13.target_section: If a worker dies in Saudi Arabia
SA3a-13.why_new: Adds to the guide's note that the cause of death is recorded in Saudi Arabia and Bangladesh does not check it [E0093].
SA3a-13.h2: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job

SA3a-14.claim: A 2023 study by RMMRU (the Refugee and Migratory Movements Research Unit) found that 31% of migrant women workers' deaths abroad were unnatural, from accidents and suicide.
SA3a-14.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: What does the migrant insurance cover?
SA3a-14.why_new: Not in either guide; bears on how often the suicide exclusion bites for women.

SA3a-15.claim: According to Prothom Alo (February 2024), Bangladesh and Saudi Arabia signed an agreement on recruiting Bangladeshi health workers in 2022, and the first group of about 60 Bangladeshi health workers went to Saudi Arabia in November 2023.
SA3a-15.why_new: The guide has no channel for doctors and nurses.

SA3a-16.claim: Saudi ambassador in Dhaka Essa Al-Duhailan told Arab News (February 2024) that Saudi Arabia had long hired no Bangladeshi health workers but had started because they now met Saudi standards, and that a Saudi health ministry team visited Bangladesh twice in 2023 and would keep visiting to recruit more.
SA3a-16.why_new: Shows the health-worker route is run with the Saudi health ministry; not in the guide.

SA3a-17.claim: Khairul Alam, additional secretary at Bangladesh's expatriates' welfare ministry, told Arab News (February 2024) that Saudi authorities had asked Bangladesh to send more than 150 trained nurses, that the ministry was examining the Saudi demand, such as whether the nurses would go to government or private hospitals, and that because the matter was new the government was drawing up a procedure to speed up recruitment of health workers.
SA3a-17.why_new: Not in the guide; would support a Need to know on how nurses apply.

SA3a-18.claim: According to the Bangladesh Medical Association (February 2024), about 30 lakh Bangladeshi workers are in Saudi Arabia, only a few of them health workers.
SA3a-18.why_new: The guide gives yearly departures but no stock of Bangladeshi workers in Saudi Arabia.

SA3a-19.claim: By BMET figures analysed by Prothom Alo (February 2024), of more than 1 crore 60 lakh workers sent abroad since 1976, 35% went to Saudi Arabia, and in the five years 2019-2023 about 55% of all workers who left went there.
SA3a-19.why_new: Long-run share not in the guide, which gives only 2025-2026 departures and 'two of every three' [E0129].

SA3a-20.claim: Migration experts told Prothom Alo in February 2024 that in the Middle East it is workers already abroad who open the way for new ones, collecting job demand there and sending it to acquaintances and relatives at home, and that about 90% of demand letters reach Bangladesh this way.
SA3a-20.why_new: The guide gives IOM's 33.2% relatives figure and the Cumilla 80% figure [RD0021, A0078]; this 90% of demand letters figure (Middle East, experts' estimate) is not there.

SA3a-21.claim: Foreign Minister Hasan Mahmud told parliament on 19 February 2024 that 9,370 Bangladeshis were held in prisons in 26 countries, the most, 5,746, in Saudi Arabia.
SA3a-21.target_section: If you or a relative is arrested
SA3a-21.why_new: The guide gives no number of Bangladeshis jailed in Saudi Arabia.

SA3a-22.claim: Foreign Minister Hasan Mahmud told Bangladeshis in Jeddah on 6 March 2024 that about 30 lakh Bangladeshis live in Saudi Arabia, and urged them to send money home through legal channels.
SA3a-22.why_new: An official (ministerial) figure for the stock of Bangladeshis in Saudi Arabia, which the guide lacks; matches the Bangladesh Medical Association's 30 lakh.

SA3a-23.claim: Probashi Kallyan Bank's managing director Md. Mujibur Rahman said in March 2024 that loan conditions for returnee women had been eased: a woman whose husband or family won't take her back can borrow without a fixed address, her loan carries no service charge, and loans up to Tk 1 lakh need no equity, though few women apply.
SA3a-23.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: What help is there when I come back?
SA3a-23.placement: other: PKB loans for returnee women
SA3a-23.why_new: The Saudi guide's PKB reintegration loan (Reintegration loan (PKB)) needs a Union Parishad address certificate and charges 0.5%+0.5% fees [E0115, E0116]; this eased rule for returnee women is not there.

SA3a-24.claim: Selim Reza, a full-time member of the Jatiya Manobadhikar Parishad (National Human Rights Council), said at a March 2024 meeting in Dhaka that when he went to Saudi Arabia for Hajj he had seen Bangladeshi workers in a terrible condition, and asked where the accountability was of those who sent them.
SA3a-24.why_new: A senior official's first-hand account; weak on detail, offered for reviewer judgement.

SA3a-25.claim: Prothom Alo reported in March 2024 that remittances from Saudi Arabia fell from USD 4.54 billion in fiscal 2021-22, when it was the top source, to USD 3.76 billion in 2022-23, and that by Bangladesh Bank figures about USD 1.79 billion came from Saudi Arabia in July 2023-February 2024, putting it third behind the UAE (about USD 2.91 billion) and the UK (about USD 1.88 billion).
SA3a-25.why_new: No remittance trend in the guide. Conflict: the Bangladesh embassy's press release (article 71b15965) gives USD 3.07 billion for 2022-23, against Bangladesh Bank's USD 3.76 billion here.

SA3a-26.claim: RMMRU founding chair Tasneem Siddiqui said in March 2024 that remittances from Saudi Arabia had fallen because many send through hundi over the exchange-rate gap and distrust of banks, and because many workers who recently went to Saudi Arabia on legal visas were not getting jobs, many of them coming home without work.
SA3a-26.why_new: Links falling Saudi remittances to hundi and to workers arriving on legal visas without jobs (the free-visa problem in What goes wrong most); not in the guide.

SA3a-27.claim: People in the sector told Prothom Alo in March 2024 that banks' official dollar rate for remittances was Tk 110, plus the government's 2.5% incentive and an equal incentive from many banks, so a legal transfer fetched over Tk 115 a dollar, and some banks short of dollars paid over Tk 120.
SA3a-27.why_new: The guide has the 2.5% government incentive [E0076] but not that banks add their own matching incentive; the 2024 rate is dated.

SA3a-28.claim: By BMET figures cited in a March 2024 opinion piece, 1 crore 45 lakh 8 thousand Bangladeshis had gone abroad with BMET clearance since 1976, 51 lakh 82 thousand of them to Saudi Arabia.
SA3a-28.why_new: Cumulative Saudi departures not in the guide. Conflict with article 1017c704 (Prothom Alo, February 2024), which puts total departures since 1976 at over 1 crore 60 lakh with 35% to Saudi Arabia (about 56 lakh).

SA3a-29.claim: By IOM figures for 2019 cited in a March 2024 opinion piece, a Bangladeshi migrant worker sent home USD 203.33 a month on average, against USD 546.10 for a Filipino worker.
SA3a-29.target_section: What reaches home, and how long the debt takes
SA3a-29.why_new: An average monthly remittance per worker (all destinations) is not in the guide; it sits beside the guide's Tk 15,000-20,000 a month figure [SB0022].

SA3a-30.claim: A March 2024 opinion piece quoted OKUP chairman Shakirul Islam as saying in a 2023 Business Standard Bangla report that in the Middle East women domestic workers face physical abuse and other problems because they don't know the language, and that men, though not directly harmed by it, lag in earnings because without the local language they stay in low-skilled work.
SA3a-30.target_section: What goes wrong most, and what people wrongly believe
SA3a-30.why_new: Language as a cause of abuse and low pay is not in the guide; the housekeeping course includes language (Step 3), but nothing for men.

SA3a-31.claim: By Bangladesh government data reported by the Guardian (March 2024), at least 13,685 Bangladeshi workers died in Saudi Arabia in 2008-2022, 1,502 of them in 2022, more than four a day; Bangladeshi authorities, working from Saudi documents, recorded 76% of deaths from January to October 2022 as 'natural', and the average age of those 'natural' deaths in 2022 was 44.
SA3a-31.target_section: If a worker dies in Saudi Arabia
SA3a-31.why_new: The guide says deaths are usually recorded as natural [E0093] but gives no death numbers. Note: the same article says about 50,000 workers went to Saudi Arabia in 2023, far below BMET's figures elsewhere; not drafted.
SA3a-31.h2: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job

SA3a-32.claim: Abdul Jalil Sheikh, 35, went to Saudi Arabia in early 2023 on a Tk 5 lakh loan and came home in a coffin within a year; the note on the coffin read 'Cause of death: natural. Post-mortem: not requested. Compensation: none', and his wife, told by co-workers he died of a stroke, was left with two children and the Tk 5 lakh debt (Guardian, March 2024).
SA3a-32.target_section: If a worker dies in Saudi Arabia
SA3a-32.why_new: Shows what a 'natural' death record means for compensation in practice; the guide has the rule [E0093] but no case.
SA3a-32.h2: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job

SA3a-33.claim: The Guardian found (March 2024) that in most cases the cause of death was not explained, Saudi death certificates giving 'natural causes', 'heart problems' or 'respiratory problems', so no post-mortem is done; FairSquare, a UK rights group, says the cause is unexplained in over half of migrant deaths in the Gulf.
SA3a-33.target_section: If a worker dies in Saudi Arabia
SA3a-33.why_new: Adds the wording of Saudi certificates and FairSquare's figure to the guide's one-line rule [E0093].
SA3a-33.h2: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job

SA3a-34.claim: Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Human Resources and Social Development said in a statement (March 2024) that it is committed to safe working conditions for all migrant workers, including more than 25 lakh Bangladeshis, that post-mortems are done where needed and death certificates issued transparently, and that it had found no negligence.
SA3a-34.target_section: If a worker dies in Saudi Arabia
SA3a-34.why_new: The Saudi labour ministry's own position on post-mortems, and an official Saudi figure (over 25 lakh) for Bangladeshi workers; neither is in the guide. Bears on the guide's Need to know on how a family can ask for a post-mortem.
SA3a-34.h2: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job

SA3a-35.claim: Rights groups told the Guardian (March 2024) that hard labour, living conditions, exploitation, stress and heat stroke may be driving the death rate, and BRAC migration programme associate director Shariful Hasan said that since workers can go only after passing a medical at a Saudi-designated centre, Bangladesh and Saudi Arabia must investigate why they die there.
SA3a-35.target_section: If a worker dies in Saudi Arabia
SA3a-35.why_new: Not in the guide; links to heat rules under Hours, rest and leave.
SA3a-35.h2: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job

SA3a-36.claim: Faisal Al-Dafayan, an assistant deputy minister at Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Human Resources and Social Development, told the Bangladesh embassy on 29 May 2024 that the ministry had recently appointed 1,200 labour inspectors to act on workers' complaints, and that they resolved about 10 lakh complaints in 2023.
SA3a-36.why_new: Scale of the Saudi labour inspection system; not in the guide.

SA3a-37.claim: At a 29 May 2024 meeting with the Saudi Ministry of Human Resources and Social Development, the Bangladesh embassy's deputy head of mission Md. Abul Hasan Mridha asked for Saudi cooperation on visa issues including assurance of work and iqama, sending women workers home when their contracts end, quick return of workers whose iqamas have expired, and settling Bangladeshi recruiting agencies' complaints on the Musaned system, and asked the ministry to name a focal point for quick solutions to workers' problems, which the assistant deputy minister agreed to.
SA3a-37.target_section: What goes wrong most, and what people wrongly believe
SA3a-37.why_new: The embassy's own list of the main problems (no work or iqama on arrival, women not sent home at contract end, expired-iqama returns) corroborates the guide's complaint types [E0128, SL0014]; the agreed ministry focal point is new.

SA3a-38.claim: The Saudi labour ministry's assistant deputy minister said in May 2024 that Bangladeshis are the largest group of foreign workers in Saudi Arabia.
SA3a-38.why_new: An official Saudi statement that Bangladeshis are the largest foreign workforce; not in the guide.

SA3a-39.claim: Under the budget proposal reported in June 2024, cash and gifts, including remittances, received from anyone other than a spouse, child or parent, such as a brother, sister or in-law, would be taxable for the recipient, and a National Board of Revenue (NBR) official said tax could be avoided only if the sender shows the money as his own and the recipient shows it as a liability in the tax return, though Prothom Alo noted the NBR had given no formal explanation and the matter was unclear.
SA3a-39.why_new: Not in the guide; Saudi workers often send to brothers' accounts. It was a proposal in June 2024: whether it was enacted is a Need to know. Better placed in CROSS-COUNTRY: How do I send money home safely?

SA3a-40.claim: Prothom Alo reported in June 2024 that many workers in Saudi Arabia and other Gulf countries send remittances to brothers', sisters', in-laws' and friends' bank accounts because in villages many elderly parents have no bank account, children are minors and wives don't open accounts.
SA3a-40.placement: other: why workers send to relatives
SA3a-40.why_new: Explains a common practice behind the proposed tax; the guide's Before you fly item 4 says to open a bank account for a family member [B0104] but not why many don't.

SA3a-41.claim: By the expatriates' welfare ministry's count, 11,25,833 workers went abroad for jobs in fiscal 2022-23, the most, nearly 4.5 lakh, to Saudi Arabia.
SA3a-41.why_new: A fiscal-year Saudi departure figure not in the guide (which gives calendar 2025 and 2026).

SA3a-42.claim: Foreign Minister Hasan Mahmud told Bangladeshis in Madinah in June 2024 that the Prime Minister had launched a special pension scheme for expatriates whose benefit even people aged 55 can take, and that offshore banking lets expatriates easily open dollar accounts.
SA3a-42.why_new: The guide's Pension section says only that there is no Saudi pension [C0109]; a Bangladesh-side pension for migrants is not mentioned. Better as CROSS-COUNTRY if a pension heading exists; how to join is a Need to know.

SA3a-43.claim: According to a June 2024 Prothom Alo guide, Bangladeshi students can't apply directly for a bachelor's at Saudi universities: they first apply for the four-level Diploma in Arabic at the university's Arabic language institute, which takes two years (one to one and a half for those who start at level two or three), and enter the degree only with satisfactory results; Arabic and Islamic subjects are taught wholly in Arabic, others in English.
SA3a-43.why_new: The guide's Student visa section doesn't mention the Arabic diploma route. Conflict: the guide says IELTS 5.5 or English-medium schooling for courses in English [D0151]; this source says Bangladeshis must go through the Arabic diploma first.

SA3a-44.claim: The same June 2024 guide says applicants must be 17 to 23 (25 at some universities) with at least GPA 4 at HSC or Alim, though some universities state no grade or accept below 4.00.
SA3a-44.why_new: Conflict: the guide gives ages 17 to 25 for a bachelor's [D0151]; the minimum GPA is not in the guide.

SA3a-45.claim: According to the June 2024 guide, the scholarship pays a monthly stipend of about SR 840, with no tuition fee, free housing and medical care, a return ticket home once a year and a preparation allowance, and some universities give married students a family visa and quarters.
SA3a-45.why_new: The guide lists scholarship items [D0148, D0154] but not the stipend amount or family visa for married students.

SA3a-46.claim: According to the June 2024 guide, applicants upload PDFs of at most 200 KB: a passport valid at least two years, a white-background photo without cap or glasses, a medical fitness certificate from the civil surgeon or any medical centre, and HSC or Alim certificates and mark sheets translated into Arabic at an approved centre, notarised, attested by the Islamic Foundation, then by the education board, the education and foreign ministries and finally the Saudi embassy in Bangladesh, plus a character certificate from the Islamic Foundation, two known scholars or a college teacher.
SA3a-46.why_new: The guide says 'attested certificates' [D0188] without the chain; whether the apostille now replaces the embassy step (as it does for work papers [B0068]) is a Need to know.

SA3a-47.claim: According to the June 2024 guide, a woman applying needs a copy of her mahram (male guardian relative) guardian's iqama, because Saudi rules do not allow women higher education without a mahram.
SA3a-47.why_new: Not in the guide; whether the rule still applies in 2026 is a Need to know.

SA3a-48.claim: Universities that take foreign students named in the June 2024 guide include the Islamic University of Madinah, King Abdulaziz University in Jeddah, Umm Al-Qura University in Makkah and Taibah University in Madinah.

SA3a-49.claim: Foreign Minister Hasan Mahmud told parliament on 1 July 2024 that 11,450 Bangladeshis were held in prisons in 31 countries, the most, 5,746, in Saudi Arabia.
SA3a-49.target_section: If you or a relative is arrested
SA3a-49.why_new: Same Saudi figure as the minister gave in February 2024 (article a5eb1d4c); a later date for the same number.

SA3a-50.claim: Foreign Minister Hasan Mahmud told parliament on 1 July 2024 that West Asia is the source of 60% of Bangladesh's remittances and that about 60% of the Bangladeshi workers employed there are semi-skilled or unskilled.
SA3a-50.why_new: An official skill-mix figure for the Middle East; the guide gives recruiters' estimate that nearly 80% going to Saudi Arabia are low-skilled [SJ0008].

SA3a-51.claim: At a 1 July 2024 political dialogue in Riyadh, Foreign Minister Hasan Mahmud asked the Saudi foreign minister for a special opportunity for Bangladeshi expatriates running businesses in Saudi Arabia to register them, according to Bangladesh's foreign ministry.
SA3a-51.target_section: Irregular routes and how they end
SA3a-51.why_new: Relates to the guide's tasattur (commercial concealment) warning [SM0020]; whether any registration window followed is a Need to know.

SA3a-52.claim: Bangladesh's foreign ministry said the two foreign ministers had a fruitful discussion in Riyadh on 1 July 2024 on forming a joint task force to bring more transparency to sending Bangladeshi workers to Saudi Arabia and stop harassment of workers by vested interests.
SA3a-52.why_new: Not in the guide; whether the task force was ever formed, and what it did, is a Need to know.

SA3a-53.claim: Foreign Minister Hasan Mahmud told Bangladeshis at the Riyadh embassy on 1 July 2024 that a Bangladesh-Saudi joint task force would work to protect people wanting to go to Saudi Arabia for jobs from fraud, and the prime minister's adviser Salman F Rahman said those wanting to go should verify that the employer is genuine before leaving.
SA3a-53.why_new: The task force announcement; whether it exists in 2026 is a Need to know. The employer check is already in the guide (Step 1, Before you pay anyone).

SA3a-54.claim: Bangladeshis in Riyadh raised with the foreign minister in July 2024 easier iqama renewal, a direct Chattogram-Riyadh flight, health insurance, a proper system for bringing bodies home, legal aid, passport renewal through the embassy, correcting NID details and family visa renewal, and he promised to address them.
SA3a-54.why_new: Lists workers' own unmet needs; NID correction through the mission matches the guide's line that a mission can't correct an existing NID [SG0018].

SA3a-55.claim: By Bangladesh Bank figures, remittances from Saudi Arabia fell by USD 1.03 billion, about 27%, in fiscal 2023-24, dropping it from first place in 2022-23 to fourth, behind the UAE, the United States and the UK.
SA3a-55.why_new: Full-year 2023-24 figure, completing the trend drafted from article 2b2f2ed1; not in the guide.

SA3a-56.claim: By BMET figures, about 39 lakh Bangladeshi workers went to Saudi Arabia from 2004 to June 2024, against about 21.5 lakh to the UAE.
SA3a-56.why_new: A 20-year comparison with the next-largest Gulf corridor; not in the guide.

SA3a-57.claim: Foreign Minister Hasan Mahmud said on 15 July 2024 that he had discussed with the Saudi ambassador in Dhaka, Essa Yousef Essa Al-Duhailan, the joint task force to protect Bangladeshis wanting Saudi jobs from fraud and the registration of businesses in Saudi Arabia in Bangladeshis' own names.
SA3a-57.target_section: Irregular routes and how they end
SA3a-57.why_new: Confirms the business-registration ask (articles db249f15, cbb5ea51) was about businesses in Bangladeshis' own names, the alternative to tasattur [SM0020]; outcome unknown.

SA3a-58.claim: A July 2024 Prothom Alo editorial, citing the daily Bonik Barta, said that during the unrest in Bangladesh all Saudi Airlines flights were cancelled on 19 and 20 July, that four of those flights had 1,200 passengers, that many travellers with only two to seven days left on their visas faced an uncertain journey to Saudi Arabia, and that the expatriates' welfare ministry said it had discussed with the Saudi embassy extending by 15 days the visas of workers that would expire in the meantime.
SA3a-58.target_section: When to pay, when to fly, and Hajj-season pauses
SA3a-58.why_new: A precedent for the guide's Need to know on extending visas of workers stranded by flight cuts (Current situation); whether the 15 days were granted is not reported.

SA3a-59.claim: Mister Ali, 38, of Adarbhita village, Madarganj, Jamalpur, who had gone to Saudi Arabia two and a half years earlier and worked as a street cleaner in a city there, was killed on 28 July 2024 when an out-of-control private car hit him from behind while he worked on the road, according to his family and local people; his younger brother Razzak Ali said the family depended on his income and demanded that his body be brought home at government cost as soon as possible.
SA3a-59.target_section: If a worker dies in Saudi Arabia
SA3a-59.why_new: A case of a road-cleaner killed at work, the occupation most men go for (What the job pays); the guide has no street-cleaner death case and covers compensation for work deaths only through GOSI [E0157].
SA3a-59.h2: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job

SA3a-60.claim: Prothom Alo reported in August 2024 that public gatherings of any kind are banned in the Middle East, that some Bangladeshis were reported arrested in Saudi Arabia for protesting in support of the July 2024 student movement, and that a UAE court sentenced 57 Bangladeshis for street protests, 53 to 10 years, one to 11 years and three to life.
SA3a-60.target_section: What can get you jailed or deported
SA3a-60.why_new: Joining a street protest is not on the guide's list of what can get a worker jailed.

SA3a-61.claim: Prothom Alo reported in August 2024 that about 17 lakh workers went to Saudi Arabia in the previous three years, yet remittances from there fell from over USD 5.5 billion a year three years earlier to about USD 3.5 billion, which it read as workers going in greater numbers but not earning well.
SA3a-61.target_section: What reaches home, and how long the debt takes
SA3a-61.why_new: Sets the rise in departures against the fall in remittances; not in the guide. Conflict: Bangladesh Bank's figure for 2021-22 was USD 4.54 billion (article 2b2f2ed1), not over USD 5.5 billion.

SA3a-62.claim: By Wage Earners' Welfare Board data, 86,621 migrants (83,719 men and 2,902 women) came home in 2023 on an outpass, the embassy travel permit issued to those returning destitute, detained or forced; Prothom Alo noted these are the only returnees counted.
SA3a-62.why_new: A yearly outpass-return figure; not in the Saudi guide's Going home without valid papers.
SA3a-62.h2: Departure bottlenecks: offloading, airport checks, bribes and deportation

SA3a-63.claim: Saudi ambassador in Dhaka Essa Yousef Essa Al-Duhailan told Chief Adviser Muhammad Yunus on 27 August 2024 that about 32 lakh Bangladeshis work in Saudi Arabia and send about USD 5 billion a year through legal channels and another USD 5 billion through informal channels.
SA3a-63.why_new: An official Saudi estimate that half of Saudi remittances go through hundi; not in the guide. Conflict: Bangladesh Bank recorded about USD 2.7 billion from Saudi Arabia in 2023-24 (articles 2b2f2ed1 and 5f8f2c2f), well below the ambassador's USD 5 billion legal figure.

SA3a-64.claim: Khokon Howlader of West Subidkhali, Mirzaganj, Patuakhali, who had lived in Saudi Arabia for seven or eight years, hanged himself on 24 September 2024 while on a video call with his wife and twin sons, according to the family; his body reached Dhaka on a Biman flight 22 days later, on 16 October.
SA3a-64.why_new: A suicide case with the time a body took to come home (22 days); the guide has no Saudi case under Mental health. The article also says he returned to Saudi Arabia on 14 October after leave, which conflicts with the 24 September date; not drafted.
SA3a-64.h2: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job

SA3a-65.claim: In a case filed on 28 October 2024 at the Barishal Human Trafficking Offence Suppression Tribunal, a father from Mehendiganj alleged that Araf Hossain alias Sifat, managing director of the recruiting agency SJ Group in Purana Paltan, Dhaka, and two local men took Tk 4.5 lakh each, Tk 1 crore 3 lakh 50 thousand in all, from 23 men from Barishal on the promise of SR 1,800 a month at a solar panel firm, Taj Al Nawar Trading East; according to the case, after they were taken to Saudi Arabia on 4 May the men were put on a Hajj project for a month and a half and paid SR 615, then 12 were caught by Saudi police as illegal migrants and sent home and 11 could not be traced.
SA3a-65.why_new: A group case of the wrong-job scam (Scams, Wrong visa or job) ending in Hajj-season work, arrest and deportation; not in the guide. Allegations only.

SA3a-66.claim: In a second case filed on 27 October 2024 at the same Barishal tribunal, a father alleged that his son Md. Rubel, on an offer from Abu Taher Sheikh, paid Tk 3.8 lakh to Md. Rana, an official of MR International in Chairmanbari, Dhaka, and Rana's sister Habiba Akter, was sent to Saudi Arabia on 15 May 2024, given no job and handed to a Saudi trafficking gang that tortured him and demanded Tk 5 lakh from his father on threat of killing him.
SA3a-66.why_new: A ransom case inside Saudi Arabia; the guide has no case of a worker held for ransom there. Allegations only.

SA3a-67.claim: In both October 2024 Barishal cases the victims' fathers filed at the Human Trafficking Offence Suppression Tribunal and the judge ordered the local police station's officer in charge to record the complaint as an FIR; in the first case he also ordered an investigation report.
SA3a-67.target_section: If an agency, broker or relative takes your money
SA3a-67.why_new: The guide mentions a police case under the trafficking law and a CR case at the magistrate's court [RC0045, RC0021], but not filing directly at the trafficking tribunal, which then orders the police to register it.

SA3b-1.claim: For Hajj 2025 Bangladesh announced government packages of BDT 478,242 (housing within 3 km of Masjid al-Haram) and BDT 575,680 (within 1.5 km) and a private general package of BDT 483,156, against 2024's government general package of BDT 578,840 and private general package of BDT 589,800.
SA3b-1.why_new: The guide gives only 2027 package prices; this gives the 2024 and 2025 prices, useful as a price history (one package about BDT 1 lakh cheaper in 2025). The 2025 packages were priced at BDT 32.50 per riyal against BDT 29.74 in 2024.

SA3b-2.claim: For Hajj 2025 the government's rule was that the whole package money be paid only into the Hajj agency's bank account or directly at the agency, with the pilgrim keeping the receipt, no dealings with middlemen, and women and children depositing together with their mahram.
SA3b-2.why_new: Guide says private-package money goes into the agency account on the Hajj portal, but not the keep-the-receipt, no-middlemen and mahram-deposits-together rules.

SA3b-3.claim: For Hajj 2025 each pilgrim had to pay the sacrifice (qurbani) cost of 1,000 riyal separately from the package, people aged 65 or over could go, and passports had to be valid to 31 December 2025.
SA3b-3.why_new: Guide does not say the sacrifice is paid on top of the package, nor the passport validity rule (given here for 2025; the current year's equivalent is a gap).

SA3b-4.claim: Pilgrims who had performed Hajj several times told Prothom Alo (November 2024) that going for less than the announced package price risks being cheated, that no agreement should be made with a middleman, broker or so-called moallem, and that pilgrims should check which agencies have complaints from the Saudi Hajj Ministry against them.
SA3b-4.why_new: Guide has no Hajj scam patterns (cheap packages, fake moallems).

SA3b-5.claim: According to experienced pilgrims quoted by Prothom Alo (November 2024), there are moallems numbered 1 to 115 for South Asian countries, the distance from the Jamarat to the pilgrim's tent in Mina depends on the price of the moallem cluster, and extra services a moallem gives for extra charges should be taken in writing because they cause disputes in Mina.
SA3b-5.placement: other: what to check in a package
SA3b-5.why_new: Ground-level detail on how Hajj packages differ; not in the guide.

SA3b-6.claim: Experienced pilgrims quoted by Prothom Alo (November 2024) said that to avoid fraud over the sacrifice it is better to buy an Islamic Development Bank (IDB) coupon, and that pilgrims should ask in advance whether the package has a 'fitra' (moving between houses in Makkah, nearer or farther from the Kaaba) before or after Hajj.
SA3b-6.placement: other: what to check in a package
SA3b-6.why_new: Insider terms (IDB coupon, fitra) not in the guide.

SA3b-7.claim: Prothom Alo reported on 1 November 2024 that 127,198 people from Bangladesh would be able to perform Hajj in 2025, with the Hajj agreement with Saudi Arabia due on 13 January 2025, Hajj visas from 19 February 2025 and Hajj flights from 29 April 2025.
SA3b-7.why_new: Guide gives the 2027 quota (78,500); this gives the 2025 quota and the usual sequence and months of the Hajj calendar (agreement January, visas February, flights late April).

SA3b-8.claim: On 11 November 2024 the chief adviser of the interim government opened a lounge for migrants at the airport.
SA3b-8.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Who helps me at the airport?
SA3b-8.why_new: Opening date of the migrants' lounge; the Saudi guide (Coming home, At Dhaka airport) describes the Probashi Lounge but not when it opened.

SA3b-9.claim: Prothom Alo reported (November 2024) that on 27 March the bag holding the passport and air ticket of Momin Sheikh (45), a Saudi-based migrant from Sirajganj, fell from the Dhumketu Express bound for Dhaka; a fellow passenger called 999 saying he would miss his 2 pm flight to Saudi Arabia without it, the Tangail railway police outpost found that a woman had picked it up, and the bag was handed back to him.
SA3b-9.why_new: The guide lists 999 for emergencies but has no evidence of what it does for a migrant; this is a case of 999 recovering a lost passport before a flight (year inferred as 2024 from a November 2024 article saying 'last 27 March').

SA3b-10.claim: In November 2024 BOESL (Bangladesh Overseas Employment and Services Limited) advertised 15 male and 15 female Nursing Specialist (BSc) posts at Afras Trading and Contracting Company in Saudi Arabia, requiring a BSc Nursing certificate from a government-approved institute, a Prometric pass certificate, at least three years' experience, ability to communicate in English and age within 40, with applications closing on 30 December 2024.
SA3b-10.target_section: NEW: Nurses and other skilled jobs (after House drivers)
SA3b-10.why_new: The guide has no nursing or other skilled-professional route, and says nothing on women going on non-domestic company visas (its Need to know asks whether a woman can go on a company visa: this ad recruited women nurses for a company). Note the guide's rule not to recommend BOESL for Saudi; this is a factual record of one ad.

SA3b-11.claim: BOESL's November 2024 ad for Saudi nursing specialists at Afras Trading and Contracting Company gave a monthly salary of SR 3,000 (BDT 95,315) plus SR 300 a month for food, 8-hour days 6 days a week, a renewable two-year contract with three months' probation, 21 days' annual leave, and housing, transport to work, primary medical care and the joining and return airfare paid by the company.
SA3b-11.target_section: NEW: Nurses and other skilled jobs (after House drivers)
SA3b-11.why_new: Wage and terms for a skilled Saudi job; the guide's wage list stops at heavy equipment operators (SR 1,500).

SA3b-12.claim: Selected candidates for BOESL's 2024 Saudi nursing posts had to pay BOESL a service charge of BDT 56,350 plus the other fees set by rule, including the GAMCA medical fee and the visa stamping fee.
SA3b-12.target_section: NEW: Nurses and other skilled jobs (after House drivers)
SA3b-12.why_new: What a worker pays on a state-agency Saudi job; not in the guide.

SA3b-13.claim: A December 2024 Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare notice to fill labour-wing posts abroad, open only to serving BCS (Bangladesh Civil Service) officers, included a Minister (Labour) post in Riyadh and a First Secretary (Labour) and a Second Secretary (Labour) post in Jeddah.
SA3b-13.placement: other: who staffs the labour wings
SA3b-13.why_new: The guide lists labour-wing contacts but not that the posts are filled by rotating BCS officers; relevant context to experts' criticism (see SA3b draft from the 18 December 2024 article).

SA3b-14.claim: Prothom Alo reported on 18 December 2024 that 60% of the workers who went abroad from Bangladesh that year went to Saudi Arabia, and more than 80% of overseas employment in the previous two months (October and November) was in Saudi Arabia.
SA3b-14.why_new: The guide's Size has 2025 and 2026 figures only; this adds 2024 share. Conflicts slightly with Ami Probashi's 62% for 2024 (see SA3b draft from the 5 February 2025 article).

SA3b-15.claim: People in the sector told Prothom Alo in December 2024 that Saudi demand for Bangladeshi workers was coming regularly because Saudi Arabia will host the 2034 football World Cup and has begun preparing football infrastructure.
SA3b-15.target_section: Is it open now, and who can go?
SA3b-15.why_new: The guide never names what drives Saudi demand (World Cup 2034 and other projects).

SA3b-16.claim: Experts told Prothom Alo in December 2024 that embassy attestation of demand letters should end and recruiting agencies be made liable instead, that labour wings fail to serve workers because administration-cadre officers work there temporarily and are transferred, and that brokers (dalals) should be brought under registration.
SA3b-16.target_section: The Bangladesh embassy's attestation, and the missing contract
SA3b-16.why_new: Insider criticism of the attestation and labour wings; the guide cites TIB on attestation for bribes but not this.

SA3b-17.claim: BAIRA (the recruiting agency owners' association) secretary general Ali Haider Chowdhury said in December 2024 that the labour market was shrinking, workers were going mainly to Saudi Arabia, and a meeting of the two countries' technical committee should be called to discuss existing problems.
SA3b-17.target_section: Is it open now, and who can go?
SA3b-17.why_new: Context on Bangladesh's dependence on Saudi Arabia in late 2024; not in the guide.

SA3b-18.claim: A writer from King Saud University in Riyadh wrote in December 2024 that most Bangladeshis in Saudi Arabia are seen doing low-level work because they lack Arabic, while Indian and Pakistani workers skilled in Arabic are seen being hired for various office jobs.
SA3b-18.why_new: Opinion piece; adds the claim that Arabic affects job level. Low evidential weight.

SA3b-19.claim: The same writer reported from field work in Saudi Arabia (December 2024) that Bangladeshis who open a baqala (small grocery shop) or other small business have to keep a Sudanese or Egyptian employee, paid a large sum, to handle daily correspondence and legal formalities.
SA3b-19.target_section: Irregular routes and how they end
SA3b-19.why_new: Ground-level detail on how Bangladeshi-run baqalas operate; relates to the guide's tasattur (commercial concealment) paragraph but the article does not say whether these shops are registered in a Saudi's name.

SA3b-20.claim: At the Bangladesh embassy in Riyadh on 18 December 2024, chargé d'affaires S M Rakib Ullah referred to 33 lakh (3.3 million) expatriate Bangladeshis in Saudi Arabia.
SA3b-20.why_new: The guide gives departures but no stock of Bangladeshis in Saudi Arabia. Other figures: 30 lakh (foreign adviser, January 2025; expatriates' adviser, 'more than 30 lakh'), and the cross-country guide's 'at least 25 lakh'.

SA3b-21.claim: The Bangladesh embassy's chargé d'affaires said on 18 December 2024 that under the Skill Verification Programme the Saudi government was holding tests in Bangladesh in 33 occupations and issuing skills certificates, and urged workers to train in a trade at a Technical Training Centre (TTC) and come with a skills certificate.
SA3b-21.why_new: Conflict in scope over time: the guide says SVP covers 108 trades by late 2026; this gives 33 occupations in December 2024, showing the list's growth.

SA3b-22.claim: The embassy's chargé d'affaires said in December 2024 that Saudi Arabia's hosting of the 2027 AFC Asian Cup, the 2029 Asian Winter Games, World Expo 2030 and the 2034 FIFA World Cup, and giga projects such as NEOM, Red Sea, Qiddiya, Green Riyadh, Amaala, Diriyah and Roshn, opened great prospects for expanding the Bangladeshi labour market.
SA3b-22.target_section: Is it open now, and who can go?
SA3b-22.why_new: Names the projects and events behind Saudi demand; not in the guide.

SA3b-23.claim: The Greater Noakhali Association-Jeddah, a Bangladeshi community association in Jeddah, says its main aims include helping unskilled people into work through training and helping distressed and helpless people, and its president Omar Faruk Chowdhury said on 20 December 2024 it would organise more training to raise members' professional skills.
SA3b-23.why_new: The guide lists no community associations; whether they actually help is unproven (no contact details in the article).

SA3b-24.claim: In an OKUP (Ovibashi Karmi Unnayan Program) survey presented on 29 December 2024 of 1,096 returnees from six Middle East countries who came for health services (returned 2020-2023, seven districts), 55% had returned from Saudi Arabia and 48% came with mental health problems, more often men; domestic workers reported mental problems most.
SA3b-24.why_new: The guide's Mental health section gives only helplines; this shows the scale among returnees.
SA3b-24.h2: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job

SA3b-25.claim: The OKUP study (December 2024) found returnees came back with back pain, workplace injuries, heart disease, kidney problems, cancer, high blood pressure, tumours and skin disease; some migrants borrowed money from home for treatment, and many came home because they could not get treatment.
SA3b-25.placement: other: what returnees come back with
SA3b-25.why_new: Evidence of what illness costs workers; not in the guide.
SA3b-25.h2: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job

SA3b-26.claim: In OKUP's survey of returnees from six Middle East countries (December 2024), 21% of 666 women said they had spent BDT 2 to 3 lakh to migrate though women should pay nothing, and 29% of men said they had spent more than BDT 6 lakh.
SA3b-26.target_section: Women domestic workers: the money should run the other way
SA3b-26.why_new: Newer figure (2020-2023 returnees) than the guide's 2020 IOM evidence that no woman went free; not Saudi-only (55% of sample from Saudi).

SA3b-27.claim: Shefali Begum of Narsingdi, who went to Saudi Arabia lured by a broker, said in December 2024 that she was made to work a lot but not fed, the householder physically abused her and beat her when she complained, broke her hand and did not get it treated; after she came home she filed a case but, under local pressure, settled with the broker for BDT 30,000 compensation and withdrew it.
SA3b-27.why_new: A case of what a domestic worker's case against a broker yields in practice (BDT 30,000 under local pressure). Placement could also be Work visa: domestic worker, If something goes wrong.

SA3b-28.claim: Mosammat Hanifa of Narayanganj said in December 2024 that she paid a broker BDT 4 lakh to go to Saudi Arabia for a company job, found no job, was kept in a room with 20 to 25 others for some days, made to work a month in pilgrims' houses and then turned out, worked illegally in various places, and came home with kidney problems and diabetes.
SA3b-28.target_section: Irregular routes and how they end
SA3b-28.why_new: Case of a woman sold a company-job visa and paying BDT 4 lakh; bears on the guide's Need to know on whether women go on company visas.

SA3b-29.claim: At the OKUP event (29 December 2024) a joint secretary of the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare, Mohammad Shahin, said a way must be found for migrants to complain immediately, and the Bangladesh Nari Sramik Kendra's executive director said women workers in the Middle East cannot even leave the house.
SA3b-29.why_new: Low priority; official acknowledgement of the complaint gap. Could be cut.
SA3b-29.h2: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job

SA3b-30.claim: Prothom Alo reported on 3 January 2025 that about 5 lakh Bangladeshi workers went to Saudi Arabia in 2023 and more than 6.25 lakh in 2024, that Saudi Arabia was the only country to take more than one lakh workers in 2024, and that more than 80% of overseas employment in the last three months was in Saudi Arabia.
SA3b-30.why_new: Guide's Size starts at 2025 (755,194); this gives 2023 and 2024.

SA3b-31.claim: Prothom Alo reported in January 2025 that there were complaints of workers in Saudi Arabia not getting work as per contract, becoming illegal, being detained by Saudi police and sent home, and that Saudi Arabia tops the list of countries from which workers return empty-handed without a passport.
SA3b-31.target_section: Irregular routes and how they end
SA3b-31.why_new: Adds that Saudi Arabia leads returns without passports (outpass returns); the guide's Irregular routes says detainees land with almost nothing but not this ranking.

SA3b-32.claim: People in the sector told Prothom Alo in January 2025 that sending workers to Saudi Arabia might fall after June 2025, while BAIRA's secretary general warned that with almost every other market closed, a Saudi closure for any reason would be a disaster.
SA3b-32.why_new: Context: the forecast fall did not happen by the guide's 2025 figure (755,194), useful to reviewers only.

SA3b-33.claim: BMET data reported in January 2025 show that 61,158 Bangladeshi women went abroad for work in 2024, down from 76,108 in 2023 and 105,466 in 2022, and that Saudi Arabia took 66% of them in 2024, more than 40,000.
SA3b-33.why_new: The guide gives no count of women going to Saudi Arabia.

SA3b-34.claim: BAIRA's secretary general Ali Haider Chowdhury said in January 2025 that the training for women going abroad had been extended from one month to two, lengthening the process.
SA3b-34.target_section: Step 3: Do the one-month housekeeping course (women)
SA3b-34.why_new: CONFLICT: the guide says the compulsory housekeeping course is one month (24 working days). On 30 January 2025 Bangladesh promised Saudi Arabia to shorten domestic-worker training (see the 1 February 2025 article draft). The current length needs checking.

SA3b-35.claim: BAIRA's secretary general said in January 2025 that Saudi employers were no longer placing demand for Bangladeshi women domestic workers as before and were taking workers from various African countries, and that negative publicity had reduced women's interest in going.
SA3b-35.why_new: Demand-side reason for the fall in women's departures; not in the guide.

SA3b-36.claim: Firoza of Manikganj, back in October 2024 after two years in Saudi Arabia, said her pay was low but regular in the first year, was raised in the second but then not paid for 11 straight months and paid all at once when she left, that there were problems with food and she was beaten, and that women should not go to Saudi Arabia for housework.
SA3b-36.why_new: Case of wages withheld until exit, a common domestic-worker pattern; the guide's domestic-worker section has no case.

SA3b-37.claim: Shahida Begum (40) of Faridpur, back in October 2024 after two years three months in one Saudi household, said she was not fed regularly, was paid little, was sometimes beaten by the kafil's son, got no treatment after spraining her leg on the stairs, and had 700 riyals (BDT 17,500) deducted from her pay for the return ticket the employer was supposed to provide.
SA3b-37.why_new: Concrete case of the return ticket being charged to the worker; the guide's domestic-worker rights say the employer pays.

SA3b-38.claim: Officials of BRAC, OKUP and the Bangladesh Nari Sramik Kendra told Prothom Alo in January 2025 that returning women workers complain of being taken on lies, being made to work in more than one house, 14 to 16 hours' work, low and irregular pay and irregular food, some also of physical and mental abuse, and that some who ran from the kafil's house were detained by police and sent home.
SA3b-38.why_new: Top complaint types for domestic workers (Middle East-wide, Saudi the main destination); the guide's Complaints covers men's company visas.

SA3b-39.claim: Saudi ambassador in Dhaka Essa Yousef Essa Alduhailan said on 28 January 2025 that the Saudi embassy had issued visas for 22 lakh (2.2 million) Bangladeshi workers in the last three years and was issuing 7,000 visas a day.
SA3b-39.why_new: Visa issuance figure from the Saudi side; not in the guide. A foreign ministry official in the same article said about 14 lakh workers went in the ambassador's roughly five years, so visas issued far exceed departures.

SA3b-40.claim: A Bangladesh foreign ministry official said in January 2025 that about 14 lakh Bangladeshi workers had gone to Saudi Arabia during the Saudi ambassador's roughly five years in Dhaka, and that worker migration never fully stopped even during the coronavirus pandemic; Foreign Adviser M Touhid Hossain spoke of 30 lakh Bangladeshis in Saudi Arabia.
SA3b-40.why_new: Stock figure 30 lakh conflicts with the embassy's 33 lakh (December 2024) and the cross-country guide's 'at least 25 lakh'.

SA3b-41.claim: A Bangladesh foreign ministry official said in January 2025 that the Saudi ambassador played an important role in including Bangladesh in Saudi initiatives such as the 'Route to Makkah Initiative'.
SA3b-41.why_new: The guide does not mention Route to Makkah (Saudi immigration pre-clearance for pilgrims in Dhaka); the article does not explain how it works, so a Need to know may be needed.

SA3b-42.claim: According to a foreign ministry press release of 29 January 2025, Expatriates' Welfare Adviser Asif Nazrul inaugurated the Bangladesh embassy in Riyadh's e-Demand Attestation System, through which Saudi companies can register online and have worker demand letters attested without going to the embassy.
SA3b-42.target_section: Step 2: See the attested demand letter
SA3b-42.why_new: The guide describes the e-demand system on beriyadh.org but not its launch date.

SA3b-43.claim: Bangladeshis in Saudi Arabia complained to Expatriates' Welfare Adviser Asif Nazrul in Riyadh in January 2025 about high air ticket prices and recruiting agencies collecting extra money, and he promised solutions.
SA3b-43.target_section: What you pay, and what you earn and keep
SA3b-43.why_new: Low priority; confirms overcharging and ticket prices as top complaints in early 2025.

SA3b-44.claim: Per a press release of 29 January 2025, Saudi recruitment companies told Adviser Asif Nazrul that they recognise skilled Bangladeshi professionals but face a lack of information, marketing and networking, slow visa processing, language barriers and a lack of pre-boarding training.
SA3b-44.target_section: Is it open now, and who can go?
SA3b-44.why_new: Saudi employers' stated barriers to hiring skilled Bangladeshis; not in the guide.

SA3b-45.claim: At a meeting in Riyadh on 30 January 2025 between Expatriates' Welfare Adviser Asif Nazrul and Saudi Human Resources Vice Minister Abdullah Abuthnain, the main topic was high iqama renewal fees and workers losing their jobs because of them; Saudi Arabia said its labour law was being reformed to protect both sides' rights.
SA3b-45.why_new: Government-level confirmation that iqama fees cost workers their jobs; the guide has the fee amounts but not this.

SA3b-46.claim: On 30 January 2025 Bangladesh raised with Saudi Arabia that attestation of professional certificates at the Saudi embassy in Dhaka was delayed because the embassy had no cultural attaché, and Saudi officials promised a quick solution.
SA3b-46.target_section: Step 6: Give the agency your papers for the visa (start before Step 5)
SA3b-46.why_new: The guide says to apostille education certificates on MyGov; this shows professional certificates were also being attested at the Saudi embassy in Dhaka, with delays. Whether Saudi embassy attestation is still needed alongside the apostille is a gap.

SA3b-47.claim: At the 30 January 2025 meeting in Riyadh, Bangladesh and Saudi Arabia discussed making sure workers receive their employment contract before leaving Bangladesh, and Saudi officials said a task force would soon be formed against illegal workers and recruitment irregularities, welcoming Bangladesh's proposal for a joint team.
SA3b-47.target_section: The Bangladesh embassy's attestation, and the missing contract
SA3b-47.why_new: Supports the guide's point on missing contracts with a bilateral acknowledgement; the task force outcome is unknown.

SA3b-48.claim: At the 30 January 2025 meeting Bangladesh promised Saudi Arabia to shorten domestic-worker training while improving its quality.
SA3b-48.target_section: Step 3: Do the one-month housekeeping course (women)
SA3b-48.why_new: Relates to the conflict on course length (BAIRA said in January 2025 it had gone from one month to two; the guide says one month).

SA3b-49.claim: On 30 January 2025 Bangladesh asked Saudi Interior Vice Minister Nasser bin Abdulaziz Al Dawood for help with quick repatriation of irregular migrants and for a royal pardon for Bangladeshi prisoners convicted of minor offences; he said he would review and consider these.
SA3b-49.target_section: If you or a relative is arrested
SA3b-49.why_new: Royal pardons for minor offences are not in the guide; outcome unknown.

SA3b-50.claim: On 30 January 2025 Bangladesh invited Saudi authorities to inspect its Technical Training Centres (TTCs) and consider skills recognition for some of them, and Saudi Arabia agreed to a possible evaluation.
SA3b-50.why_new: Background to whether TTC certificates count in Saudi Arabia; outcome unknown.

SA3b-51.claim: According to Khilgaon police in Dhaka, on 11 January 2025 an organised gang of expatriate Bangladeshis kidnapped Russell, a Bangladeshi long resident in Saudi Arabia, from Riyadh, tortured him and demanded BDT 35 lakh ransom from his family, who deposited it into a bank account the gang gave them.
SA3b-51.target_section: NEW: If you or a relative is kidnapped (after If you or a relative is arrested)
SA3b-51.why_new: The guide has nothing on Bangladeshi gangs kidnapping Bangladeshis in Saudi Arabia for ransom paid at home.

SA3b-52.claim: After Russell's father-in-law filed a case at Khilgaon police station in Dhaka on 21 January 2025, police arrested three men in Lakshmipur and Brahmanbaria on 31 January, and BDT 12 lakh of the BDT 35 lakh ransom was frozen by court order.
SA3b-52.target_section: NEW: If you or a relative is kidnapped (after If you or a relative is arrested)
SA3b-52.placement: other: what the family can do
SA3b-52.why_new: Shows a family in Bangladesh can file a case at a Bangladeshi police station over a kidnapping in Saudi Arabia, and ransom paid into Bangladeshi accounts can be partly frozen.

SA3b-53.claim: The 2024 annual report of the digital migration platform Ami Probashi says 1,009,146 Bangladeshi workers went abroad in 2024, 27% fewer than the 1,390,811 of 2023, and that Saudi Arabia was again the top destination with 62% of them.
SA3b-53.why_new: 2024 Saudi share; conflicts slightly with Prothom Alo's 60% (December 2024, 11 months' data).

SA3b-54.claim: According to Ami Probashi's 2024 annual report, enrolment in Technical Training Centre courses fell to 112,166 in 2024 from 236,270 in 2023, while BMET registrations rose to 798,276 from 660,088, with women's share of registrations rising from 2.78% to 4.79%.
SA3b-54.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: How do I join a TTC course?

SA3b-55.claim: In a memorandum to the expatriates' welfare secretary on 5 February 2025, several BAIRA leaders said that for Saudi Arabia the rule had become that any visa lot of more than one must be attested by the embassy, whereas earlier this exemption applied up to 25, and demanded that 24-person visas be treated as a single item and given emigration clearance without embassy attestation.
SA3b-55.target_section: The Bangladesh embassy's attestation, and the missing contract
SA3b-55.why_new: CONFLICT: the guide says the embassy attests single visas too since 2025; here, a single one-worker visa is exempt and lots of 2+ need attestation. Also 'up to 25' here vs 'up to 24' in the 11 March 2025 article, and the guide's BMET definition of a group visa as 25 or more.

SA3b-56.claim: BAIRA leaders alleged in a memorandum on 5 February 2025 that every year a syndicate hoards air tickets and sells each at double the price or more, ruining poor outgoing workers.
SA3b-56.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Who pays for the air ticket?
SA3b-56.why_new: Ticket hoarding not in either guide; applies to Gulf routes generally.

SA3b-57.claim: Saudi ambassador in Dhaka Essa Yousef Essa Alduhailan said on 5 February 2025 that Saudi Arabia had asked Bangladesh to renew the Bangladeshi passports of 69,000 Rohingya living in Saudi Arabia, only for legal processes, and would not send them back to Bangladesh.
SA3b-57.target_section: Renewing your passport and getting an NID
SA3b-57.why_new: Not in the guide; relevant to Rohingya holding Bangladeshi passports in Saudi Arabia. Outcome unknown.

SA3b-58.claim: According to the CID (February 2025), a trafficking ring promising jobs in Russia at BDT 2 to 2.5 lakh a month first sent 10 Bangladeshis to Saudi Arabia on Umrah visas, had them perform Umrah, then took them to Russia, sold them to a 'Sultan' who handed them to Russian soldiers, and they were forced to fight against Ukraine; one, Humayun Kabir of Singra, Natore, was killed and another badly injured.
SA3b-58.why_new: The guide's Umrah section has no case of the Umrah visa used as a transit route for trafficking; the cross-country guide mentions RMMRU saying many go to Russia via Saudi tourist or Umrah visas but not this case.

SA3b-59.claim: According to the CID (February 2025), a second group of 10 trafficked Bangladeshis was in Saudi Arabia after refusing to go on to Russia on learning they would be forced to fight; their passports were taken, so they could neither work nor come home, and the CID was trying to bring them back.
SA3b-59.why_new: Shows people stranded in Saudi Arabia on Umrah visas without passports; links to Going home without valid papers.

SA3b-60.claim: The CID arrested a woman (named Fabiha Jerin and also Tamanna in its statements), a partner in Dream Home Travels and Tours Ltd, at Dhaka airport on 5 February 2025 as she was about to flee to Nepal, in a case filed at Banani police station by the wife of a wounded victim; the CID said she confessed and that her brother Tuhin, in Russia, had encouraged people to go to the war.
SA3b-60.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Russia: recruited into the war
SA3b-60.why_new: Named travel agency and arrest not in the cross-country guide.

SA3b-61.claim: Bangladesh's ambassador to Saudi Arabia, Mohammad Delwar Hossain, said at a Jeddah consulate seminar in late February 2025 that bringing skilled people to Saudi Arabia was their number one manpower priority, and that talks across Saudi Arabia showed skilled professionals were an important obstacle.
SA3b-61.target_section: Is it open now, and who can go?
SA3b-61.why_new: Official mission priority; not in the guide.

SA3b-62.claim: Bangladeshi community leaders at a Jeddah consulate seminar in late February 2025 demanded that no migrant worker be harassed when renewing a passport at the missions abroad, and that the government budget cover sending home the bodies of migrants who die abroad.
SA3b-62.target_section: Renewing your passport and getting an NID
SA3b-62.why_new: Indicates harassment at missions during passport renewal; the guide's passport-renewal steps don't mention it.

SA3b-63.claim: The ambassador said in February 2025 that, as community leaders told him, five thousand Bangladeshi businesspeople were already registered in Saudi Arabia.
SA3b-63.why_new: Low priority; count of registered Bangladeshi businesspeople.

SA3b-64.claim: Prothom Alo reported in March 2025 that Md. Kawsar (30), a construction worker from Trishal, Mymensingh, had gone to Saudi Arabia about 16 months earlier for BDT 7 lakh in all, BDT 5 lakh of it taken as dadon (an informal loan) costing BDT 10,000 a month per lakh, and that his family took a further BDT 2.10 lakh from two NGOs to pay the dadon.
SA3b-64.why_new: The guide says moneylenders charge 'far higher interest' without a figure; this gives the word dadon and a rate (10% a month).

SA3b-65.claim: Prothom Alo reported in March 2025 that the BDT 50,000-55,000 Kawsar sent home each month from Saudi Arabia all went on interest, and his wife said he was to come home after the loan was repaid.
SA3b-65.target_section: What reaches home, and how long the debt takes
SA3b-65.why_new: Concrete case of debt eating all remittances.

SA3b-66.claim: Relatives, citing Kawsar's acquaintances in Saudi Arabia, said he died on 3 March in an accident while working on a gas transmission line in Dammam, where he worked for a company named Sacco (সাক্কো); the family learned of the death through a neighbour who is also a migrant, and as of 10 March 2025 the body had not come home and his father did not know through which Bangladeshi agency or when it would be returned.
SA3b-66.target_section: If a worker dies in Saudi Arabia
SA3b-66.why_new: Case showing families often hear of a death informally and don't know the repatriation route.
SA3b-66.h2: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job

SA3b-67.claim: On 10 March 2025 Kawsar's father applied in writing for the body at the Wage Earners' Welfare Board's welfare centre in Mymensingh city, whose assistant director said the centre would forward the application to the Welfare Board, which would then make all arrangements.
SA3b-67.target_section: If a worker dies in Saudi Arabia
SA3b-67.why_new: Answers part of the guide's Need to know ('How does the family apply to the Welfare Board to have the body brought home: in person, by email or on its portal?'): a written application in person at a district welfare centre is accepted and forwarded.
SA3b-67.h2: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job

SA3b-68.claim: Prothom Alo reported on 11 March 2025 that since 22 December the government has required the Bangladesh embassy's attestation of any Saudi demand letter for more than one worker, whereas earlier letters for up to 24 workers did not need it (former BAIRA joint secretary general Fakhrul Islam said only BMET's attestation was taken), that BAIRA members blamed this attestation complication for falling departures, and that departures to Saudi Arabia, over 80,000 a month on average since October, fell by half in February.
SA3b-68.why_new: CONFLICT: the guide dates the single-visa attestation stall 'from late January' 2025 and says single visas need attestation 'since 2025'; this article gives 22 December 2024 and says a one-worker letter is exempt.

SA3b-69.claim: BMET figures reported in March 2025 show 44,229 workers went to Saudi Arabia in September 2024, 83,582 in October 2024, about the same for the next two months, 76,618 in January 2025 and 44,258 in February 2025.
SA3b-69.why_new: Monthly departures show the size of the early-2025 stall; not in the guide.

SA3b-70.claim: BAIRA members said in March 2025 that 85% of workers sent from Bangladesh to Saudi Arabia go on small demand letters for 1 to 24 workers.
SA3b-70.why_new: Agency-side estimate of the single-visa share; fits the guide's BMET five-year figure (21.36 lakh single vs 90,000 group) and partly answers its Need to know on single-visa clearances.

SA3b-71.claim: Former BAIRA joint secretary general Fakhrul Islam said in March 2025 that the embassy lacks the capacity to attest every worker's demand letter, so the sudden rule change had cut departures.
SA3b-71.target_section: The Bangladesh embassy's attestation, and the missing contract
SA3b-71.why_new: Agency-side view of the attestation bottleneck, relevant to how long attestation takes (the guide's Need to know on processing time).
