SA3c-1.claim: A Prothom Alo editorial of 13 March 2025 said that under a rule the Bangladesh government introduced on 22 December 2024, a Saudi demand letter for one worker needs no attestation by the Bangladesh embassy but any letter for more than one worker must be attested, whereas before demand letters for up to 24 workers needed no attestation.
SA3c-1.why_new: CONFLICT: the guide dates the single-visa attestation stall 'from late January' 2025 [SB0031] and says attestation applies 'for single visas too since 2025' [A0087]; this editorial dates the rule from 22 December 2024 and says a one-worker letter is still exempt, the change being that 2-24 worker letters now need attestation.

SA3c-2.claim: From October 2024 more than 80,000 workers a month on average went to Saudi Arabia, but in February 2025 the number fell to half, which members of BAIRA (the Bangladesh Association of International Recruiting Agencies) blamed on delays in attesting demand letters, a Prothom Alo editorial said in March 2025.
SA3c-2.why_new: Gives the size of the early-2025 attestation stall (monthly departures halved in February 2025); the guide names the stall but not its effect.

SA3c-3.claim: BAIRA members said in March 2025 that 85% of workers going from Bangladesh to Saudi Arabia go on small demand letters for 1 to 24 workers, so embassy attestation delays had stopped visas being processed.
SA3c-3.why_new: Adds the recruiters' estimate of the share going on small (single-visa) demand letters; the guide gives only BMET's five-year single vs group totals [RD0015].

SA3c-4.claim: Bangladesh Bank governor Ahsan H Mansur said at several recent events (reported 19 March 2025) that not all remittances from Saudi Arabia come directly to Bangladesh but come via Dubai, that a dishonest ring buys remittances from Saudi Arabia, hoards them and sells them to Bangladeshi banks at a higher price, and that banks would not be allowed to buy dollars at higher prices from such firms.
SA3c-4.placement: other: why the legal channel is hard to trace
SA3c-4.why_new: The guide covers hundi and costs but not this routing of Saudi remittances through Dubai aggregators; low direct use to a worker, background only.

SA3c-5.claim: Under Saudi labour law the employer or the Saudi government must bear a worker's cost of going home, and the Saudi human resources ministry's spokesperson Mike Goldstein told the New York Times (abridged in Prothom Alo, March 2025) that under no circumstances will a worker bear the cost of repatriation, but returned workers and labour-rights groups said workers are in practice forced to pay and those who cannot are sometimes held.
SA3c-5.placement: under Work visa: domestic worker; other: who pays the ticket home in practice
SA3c-5.why_new: The guide says a domestic worker leaving without a valid reason pays her own ticket [D0019]; this adds the ministry's stated rule and the reported practice. The workers in the article are Kenyan and Ugandan, not Bangladeshi.

SA3c-6.claim: The Saudi government had tasked an organisation called Sakan with housing and legal help for foreign workers in difficulty; the ministry spokesperson told the New York Times that the government stopped Sakan's funding in 2023 and that another organisation, Samasco, now does this work; three Kenyan women in a Samasco shelter said they would not be allowed home unless each paid USD 400, and Samasco did not respond.
SA3c-6.placement: under Work visa: domestic worker; Complain in this order, item 2 (shelters)
SA3c-6.why_new: New: names Samasco as the Saudi-funded shelter operator for foreign workers (Sakan before 2023), with an allegation of a USD 400 exit charge; the guide lists only the Bangladesh embassy's safe homes.

SA3c-7.claim: Ugandan domestic worker Mary Nisimenta told the New York Times that after she jumped from a three-storey roof in Najran to escape her employer and was treated for a spinal injury, she reported the abuse to the police and the doctor, who told her to go back to work; when she refused, the Saudi placement agency sent her home.
SA3c-7.placement: under Work visa: domestic worker; other: reporting abuse to police or a doctor
SA3c-7.why_new: Shows what reporting abuse to Saudi police or hospital staff can lead to; the guide does not cover this. Not a Bangladeshi case.

SA3c-8.claim: Ugandan domestic worker Farida Nassanga told the New York Times that her employer's husband raped her in Saudi Arabia, and that when she became pregnant the employer blamed her and put her on a flight home.
SA3c-8.why_new: Adds a case of what happened to a worker made pregnant by rape (sent home); the guide notes only the legal risk [SG0008]. Not a Bangladeshi case.

SA3c-9.claim: In cases the New York Times investigated, Saudi authorities declared the deaths of foreign domestic workers natural despite signs of violence: Ugandan Aisha Meeme's Saudi autopsy found three broken ribs and severe electrical burns on her ears, hands and feet, and her husband said the employer offered him the choice of her body or her USD 2,800 in unpaid wages.
SA3c-9.target_section: If a worker dies in Saudi Arabia
SA3c-9.why_new: Supports the guide's line that cause of death is usually recorded as natural [E0093] with a documented example, and adds the body-or-wages trade-off offered to a family. Not a Bangladeshi case.
SA3c-9.h2: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job

SA3c-10.claim: By Saudi government figures about 5 lakh workers from Kenya and Uganda, mostly women domestic workers, work in Saudi Arabia, and at least 274 Kenyan workers, mostly women, died there in the five years to early 2025, 55 of them in 2024, double the year before, the New York Times reported.
SA3c-10.why_new: Corridor comparison (East African competition for domestic-worker jobs); the guide has no comparison with other sending countries for domestic work. Low priority.

SA3c-11.claim: ATAB (the Association of Travel Agents of Bangladesh) said in March 2025 that Dhaka-Saudi fares, which reached up to Tk 1,90,000 in December 2024 and February 2025 because of 'group booking schemes', had fallen to Tk 48,000-50,000, with some airlines selling Dammam and Riyadh tickets for as little as Tk 35,000, after the civil aviation ministry's 11 February 2025 directives made a passenger's name, passport details and passport copy compulsory at booking.
SA3c-11.why_new: The guide already has Tk 48,000-50,000 [G0021] and the name-and-passport booking rule [G0020]; this adds the Tk 1.9 lakh peak from group-booked seats, the Tk 35,000 low and the 11 February 2025 directive date. Guide dates the Tk 48-50k fare May 2025; this source is March 2025.

SA3c-12.claim: A banker's column in Prothom Alo in April 2025 said about 28 lakh Bangladeshis live in Middle Eastern countries, more than 21 lakh of them in Saudi Arabia, making Bangladesh third among Saudi Arabia's foreign workforces after India and Pakistan.
SA3c-12.why_new: The guide gives departures but no stock of Bangladeshis in Saudi Arabia. CONFLICT within this batch: 21 lakh+ here, about 32 lakh (Foreign Adviser, SA3c drafts from 79b9bcde), about 35 lakh working (religious affairs adviser, 851093ae), more than 30 lakh (Asif Nazrul, bb65a329). A reviewer should pick an official figure.

SA3c-57.claim: A banker's column in April 2025 described the incentive for remittances through banking channels as 2.5% and proposed raising it to 3.5%.
SA3c-57.why_new: Supports the guide's 2.5% [E0076]; conflicts with the ministry's 2% in June 2025 (5afce1f2).

SA3c-13.claim: A Prothom Alo check in April 2025 found a direct Dhaka-Jeddah ticket for 1 May 2025 priced at USD 552 (about Tk 67,000), against USD 307 (about Tk 37,500) from New Delhi to Jeddah the same day.
SA3c-13.why_new: Adds a dated Dhaka-Jeddah market fare; the guide gives Tk 48,000-50,000 [G0021], lower than this fare.

SA3c-14.claim: The civil aviation ministry's February 2025 directives require tickets to be sold at the Civil Aviation Authority of Bangladesh's approved fares and discounted tickets to be given to migrant workers, and Biman's managing director, Md Safiqur Rahman, said in April 2025 that discounted tickets were being given to workers going abroad.
SA3c-14.why_new: Partly answers the guide's Need to know 'Does the fare still apply?' under item 6 (as of April 2025, from the directive and Biman); gives no amount.

SA3c-15.claim: Ticket agencies told Prothom Alo in April 2025 that under the previous Awami League government a ring formed in which Biman itself held back cheap tickets and released only expensive ones, and that this had not fully stopped; the article said trading in Saudi tickets began in late 2024, and people in the sector said ticket blocking had fallen a lot since the civil aviation ministry's February 2025 directives.
SA3c-15.why_new: Explains the late-2024 Saudi ticket racket behind the fare spike; the guide has only the booking rule [G0020].

SA3c-16.claim: Mizanur Rahman (62) of Noakhali, a day labourer in Jubail who had worked in Saudi Arabia since 1993 and who, his family said, had been without valid papers since 2017, was admitted to Jubail General Hospital after a stroke on 28 February 2025; his family said his first week's hospital bill was waived but his treatment largely stopped afterwards because there was no guarantee the bill would be paid.
SA3c-16.why_new: The guide's Injured or ill covers insured workers; nothing on hospital treatment for a worker without papers. Adds a case.
SA3c-16.h2: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job

SA3c-17.claim: Mizanur's wife said the Bangladesh embassy in Saudi Arabia told the family it would arrange to send him home once a compensation case his employer had filed against him was resolved; the family said the employer had since died but the case remained, and she said she did not know how to resolve it from Bangladesh.
SA3c-17.placement: To get home (worker with a case against him)
SA3c-17.why_new: Shows an employer's case blocking repatriation of a sick worker, as with matloob [SM0046]; the guide does not cover this for a sick worker.
SA3c-17.h2: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job

SA3c-18.claim: The Wage Earners' Welfare Board cannot directly help workers without valid papers, so it forwarded Mizanur's wife's 9 April 2025 application, made with help from BRAC's Migration Programme, to the expatriates' ministry, which wrote to the embassy's labour wing on 16 April 2025 asking it to send him home urgently.
SA3c-18.placement: To get home (worker without valid papers)
SA3c-18.why_new: The guide's To get home route needs BMET clearance or Board membership [E0014]; this shows the route for an undocumented sick worker (Board forwards to ministry, ministry writes to labour wing), parallel to the guide's route for bodies [E0091].
SA3c-18.h2: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job

SA3c-19.claim: Foreign Adviser Touhid Hossain said in April 2025 that about 80% of the problems Bangladeshi migrant workers face arise from processes in Bangladesh before they leave and 20% in the destination country, citing Saudi Arabia, where about 32 lakh Bangladeshis live, as an example of a mission's workload.
SA3c-19.target_section: What goes wrong most, and what people wrongly believe
SA3c-19.why_new: An official's estimate of where migrant problems originate; not in the guide. Opinion-level, low priority.

SA3c-20.claim: Foreign Adviser Touhid Hossain said in April 2025 that about 32 lakh Bangladeshis live in Saudi Arabia and asked how a mission's 50 officials could handle the problems of so many people.
SA3c-20.why_new: Stock figure and embassy staffing (50 officials); the guide has neither. CONFLICT with other stock figures in this batch (21 lakh+, 30 lakh+, 35 lakh).

SA3c-21.claim: For Hajj 2025, from 1 Zilqad (29 April) to 14 Zilhajj (10 June), Saudi Arabia barred anyone from entering or staying in Makkah and the surrounding holy sites without a valid permit to work at the holy sites, a Makkah-registered iqama or an official Hajj permit, and said visit-visa holders would be under the closest surveillance.
SA3c-21.placement: other: Hajj-season restrictions in Saudi Arabia
SA3c-21.why_new: The guide gives the SR 20,000 fine and ban for Hajj on another visa [D0109, D0110] but not the Makkah entry rule, which also binds iqama holders living outside Makkah.

SA3c-22.claim: Saudi Arabia's interior ministry said for Hajj 2025 that anyone who helps a person perform Hajj without a permit faces a fine of up to SR 100,000, and that if the offence is proved the helper's own vehicle will be confiscated by court order.
SA3c-22.target_section: What can get you jailed or deported
SA3c-22.placement: other: helping someone do Hajj without a permit
SA3c-22.why_new: New: the penalty for workers in Saudi Arabia who drive, house or help relatives doing Hajj without a permit; the guide covers only the pilgrim's own penalty.

SA3c-23.claim: Bangladesh's religious affairs ministry on 2 May 2025 asked Bangladeshis in Saudi Arabia not to sponsor, transport, help into the restricted Hajj area, or house in hotels or homes any visit-visa holder breaking the Hajj rules, and not to perform Hajj without a permit.
SA3c-23.target_section: What can get you jailed or deported
SA3c-23.placement: other: helping someone do Hajj without a permit
SA3c-23.why_new: Lists the acts that count as helping; not in the guide.

SA3c-24.claim: Religious affairs adviser A F M Khalid Hossain said in May 2025 that about 35 lakh Bangladeshis work in Saudi Arabia and that the highest remittance comes from Saudi Arabia.
SA3c-24.why_new: Stock figure; CONFLICT with 21 lakh+ (column), 32 lakh (Foreign Adviser) and 30 lakh+ (Asif Nazrul) in this batch; the guide gives no stock.

SA3c-25.claim: The family of cousins Sohel Molla and Iqbal Molla of Jaldia village, Sultanpur union, Rajbari Sadar paid neighbour Moniruddin Molla and his brother-in-law Mamun Molla Tk 6 lakh in cash on 5 March 2024 and Tk 4 lakh through a bank on 26 May 2024 for good jobs in Saudi Arabia, where, the family says, the two got no work and were abused by the broker ring.
SA3c-25.target_section: If an agency, broker or relative takes your money
SA3c-25.why_new: New case of neighbours acting as brokers (Tk 5 lakh a head, paid partly by bank), adding to the guide's relative/neighbour fraud cases.

SA3c-26.claim: Sohel's father Kamal Molla said the brokers took a further Tk 2 lakh from the family on 7 February 2025 on a promise of work for the two men, after which the men lost contact with their families, and Sohel's wife Rina Akter said in May 2025 that the brokers were now demanding Tk 10 lakh more to bring them back.
SA3c-26.target_section: If an agency, broker or relative takes your money
SA3c-26.why_new: Shows the follow-on demands (money for work after arrival, then money to bring the men home); the guide's free-visa section has post-arrival payments but not ransom-style demands to return a worker.

SA3c-27.claim: On 27 April 2025 Rina Akter filed a case under the human trafficking prevention and suppression law against Moniruddin and Mamun at Rajbari's human trafficking offences tribunal, which ordered PBI (the Police Bureau of Investigation) Faridpur to investigate; Mamun said the men had refused to work at the company they were given and their passports were returned from the company through the agency.
SA3c-27.target_section: If an agency, broker or relative takes your money
SA3c-27.why_new: Example of a family going straight to the trafficking tribunal (complaint case) and the court sending it to PBI; the guide mentions the trafficking law route [RC0045] without a Saudi example of a tribunal filing.

SA3c-28.claim: Expatriates' welfare adviser Asif Nazrul told Saudi Arabia's vice minister of human resources, Abdullah bin Nasser Abuthnain, in Riyadh in May 2025 that women domestic workers would complete the one-month training before getting a Saudi visa and be sent within two weeks of the visa after a short training, and that the ministry was committed to shortening domestic workers' training; the Saudi vice minister welcomed this.
SA3c-28.target_section: Step 3: Do the one-month housekeeping course (women)
SA3c-28.why_new: Changes the order of steps for women (course before the visa, flight within two weeks of it); the guide puts the course at Step 3 without saying it must come before the visa. Need to know: was this implemented?

SA3c-29.claim: According to a press release reported in May 2025, Asif Nazrul thanked the Saudi side for forming the working team of officials from the Saudi Ministry of Human Resources and Social Development and the Bangladesh embassy, promised at a 30 January 2025 meeting, to solve specific problems of irregular Bangladeshi workers in Saudi Arabia, and a high-powered task force had already been formed under the latest Foreign Office Consultations to solve the problem of illegal workers and remove recruitment irregularities.
SA3c-29.why_new: New: the joint working team and task force on irregular workers; the guide's amnesty section does not mention them. Need to know: what did they deliver?

SA3c-30.claim: In the May 2025 Riyadh meeting Asif Nazrul proposed that Saudi Arabia verify an employer's capacity and whether work actually exists before issuing a work visa, and that employment contracts be signed online before the worker arrives; these were proposals, not agreed measures.
SA3c-30.target_section: The Bangladesh embassy's attestation, and the missing contract
SA3c-30.why_new: Shows Bangladesh's ask on the missing-contract and no-job problems; status only, no rule changed.

SA3c-31.claim: Asif Nazrul thanked Saudi Arabia in May 2025 for hosting more than 30 lakh Bangladeshis.
SA3c-31.why_new: Stock figure; CONFLICT with 21 lakh+, 32 lakh and 35 lakh in this batch.

SA3c-32.claim: Expatriates' welfare adviser Asif Nazrul said on 6 May 2025, after a visit to Saudi Arabia, that an opportunity had been created to regularise women workers living illegally in Saudi Arabia; he gave no procedure.
SA3c-32.why_new: The guide says it is not known how an undocumented woman domestic worker gets an exit visa; this reports a regularisation chance (no how). Need to know: what is the procedure, and is it still open?

SA3c-33.claim: According to Motiur Rahman's family, Motiur, a manpower trader from Raninagar, Naogaon, sent Sajib of Talson village, Adamdighi, Bogura, to Saudi Arabia two years earlier, where Sajib got no iqama because of problems with his papers; Sajib's uncle Jahangir Alam said in May 2025 that the company Sajib was sent to had still not given him an iqama and that Motiur had promised one and kept making excuses.
SA3c-33.target_section: If a relative or friend offers you a visa
SA3c-33.placement: If it turns out to be a free visa (Cases)
SA3c-33.why_new: Another no-iqama case after a broker's visa. CONFLICT within sources: this report says Sajib went two years earlier; the next day's report (f180ac18) quotes his father as saying 40 days earlier.

SA3c-34.claim: Manpower businessman Motiur Rahman said that on 18 May 2025 seven masked young men beat him on a train after Altafnagar station and tried to push him off until he fell at Nasratpur station, Adamdighi, Bogura, and he filed an attempted-murder case at Santahar Junction GRP (railway police) station naming as main accused Sumon, brother-in-law of Sajib, a man Motiur had sent to Saudi Arabia who had not found work; Sajib's father said his son had gone 40 days earlier, still had no work and Motiur was hiding from the family, but denied any part in the attack.
SA3c-34.why_new: Shows village-level disputes between families and brokers when a worker gets no job or iqama; low priority for a migrant's decisions.

SA3c-35.claim: Saiful Islam (28) of East Belagaon, Juri, Moulvibazar, a labourer on a poultry farm near Riyadh for about three years, whose employer had just given him three months' leave, was killed on 20 May 2025 when the goods truck he and a co-worker were riding to Riyadh on their weekly day off hit a camel on the road and overturned; his body was kept at a Riyadh hospital morgue.
SA3c-35.target_section: If a worker dies in Saudi Arabia
SA3c-35.why_new: A road-death case for a farm worker; the guide has no case of a non-work road death. Low priority; may also show farm workers riding goods trucks.
SA3c-35.h2: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job

SA3c-36.claim: Abdul Jabbar Sardar, a farm labourer from Hiranandapur, Tanore, Rajshahi, borrowed Tk 7 lakh and went to Saudi Arabia on 16 January 2018, where, his wife Adori Khatun said, he was put to work as a cleaner on landing, later realised brokers had 'sold' him as an airport cleaner, and after three years of unpaid work was sent away empty-handed; the loan was still unpaid in May 2025.
SA3c-36.target_section: Irregular routes and how they end
SA3c-36.why_new: New case: three years' unpaid work as an airport cleaner, then cast out undocumented.

SA3c-37.claim: Believing Saudi police would send him home if they caught him, Jabbar gave himself up to the police, who took his fingerprints and released him, leaving him with no money for food, his wife said.
SA3c-37.why_new: Counters a common belief that surrendering to police gets an undocumented worker deported home; the guide does not address self-surrender.

SA3c-38.claim: His wife said that after Jabbar, who worked at a tile factory owned by an Indian national and had no papers, was badly injured in a road accident on 10 May 2024 and put in a Saudi hospital ICU, those she spoke to three months later asked Tk 70 lakh to send him home because he had no papers, and later people she was connected with, whom she could not identify, asked Tk 70 lakh and then Tk 19,000 for the airfare, which she could not raise.
SA3c-38.placement: To get home (worker without valid papers)
SA3c-38.why_new: Shows what families are asked to pay to repatriate an injured undocumented worker; the guide has no figure.
SA3c-38.h2: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job

SA3c-39.claim: Jabbar's wife said her application to the Wage Earners' Welfare Board brought no result until the Tanore UNO (Upazila Nirbahi Officer, the sub-district's chief executive), whose office she waited 22 days to enter, reached the Bangladesh embassy after 15 days of trying.
SA3c-39.why_new: Shows the UNO as an alternative push when the Board stalls; the guide's 'If the Board doesn't deliver' lists only Board/ministry/GRS. CONFLICT with the Board's own account in f8925d9a (it wrote to the embassy and sent a reminder on 9 April 2025).
SA3c-39.h2: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job

SA3c-40.claim: When Jabbar was flown home unconscious in May 2025, the escorts who had promised to bring him to a hospital with a doctor and nurse and to give some money gave nothing and left him at the airport, and a private hospital in Dhaka cost Tk 70,000 for seven hours before his wife hired an oxygen-equipped vehicle to Rajshahi for Tk 25,000, she said.
SA3c-40.why_new: The guide says the Board's airport desk takes injured returnees to hospital by ambulance [E0014, E0040]; this case (undocumented, not Board-registered as far as reported) got no such help.

SA3c-41.claim: Asif Nazrul said on 31 May 2025 that Saudi Arabia had assured him it would regularise Bangladeshis who were irregular workers there and had already started doing so.
SA3c-41.why_new: Official claim of a 2025 regularisation for irregular workers (not only women); the guide's amnesty section has only the employer-led permit regularisation to end-2026 [G0014]. Need to know: was this the same scheme?

SA3c-42.claim: Jabbar's wife applied in writing to the Wage Earners' Welfare Board's director general on 13 January 2025; the Board wrote to the embassy, sent a reminder on 9 April, and he was flown home unconscious on 23 May 2025, after more than a year in a Saudi ICU, the Board's assistant director Main Uddin and the family said.
SA3c-42.why_new: Gives a real timeline (about four months) for the Board's bring-home route; the guide gives no time.
SA3c-42.h2: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job

SA3c-43.claim: The Welfare Board's assistant director Main Uddin said in June 2025 that Jabbar's family could now apply for treatment help, and that if he was a registered worker the Board could give up to Tk 1.5 lakh quickly.
SA3c-43.why_new: CONFLICT: the guide says the Board pays up to Tk 2 lakh in treatment money after coming home [E0014]; a Board official said up to Tk 1.5 lakh in June 2025.
SA3c-43.h2: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job

SA3c-44.claim: CID (the police Criminal Investigation Department) said in June 2025 that a ring lured 10 people with jobs as cleaners or cooks in a chocolate factory in Russia at Tk 2-2.5 lakh a month, sent them first to Saudi Arabia on Umrah visas, had them perform Umrah, then took them to Russia and sold them to a man called Sultan, who handed them to the Russian army.
SA3c-44.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Russia: recruited into the war
SA3c-44.why_new: The cross-country Russia section has RMMRU's general statement that many go via Saudi Arabia on tourist or Umrah visas [RU0030]; this adds a documented CID case with the job lure and pay promised.

SA3c-45.claim: A second group of 10 recruited by the same ring was in Saudi Arabia in June 2025: when it became known that recruits were forced to fight, they refused to go on to Russia, their passports were taken from them, and they could neither work in Saudi Arabia nor go home, CID said.
SA3c-45.why_new: New: Umrah visas used as the first leg of trafficking to Russia, leaving men stranded in Saudi Arabia without passports; the guide's Umrah section has no scams beyond fake agencies.

SA3c-46.claim: CID arrested Fabiha Jerin alias Tamanna, a partner of Dream Home Travels and Tours Limited of Banani, Dhaka, at Dhaka airport on 5 February 2025 as she was fleeing to Nepal, and arrested the alleged ringleader Muhammad Alamgir Hossain (40) of Lohagara, Chattogram at Chattogram's Shah Amanat airport in June 2025; CID said Alamgir, who went to Russia on a student visa in 2008 and became a citizen by marriage, had taken 50 people to Russia on three visa categories.
SA3c-46.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Russia: recruited into the war
SA3c-46.why_new: Names a travel agency and ringleader in the Russia route not in the cross-country section.

SA3c-47.claim: By BMET figures total departures of Bangladeshi workers fell from 13 lakh in 2023 to 10 lakh in 2024 because the Malaysia, UAE and Oman markets were closed, while, according to information gathered by Prothom Alo and unnamed sources, about 5 lakh workers went to Saudi Arabia in 2023 and about 6.25 lakh in 2024, Saudi Arabia being the only country to take more than 1 lakh.
SA3c-47.why_new: The guide gives 2025 and 2026 departures only; adds 2023 and 2024.

SA3c-48.claim: Prothom Alo reported in June 2025 that 34% of all Bangladeshi workers who have gone abroad so far went to Saudi Arabia and 73% of those who left in the five months to May 2025 went there, and by BMET data 3 lakh of the 4.2 lakh workers who left in the first five months of 2025 went to Saudi Arabia, followed by Qatar with 40,000 and Singapore with over 26,000.
SA3c-48.why_new: Adds the all-time share (34%) and the early-2025 share (73%); the guide says 'two of every three' for 2025-2026.

SA3c-49.claim: By BMET data, 17,786 of the 24,617 Bangladeshi women who went abroad for work in January-May 2025 went to Saudi Arabia, and women's departures overall fell from 1,05,466 in 2022 to 76,108 in 2023 and 61,158 in 2024.
SA3c-49.why_new: The guide gives no count of women going to Saudi Arabia.

SA3c-50.claim: Former BAIRA secretary general Ali Haider Chowdhury said in June 2025 that Saudi visas had been closed for a month, new demand had also fallen, and Saudi Arabia might introduce more screening in recruitment when it made an announcement expected in July.
SA3c-50.why_new: Confirms the June 2025 visa closure the guide ties to the Hajj season [SB0043, E0123], and adds falling demand.

SA3c-51.claim: Sector people said in June 2025 that most workers going to Saudi Arabia get the recruitment demand letter through acquaintances or relatives, and that a class of brokers has grown up around this who pass off fake appointment letters, so some reach Saudi Arabia, find no work and are cheated.
SA3c-51.why_new: Supports the guide's relatives channel [A0078] for 2025 and adds fake appointment letters passed through it.

SA3c-52.claim: Sumaiya Islam, executive director of Bangladesh Nari Sramik Kendra (BNSK, a women migrant workers' organisation), said in June 2025 that domestic work in Saudi homes pays little for the labour it demands, that necessary support for women workers in the Middle East has not been ensured, and that Middle Eastern countries are taking workers from Africa instead.
SA3c-52.why_new: An NGO view on the domestic-worker corridor; opinion, low priority.

SA3c-53.claim: The expatriates' ministry said on 24 June 2025 that Saudi recruitment had slowed somewhat because of complications in the visa process, vaccine-related restrictions and changes in Saudi labour policy, that construction projects for the 2034 World Cup were nearing completion and cutting labour demand, and that in June 2024 Saudi Arabia temporarily suspended visa processing for Bangladeshi workers, as it has done before, this time as it seeks under Vision 2030 a more technology-based, localised workforce that prioritises women workers.
SA3c-53.why_new: Official reasons for the mid-2025 stall. The ministry's text says June 2024, but the report it answers (a89dbb34, same day) puts the pause in June 2025; likely a misprint. 'Vaccine-related restrictions' are unexplained: Need to know which vaccine rule (possibly meningitis or polio) affected workers.

SA3c-54.claim: The expatriates' ministry said in June 2025 that an earlier productive meeting with the Saudi government led by adviser Asif Nazrul had brought positive responses, that a government-level memorandum of understanding with Saudi Arabia was at the final stage of signing, and that sending more skilled and unskilled workers to Saudi Arabia had been discussed with the Saudi government.
SA3c-54.why_new: Background to the 6 October 2025 agreement the guide cites [SB0001]; low priority.

SA3c-55.claim: The expatriates' ministry said in June 2025 that, following the adviser's talks, an opportunity had been created to regularise women workers living illegally in Saudi Arabia; it gave no procedure, deadline or cost.
SA3c-55.why_new: Official ministry confirmation of the women's regularisation chance (see also SA3c draft from 44b3e5e8); the guide says how undocumented women domestic workers get out is not known.

SA3c-56.claim: The expatriates' ministry said in June 2025 that the government continues a 2% cash incentive on remittances sent through banks.
SA3c-56.why_new: CONFLICT: the guide says the family gets a 2.5% government incentive [E0076], and an April 2025 column in this batch (85959aa3) also says 2.5%; the ministry says 2%. Check the current rate.

SA3d-1.claim: In July 2025 Expatriates' Welfare Adviser Asif Nazrul said that in one place in Saudi Arabia Bangladeshi thugs go and attack other Bangladeshis to snatch and loot their money.
SA3d-1.why_new: The guide says nothing about Bangladeshi gangs robbing other Bangladeshi workers in Saudi Arabia; the place is not named.

SA3d-2.claim: Sakibur Rahman (25) of Mohuripara, Pekua, Cox's Bazar, who went to Saudi Arabia on 6 June 2025, died on the spot in a road accident in Mahil city on 23 July 2025 while learning to drive, and a relative was injured, his elder brother told Prothom Alo.
SA3d-2.why_new: Driving section has blood-money and insurance rules but no case of a new arrival killed while learning to drive; licence/learning rules are a gap.

SA3d-3.claim: In July 2025 Magnama Union Parishad panel chairman Badiul Alam said papers were being collected to bring Sakibur Rahman's body home, and that such a death a month and a half after going abroad was hard to accept.
SA3d-3.target_section: If a worker dies in Saudi Arabia
SA3d-3.why_new: Shows the Union Parishad's role in gathering papers for repatriation; the guide lists the heirship certificate but no case.
SA3d-3.h2: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job

SA3d-4.claim: In August 2025 Asif Nazrul said an agreement on migrant workers and employment was being signed with Saudi Arabia, the first ever on migrant workers, that it would increase workers' safety and protection there, that the previous government had tried many times and failed, and that India and Pakistan do not have such an agreement with Saudi Arabia.
SA3d-4.why_new: Guide states only the signing date and that private agencies carry it; adds what it was meant to change and the India/Pakistan comparison.

SA3d-5.claim: Asif Nazrul said in August 2025 that he had seen migrant workers at one place in Saudi Arabia living in conditions worse than anyone lives in Bangladesh's worst slum.
SA3d-5.why_new: No first-hand official account of housing conditions in the guide.

SA3d-6.claim: Asif Nazrul said in August 2025 that people spend Tk 8 to 10 lakh to go abroad and many get no work when they arrive.
SA3d-6.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: How much does it really cost to go?
SA3d-6.why_new: An adviser's own cost estimate (no country named), higher than the survey averages the cross-country doc gives.

SA3d-7.claim: Prothom Alo reported in August 2025 that a joint task force had been formed to resolve the problems of Bangladeshis in Saudi Arabia.
SA3d-7.why_new: The guide does not mention the joint task force; its membership and how a worker reaches it are unknown (Need to know).

SA3d-8.claim: The Expatriates' Welfare Ministry's one-year report (August 2025) said measures had been taken to regularise irregular women workers in Saudi Arabia, Jordan and Oman.
SA3d-8.why_new: Guide says women domestic workers are excluded from SEP and asks how they get an exit visa; this names a regularisation measure for irregular women without details.

SA3d-9.claim: The Expatriates' Welfare Ministry said in August 2025 that legal consultancy firms had been appointed in Qatar, Oman, Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Kuwait.
SA3d-9.why_new: The guide has no mention of a ministry-appointed law firm in Saudi Arabia; name and access route are a gap.

SA3d-10.claim: Prothom Alo reported in August 2025 that under an agreement between BMET and the Saudi company Takamol, 15 TTCs and BRTC training centres had gained the capacity to run skill tests in the past year.
SA3d-10.why_new: Conflict: guide says the test runs at 27 TTCs and BRTC Gazipur (later source); this is the August 2025 count.

SA3d-11.claim: Prothom Alo reported in August 2025 that after Bangladeshis abroad protested last year in support of the uprising, 188 people were freed from the UAE and 12 from Saudi Arabia and returned home.
SA3d-11.why_new: Guide has nothing on Bangladeshis jailed in Saudi Arabia for political protest; relevant to what can get you jailed.

SA3d-12.claim: Prothom Alo reported in August 2025 that demand for unskilled workers has fallen in Saudi Arabia, the largest labour market.
SA3d-12.why_new: Guide gives numbers but not the stated fall in demand for unskilled workers.

SA3d-13.claim: Prothom Alo reported in August 2025 that BOESL, the government agency, sent 16,066 workers to various countries in FY2024-25, 4% more than the year before.
SA3d-13.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Can I go through the government agency, BOESL?
SA3d-13.why_new: Cross-country gives BOESL's 14-year total but not the FY2024-25 figure.

SA3d-14.claim: Asif Nazrul said on 20 August 2025 that the interim government had shut the private app 'Ami Probashi' and built an integrated government online platform on which BMET issues emigration clearance 100% online.
SA3d-14.why_new: Conflict: the guide's PDO enrolment step (Step 8) still tells workers to enrol through the Ami Probashi app [B0166]; the minister says the app was shut.

SA3d-15.claim: Physician Arifur Rahman, now Premier Bank chairman, told Prothom Alo (August 2025) that years ago a contractor named Al Khodari, who had the Saudi government contract to clean Dammam, needed 2,700 people from Bangladesh and later divided that job among several people, and that a later job for 4,000 people was also shared among several businessmen who approached him.
SA3d-15.target_section: The root: a visa the sponsor owns
SA3d-15.why_new: Historical example (before 2010) of how a large Saudi demand was split among Bangladeshi recruiters; date not stated in the article.

SA3d-16.claim: Arifur Rahman said that while working as a doctor in Saudi Arabia he was taken by Saudi police and questioned as a suspect after a complaint that he, a doctor, was involved in recruiting workers, a breach of his iqama rules he did not know of; he was released after about three months as the allegation was not proved.
SA3d-16.target_section: What can get you jailed or deported
SA3d-16.why_new: A case of detention for work outside the iqama's profession; undated (before 2010).

SA3d-17.claim: A nursing teaching assistant at Bangladesh Medical University wrote in September 2025 that nurses can get work in Saudi Arabia and the Middle East by taking the 'Prometric' exam, and that demand for male nurses abroad is rising.
SA3d-17.why_new: The guide has nothing on nurses or the Prometric licensing exam; route, fee and agency rules are a gap.

SA3d-18.claim: According to the Expatriates' Welfare Ministry (October 2025), recruitment to Saudi Arabia began informally in 1976 with no formal agreement on general workers; two special agreements were signed before 2025, on domestic worker recruitment in 2015 and on skill verification in 2022.
SA3d-18.why_new: Guide cites the 2015 domestic agreement's wage (D0193) but not the 1976 start or the 2022 skill-verification agreement.

SA3d-19.claim: At the bilateral meeting before the 6 October 2025 signing in Riyadh, Asif Nazrul asked that employment contracts be correct, that employers carry out the duty of renewing the iqama, and that workers wanting to go home get an exit visa quickly; Saudi Minister of Human Resources Ahmed bin Sulaiman Al-Rajhi told officials to take effective steps on these.
SA3d-19.why_new: Shows the three problems Bangladesh raised (contracts, iqama renewal, exit visas); guide records only the signing.

SA3d-20.claim: Former BAIRA secretary general Ali Haider Chowdhury said in October 2025 that workers are usually sent under memoranda of understanding with no legal obligation, while the agreement gives workers sent to Saudi Arabia legal protection and lets the government go to court for a worker if needed.
SA3d-20.placement: other: legal effect of the agreement
SA3d-20.why_new: New claim about the agreement's legal effect; whether the government has gone to court for any worker under it is a Need to know.

SA3d-21.claim: In October 2025 Bangladesh's ambassador to Saudi Arabia was Md. Delwar Hossain, the deputy chief of mission S M Nazmul Hasan and the labour counsellor Muhammad Rezae Rabbi.
SA3d-21.why_new: Contacts list the labour counsellor's phone and email but not names.

SA3d-22.claim: Md. Habib Khan (21) of Nabakalas, Matlab Dakshin, Chandpur, borrowed Tk 5.5 lakh and went to Saudi Arabia in November 2023 on a 'free visa' through a Narayanganj broker named Md. Rashed; after working a while at a residential hotel in Mecca he left, then under a local broker got only occasional small jobs with little pay and spent most of his time idle, according to his family and local sources.
SA3d-22.why_new: A dated free-visa case showing the local-broker stage in Saudi Arabia; the guide's free-visa section has no such case.

SA3d-23.claim: Habib Khan died of a heart attack in a Mecca hospital in October 2025 with his Tk 5.5 lakh loan still unpaid; his father said worry over lack of work made him ill, and the family was waiting for the body.
SA3d-23.target_section: If a worker dies in Saudi Arabia
SA3d-23.why_new: Case linking a free visa, debt and a young worker's death; guide's death section has procedure, no case.
SA3d-23.h2: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job

SA3d-24.claim: Bangladesh Bank Governor Ahsan H. Mansur said on 7 October 2025 that expatriates in Saudi Arabia pay 6 to 10 percent to send remittances, comparatively much higher, a huge burden on them.
SA3d-24.why_new: Consistent with the guide's 7-9% app range [E0080]; adds the central bank's own estimate.

SA3d-25.claim: Policy Exchange chairman Masrur Reaz said on 7 October 2025 that about 21 lakh Bangladeshis work in Saudi Arabia, only 22 percent of them skilled.
SA3d-25.why_new: Guide gives yearly departures but no stock of Bangladeshis in Saudi Arabia or skill share; another column (891d19ee) says 25 lakh.

SA3d-26.claim: The Bangladesh Bank Governor said in October 2025 that Saudi Arabia is Bangladesh's biggest source of remittances and of foreign currency inflow.
SA3d-26.why_new: Remittance share not in guide; RMMRU (df8d2ef1) gives 15.52% in 2025.

SA3d-27.claim: A Prothom Alo opinion column (October 2025) stated there are about 25 lakh Bangladeshi expatriates in Saudi Arabia.
SA3d-27.why_new: Stock figure not in guide; conflicts with the 21 lakh given at the October 2025 business summit (97cc1097).

SA3d-28.claim: According to an October 2025 column, the Election Commission planned to pilot voting by Bangladeshis abroad in Saudi Arabia, Malaysia, the UAE and the UK, first at embassy booths, with voters registering online in advance and then voting on the set day after passport and NID checks.
SA3d-28.why_new: Guide has nothing on voting from Saudi Arabia; this was a plan, and how it was actually run is a Need to know.

SA3d-29.claim: Sarowar Hossain Rabbi (27) of Dakshin Panan, Hossainpur, Kishoreganj said in October 2025 that he had been unable to go to Saudi Arabia for three or four months for lack of Tk 1 lakh, that his visa and medical would both expire on 30 October, and that his visa had expired twice before.
SA3d-29.target_section: When to pay, when to fly, and Hajj-season pauses
SA3d-29.why_new: A case of a visa expiring repeatedly while the worker raises money; guide notes expired work visas are hard to renew but has no case, and doesn't say the medical expires too.

SA3d-30.claim: OKUP's survey of 1,084 households of workers who went to Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, the UAE and Saudi Arabia in 2022 (released 19 October 2025) found that 43% got no work, 57% got a work permit, 21% found no work and paid about Tk 1.5 lakh more for an iqama, 4% paid Tk 44,000 to get work, 4% came home at their own cost, and 14% could not pay for a permit or the trip home and stayed on undocumented.
SA3d-30.why_new: Five-country survey, not Saudi-only; guide has OKUP's complaint study (47% no permit) but not these outcome shares.

SA3d-31.claim: In OKUP's 2022 Gulf survey (released October 2025), 72% of free-visa workers took loans, 11% mortgaged land and 6% sold land, and those who came home without work could not recover mortgaged land.
SA3d-31.why_new: Adds land mortgage and sale shares; guide gives 81% borrowing (BBS) and lender types only.

SA3d-32.claim: Of the 51% (554) of workers in OKUP's 2022 Gulf survey who went knowingly on a free visa, 54% went through illegal broker networks, 7% directly through a recruiting agency, 8% through a family member and 31% through distant relatives.
SA3d-32.why_new: Answers in part the guide's Need to know on channel shares, though for five Gulf countries combined; cross-country has only the 51%.

SA3d-34.claim: The Bangladesh Consulate in Jeddah runs a toll-free hotline, 8002440051, which expatriates can call free for immediate help every day from 8 am to 9 pm Saudi time except weekly and other holidays (October 2025).
SA3d-34.why_new: The Jeddah consulate's toll-free hotline is missing from Contacts, which has only direct numbers for Jeddah.

SA3d-35.claim: Prothom Alo reported in October 2025 that workers seeking special exit, and domestic workers, call the Jeddah consulate's hotline from Jeddah and from outside Jeddah to get service through the Labour Welfare Wing.
SA3d-35.why_new: Guide says sponsors under Makkah, Madinah and other western labour offices aren't covered by SEP and to contact the Jeddah labour wing; this gives the hotline route used for special exit and by domestic workers.

SA3d-36.claim: The Jeddah hotline began in April 2019 as a pilot under a ministry-ILO agreement, is now funded by the Wage Earners' Welfare Board, and had received more than 2 lakh calls by October 2025; a Bisha worker said it took several tries to get through and operators could not check his e-passport status, telling him to check online himself.
SA3d-36.why_new: What the hotline can and can't do in practice; not in the guide.

SA3d-37.claim: More than 10 lakh Bangladeshis work in Jeddah and Saudi Arabia's western region, served by the Bangladesh Consulate in Jeddah (October 2025).
SA3d-37.why_new: Regional stock figure not in guide.

SA3d-38.claim: Nurul Alam (38) of Akbarpara, Adhunagar, Lohagara, Chattogram, who went to Saudi Arabia 18 years earlier, learned tailoring, worked about 10 years at a firm, then ran his own cloth business in Mahail, Abha (Asir province), delivering cloth to shops in his own microbus; a relative said he was killed on the spot on Thursday night in early December 2025 in a collision with a cargo lorry on his way home after deliveries.
SA3d-38.why_new: Another road death case; also a long-stayer running his own business (the article doesn't say under what status, relevant to tasattur).

SA3d-39.claim: In December 2025 family members said Nurul Alam's father was rushing to send the papers needed to bring the body home, and no one yet knew when it would arrive; the Adhunagar Union Parishad chairman said the Union Parishad and upazila administration were giving all necessary help.
SA3d-39.target_section: If a worker dies in Saudi Arabia
SA3d-39.why_new: Shows the family-side paper gathering and uncertainty over timing; guide has a Need to know on how long it takes.
SA3d-39.h2: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job

SA3d-40.claim: According to BMET data reported in December 2025, about 26% of the 11,98,900 workers who went abroad in FY2023-24 were skilled, against 18% of the 10,15,312 in FY2024-25, when 59% went as low-skilled and only 3% as professionals.
SA3d-40.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Is there a job for someone with no skills?
SA3d-40.why_new: Skill-mix figures not in the cross-country doc.

SA3d-41.claim: RMMRU's acting executive director Tasneem Siddiqui said in December 2025 that the skills of TTC-trained workers are not internationally recognised.
SA3d-41.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: How do I join a TTC course?
SA3d-41.why_new: Limits of TTC certificates not stated in cross-country doc.

SA3d-42.claim: The ILO country director and IOM chief of mission wrote in December 2025 of a worker, Shafiqul, who borrowed about USD 5,000 (over Tk 5 lakh), the price village brokers demanded, for an ordinary construction job in Saudi Arabia the year before, and on Tk 30,000-40,000 a month spent almost his whole first year repaying it.
SA3d-42.target_section: What reaches home, and how long the debt takes
SA3d-42.why_new: A case consistent with the guide's repayment estimate, from ILO/IOM heads.

SA3d-43.claim: The ILO and IOM heads in Bangladesh wrote in December 2025 that, according to the Labour Force Survey 2024, the average cost of migration is over USD 3,500 (Tk 4.62 lakh), about 10 months' earnings, and that Bangladeshi workers pay two to three times what Indian or Nepali workers pay for the same jobs in the GCC countries and Malaysia.
SA3d-43.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: How much does it really cost to go?
SA3d-43.why_new: National average and the India/Nepal comparison are not in the cross-country doc.

SA3d-44.claim: Monowara Begum, a waste picker in Rajshahi city, said in December 2025 that sending her elder son (26, SSC pass) to Saudi Arabia through a broker cost Tk 9 lakh, that he gets 'a lakh taka' in salary, and that he will come home in two years.
SA3d-44.target_section: The legal maximum and what people really pay
SA3d-44.why_new: Case at the top of the guide's Tk 9 lakh range; job and departure year not stated.

SA3d-45.claim: Abul Hashem (42) of Telibila, Chorombo, Lohagara, Chattogram, who went to Saudi Arabia in 2005 and owned two shops in Mecca, was forced to wind up the business and come home after a stomach cancer diagnosis in 2021, spent about Tk 68 lakh on treatment, and now farms two acres with technical advice, incentives and training from the upazila agriculture office (January 2026).
SA3d-45.why_new: Shows the upazila agriculture office as a source of reintegration help; guide lists PKB, BRAC and the Board only.

SA3d-46.claim: RMMRU's report released on 7 January 2026 said 1,130,757 workers went abroad in 2025, 67% of them (754,369) to Saudi Arabia, followed by Qatar 10%, Singapore 6%, Kuwait 4% and the Maldives 4%.
SA3d-46.why_new: Conflict: guide gives BMET's 755,194 to Saudi Arabia of 1,132,360 [SB0017]; RMMRU gives 754,369 of 1,130,757.

SA3d-47.claim: RMMRU said in January 2026 that of 2025's USD 32.82 billion in remittances, the highest in 25 years, Saudi Arabia sent the largest share among the top 10 countries, 15.52%, followed by the UAE at 12.58%.

SA3d-48.claim: RMMRU said in January 2026 that Bangladesh's licensed recruiting agencies, once limited to 850-900, were raised to 2,300 by the previous government, and 252 new licences were approved in 2025 with 300 more in process, against 192 agencies in India, 464 in Pakistan, 416 in Nepal and 248 in Sri Lanka.
SA3d-48.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: How do I check whether an agency is real?
SA3d-48.why_new: The Saudi guide gives 2,807 licensed agencies (later source); the growth and comparison are new.

SA3d-54.claim: Asif Nazrul said at the Global Labour Market Conference in Riyadh on 26 January 2026 that under the Skill Verification Programme agreement with Takamol, Bangladesh now gives skill certificates in various occupations to 60,000 workers a month in line with Saudi demand.
SA3d-54.why_new: Monthly certification volume not in guide.

SA3d-49.claim: Asma Begum, a woman returnee from Saudi Arabia, said at a December 2025 roundtable that she paid Tk 45,000 through a broker to go, was subjected to much abuse while working there, was ill for six months after coming home with high treatment costs, and has not fully repaid the loan she took to go.
SA3d-49.target_section: Women domestic workers: the money should run the other way
SA3d-49.why_new: A named returnee case of a woman paying when she should pay nothing; job type not stated (likely domestic, not confirmed).

SA3d-50.claim: BRAC associate director Shariful Hasan said in December 2025 that brokers and even relatives often effectively sell women domestic workers under the name of sending them free, and that when they are abused abroad, intervention by the embassy or authorities is limited, with no trial and no accountability.
SA3d-50.placement: other: domestic workers, what help reaches them
SA3d-50.why_new: Evidence on what help actually reaches abused domestic workers (Work visa: domestic worker, If something goes wrong).

SA3d-51.claim: Syed Saiful Haque, chairperson of WARBE and a returnee who spent about 10 years in Saudi Arabia, said in December 2025 that the government has twice banned women from going abroad and twice lifted the ban.
SA3d-51.target_section: Is it open now, and who can go?
SA3d-51.why_new: Past bans on women going abroad (not Saudi-specific) are not in the guide; dates not given.

SA3d-52.claim: Hasan Imam of the Center for Development Communication said in December 2025 that the government's reintegration policy, begun in 2022, received final approval in 2025, with six objectives: employment and financial self-reliance, entrepreneurship, social reintegration and health care, psychosocial support, support for exploited and abused women, and sustainability.
SA3d-52.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: What help is there when I come back?
SA3d-52.why_new: Cross-country mentions a reintegration policy without its approval date or objectives.

SA3d-53.claim: BRAC's Shariful Hasan said in December 2025 that there is no clear gender-sensitive SOP at the airport for a dignified return, and that immigration or police often do not treat women returning with abuse and trauma humanely.
SA3d-53.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Who helps me at the airport?
SA3d-53.why_new: What women returnees meet at the airport in practice; not in cross-country doc.

MY3f-1.claim: On 24 March 2026 the state minister for expatriates' welfare, Md Nurul Haque Nur, said government-level talks were under way to open the Malaysian and Vietnamese labour markets quickly and that he hoped for a positive response soon.
MY3f-1.target_section: Is it open now, and who can go?
MY3f-1.why_new: Adds a dated March 2026 point to the Status timeline, which jumps from 31 May 2024 to June 2026.

MY3f-2.claim: On 24 March 2026 the state minister for expatriates' welfare, Md Nurul Haque Nur, said the Prime Minister had directed that students going abroad for higher study (to South Korea, Japan, China, Germany and other countries) get loans of up to Tk 10 lakh through Probashi Kallyan Bank as proof of bank solvency, paid not in cash but against tuition fees or other required payments.
MY3f-2.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Can I get a government loan to go abroad?
MY3f-2.why_new: The cross-country doc has no PKB loan for students' solvency proof.

MY3f-3.claim: On 24 March 2026 the state minister for expatriates' welfare said the government was working, as part of its 180-day action plan, to fix migration costs, and that once final this would stop extra money being taken.
MY3f-3.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: How much does it really cost to go?
MY3f-3.why_new: A dated government commitment to fix costs; check whether any fixed cost was later issued.

MY3f-4.claim: Prothom Alo, reviewing the case documents, reported on 25 March 2026 that Altab Khan, owner of a firm named Afia Overseas, filed the human-trafficking case over Malaysia recruitment at Paltan police station, Dhaka, naming 103 accused, on 3 September 2024, after the fall of the Awami League government.
MY3f-4.target_section: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut
MY3f-4.placement: The cases against the syndicate (conflict: date of Paltan case)
MY3f-4.why_new: CONFLICT: the guide (The cases against the syndicate, '3 September 2025' entry and the March 2026 entry) dates the Paltan case to 3 September 2025; this article says 3 September 2024, which fits the CID final report of 15 July 2025.

MY3f-5.claim: The accused in the Paltan Malaysia-trafficking case include former expatriates' welfare minister Imran Ahmed, former senior secretary of the expatriates' welfare ministry Ahmed Munirus Salehin, former Feni MP Nizam Hazari and former Dhaka-20 MP Benzir Ahmed, with Lt Gen (retd) Masud Uddin Chowdhury as accused no. 3, according to the case documents reported by Prothom Alo in March 2026.
MY3f-5.target_section: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut
MY3f-5.why_new: The guide names neither the former minister nor the former senior secretary among the accused.

MY3f-6.claim: The Paltan case was first investigated by Paltan police and then the CID, which on 15 July 2025 filed a final report calling the case false and recommending action against the complainant; the complainant filed a no-confidence petition, and the court ordered the DB (Detective Branch) to reinvestigate, Prothom Alo reported in March 2026.
MY3f-6.target_section: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut
MY3f-6.why_new: New: the CID first closed the case as false; the guide has only the March 2026 arrest and remand.

MY3f-7.claim: The CID's supervising officer, Additional Special SP Mostafizur Rahman, said that when the CID took the case 76 of the 103 accused were on bail and the rest absconding, so they could not be questioned, that the complainant could not produce enough evidence, and that a Penal Code extortion section in the case also got a final report, which the court accepted; the complainant, Altab Khan, said the CID had compromised with the accused and never told him the result.
MY3f-7.target_section: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut
MY3f-7.why_new: Shows why trafficking cases over Malaysia stall; not in the guide.

MY3f-8.claim: In December 2025, after the DB began reinvestigating, accused no. 12 in the Paltan case, S M Rafiq, gave a confessional statement in court, which a DB officer said contains information that human trafficking and embezzlement of a huge sum took place in the name of sending workers to Malaysia.
MY3f-8.target_section: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut
MY3f-8.why_new: The confession is not in the guide.

MY3f-9.claim: DMP Detective Branch Joint Commissioner Mohammad Nasirul Islam said in March 2026 that a ring was built around sending workers to Malaysia under the previous government, that Masud Uddin Chowdhury was a powerful member of it, and that he was being questioned about the ring and the source of his power.
MY3f-9.target_section: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut
MY3f-9.why_new: Guide quotes a DB additional commissioner and an unnamed joint commissioner; this names the joint commissioner and his allegation.

MY3f-10.claim: BMET data cited in a Prothom Alo editorial of 28 March 2026 show that the number of workers taking clearance to go abroad in the first 10 days of March 2026 fell by about 50 percent from the same period a year earlier, after the Middle East war closed airspace and several hundred flights from Dhaka's Shahjalal airport were cancelled.
MY3f-10.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Which countries can I go to for work right now?
MY3f-10.why_new: Adds the March 2026 war-related drop; the cross-country doc gives Jan-Aug totals only.

MY3f-11.claim: According to a Prothom Alo editorial of 28 March 2026, 67 percent of the workers who went abroad in 2025 went to Saudi Arabia and about 90 percent to just five countries, although 168 countries are on the list of destinations.
MY3f-11.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Which countries can I go to for work right now?
MY3f-11.why_new: Concentration figures for 2025 not in the cross-country doc.

MY3f-12.claim: On the afternoon of 30 March 2026 the Coast Guard raided a house in Dakshin Lombori, Teknaf, which it called a traffickers' den, and rescued seven people including women and children who had been brought there, with promises of a better life, high-paid jobs and a cheap passage, to be taken to Malaysia by sea; the traffickers fled and the seven were handed to Teknaf Model Police Station.
MY3f-12.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
MY3f-12.why_new: A 2026 case not in the Cases list (which has a December 2024 Dakshin Lambari Para case).

MY3f-13.claim: A Prothom Alo column of 3 April 2026 by Mohammad Jalal Uddin Sikder of North South University cites a 21 May 2020 statement of the UN human rights office (OHCHR), 'Malaysia: Stop crackdown on migrants, journalists and civil society', saying that during COVID-19 migrant workers in Malaysia were blamed for spreading the virus, detained, and many sent back.
MY3f-13.target_section: What goes wrong most, and what people wrongly believe
MY3f-13.why_new: The guide has no COVID-period crackdown; low priority, may not change what a worker does.

MY3f-14.claim: By BMET data cited in a Prothom Alo column of 3 April 2026, 11,16,399 Bangladeshis migrated in 2025, about 82.4 percent of them (9,19,981) to the Middle East or GCC countries, and of USD 32.8 billion in remittances in 2025 about 46 percent (USD 15.07 billion) came from GCC countries (Bangladesh Bank, 2026).
MY3f-14.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Which countries can I go to for work right now?
MY3f-14.why_new: CONFLICT: the minister told parliament on 5 April 2026 that 11,32,519 went in 2025 (draft from article 2847a95a).

MY3f-15.claim: On 5 April 2026 the expatriates' welfare minister, Ariful Haque Chowdhury, told parliament that the government was not interested in sending workers to Malaysia through a syndicate of a limited number of recruiting agencies as before, that it was trying to keep the market open to all eligible licensed agencies, and that it was corresponding with the Malaysian authorities through the Bangladesh High Commission.
MY3f-15.target_section: Is it open now, and who can go?
MY3f-15.why_new: The guide has the minister's 5 November 2026 wish that every licensed agency be allowed in; this shows the same position stated in April, before Malaysia chose 25.

MY3f-16.claim: The expatriates' welfare minister told parliament on 5 April 2026 that 11,32,519 workers went abroad for jobs in 2025, 62,352 of them women, and that more than 1.5 crore Bangladeshi workers were then working in 176 countries.
MY3f-16.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Which countries can I go to for work right now?
MY3f-16.why_new: Official 2025 totals; CONFLICT with 11,16,399 cited from BMET in a 3 April 2026 column (article fa1e9f68).

MY3f-17.claim: On 9 April 2026 Bangladesh and Malaysia held a bilateral labour-migration meeting in Putrajaya, led by Malaysia's Human Resources Minister Ramanan Ramakrishnan and Bangladesh's expatriates' welfare minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury, and agreed to speed up reopening the market to Bangladeshi workers based on Malaysia's sector-wise demand, with a fair, ethical and transparent recruitment process, the Prime Minister's adviser Mahdi Amin said.
MY3f-17.target_section: Is it open now, and who can go?
MY3f-17.why_new: The Status timeline has no April 2026 entry; the guide cites only 'April 2026 both governments said employers will bear the full cost' [A0097].

MY3f-18.claim: The two governments' joint press statement of 9 April 2026 said steps would be taken to cut migration cost by reducing intermediaries, to use credible recruiting agencies, and to complete quickly the recruitment of workers who are stuck.
MY3f-18.target_section: Is it open now, and who can go?
MY3f-18.why_new: Commitment to the stuck workers and to fewer intermediaries is not in the guide.

MY3f-19.claim: The joint statement of 9 April 2026 said Malaysia had begun introducing an AI-based, technology-driven recruitment system for all source countries, meant to cut middlemen and migration cost and bring the cost to workers to zero in line with the ILO 'employer pays' principle, and Bangladesh said it fully supported such a digital platform as a global initiative involving all sending countries.
MY3f-19.target_section: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut
MY3f-19.why_new: The guide mentions TURAP (Step 1) but not that Bangladesh endorsed Malaysia's new system in April; relevant to who will control recruitment.

MY3f-20.claim: At the 9 April 2026 Putrajaya meeting the two sides discussed concerns about the ongoing human-trafficking cases, and Bangladesh reaffirmed its commitment to rule of law, due process, accountability and timely justice, the joint statement said.
MY3f-20.target_section: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut
MY3f-20.why_new: Links the trafficking cases to the reopening talks; the guide has Malaysia's 2025 call to withdraw allegations but nothing from 2026.

MY3f-21.claim: On 12 April 2026 the Prime Minister's adviser Mahdi Amin said reopening the Malaysian market was a procedural matter being worked on as fast as possible, gave no date, and said Bangladesh had asked Malaysia to do whatever was needed to make the process syndicate-free.
MY3f-21.target_section: Is it open now, and who can go?
MY3f-21.why_new: Dated April 2026 status point; Bangladesh's ask to Malaysia on the syndicate is not in the guide.

MY3f-22.claim: Speaking in Sylhet on 12 April 2026 about his Malaysia visit, the expatriates' welfare minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury said 'we have signed a joint venture, it is in our favour' and called the meeting very fruitful, without saying what was signed.
MY3f-22.target_section: Is it open now, and who can go?
MY3f-22.why_new: The minister claims something was signed in April; the joint statement (article dc450226) mentions no signed agreement. A reviewer may want a Need to know on what, if anything, was signed.

MY3f-23.claim: Prime Minister Tarique Rahman told parliament on 15 April 2026 that the government was working to open the Malaysian labour market and that the minister and adviser in charge of the expatriates' welfare ministry had visited Malaysia on 8 to 11 April.
MY3f-23.target_section: Is it open now, and who can go?
MY3f-23.why_new: Gives the dates of the April ministerial visit.

MY3f-24.claim: Prime Minister Tarique Rahman told parliament on 15 April 2026 that steps had been taken to sign bilateral agreements to expand labour markets in Serbia, Greece, North Macedonia, Romania, Portugal, Brazil and Russia, and a recruitment agreement to open Thailand's labour market.
MY3f-24.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Which countries can I go to for work right now?
MY3f-24.why_new: Planned agreements (not open routes); the cross-country list has none of these.

MY3f-25.claim: According to UNHCR, reported by Prothom Alo on 17 April 2026, about 900 Rohingya refugees went missing or died in the Andaman Sea and Bay of Bengal in 2025, the deadliest year on record for sea journeys in South and South-East Asia, with one in seven of the more than 6,500 who attempted the crossing dying or going missing.
MY3f-25.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
MY3f-25.why_new: 2025 UNHCR figures; the section has 2023 figures only.

MY3f-26.claim: UNHCR said that more than half of the Rohingya crossing by sea in recent years were women and children, that more than 2,800 had taken the journey in 2026 up to 13 April, and that the boats usually leave Cox's Bazar in Bangladesh or Rakhine State in Myanmar for Indonesia or Malaysia.
MY3f-26.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
MY3f-26.why_new: 2026 year-to-date figure not in the cross-country doc.

MY3f-27.claim: UNHCR said an overloaded boat that left Bangladesh on 26 March 2026 sank in rough sea with about 250 people missing, and only nine were rescued alive near the Andaman Islands on 9 April.
MY3f-27.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
MY3f-27.why_new: Same sinking as article 646aca07, which says it sank on 8 April and that the missing Pekua men left on 4 April; the 26 March departure date differs.

MY3f-28.claim: On 18 April 2026 the Prime Minister's adviser Mahdi Amin said a collateral-free bank guarantee of up to Tk 10 lakh had been arranged for higher study abroad, and that a 'Probashi Card' for expatriates was being introduced.
MY3f-28.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Can I get a government loan to go abroad?
MY3f-28.why_new: Pairs with the 24 March student-loan statement; the Probashi Card is not described in the cross-country doc (it has 'Probashi card' only in other contexts; check).

MY3f-29.claim: A Malaysia-bound trawler that left the Teknaf coast of Cox's Bazar, carrying at least 250 Bangladeshi and Rohingya men and women, sank in the Andaman Sea on the morning of 8 April 2026 in strong wind, rough sea and overloading; nine were rescued and the Coast Guard said no trace of the missing or the wreck had been found.
MY3f-29.target_section: What goes wrong most, and what people wrongly believe
MY3f-29.placement: Irregular routes, and where an irregular stay ends (new bullet: by sea)
MY3f-29.why_new: The country guide's Irregular routes list has land and airport routes but no sea route; a one-line pointer to the cross-country section may belong there.

MY3f-30.claim: The nine survivors of the 8 April 2026 sinking, picked up from water drums and pieces of wood near the Andaman Islands on 9 April by the Bangladesh-flagged merchant ship Meghna Pride and handed to the Coast Guard, were taken to Teknaf police: the three Rohingya were sent back to the camps after giving statements in court, and the six Bangladeshis were charged under the trafficking prevention law and sent to jail, with 10 to 15 unnamed accused added, police inspector Sukanta Chowdhury said.
MY3f-30.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
MY3f-30.why_new: New and decision-relevant: Bangladeshi survivors themselves were charged under the trafficking law and jailed.

MY3f-31.claim: Brokers target unemployed, needy young men of poor families and offer to take them to Malaysia by boat for free, saying they can pay after reaching Malaysia and promising very high wages, Parvez Siddiqui, executive director of the NGO Films for Peace Foundation, said in April 2026; the wife of one missing man, Belal Uddin, said he went because brokers told him he could go without money.
MY3f-31.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
MY3f-31.why_new: The 'go free, pay on arrival' lure is not in the How it is sold paragraph, which gives up-front prices.

MY3f-32.claim: Seven young men from Hajipara, Miapara and Natun Ghona villages of Rajakhali union, Pekua, Cox's Bazar, left the Teknaf coast on 4 April 2026 on one of three trawlers that left for Malaysia at about the same time, phoned home until 8 April and have not been heard from since; the Teknaf brokers stopped answering their phones, and one missing man's uncle said Teknaf police only took photos and addresses and sent the family away.
MY3f-32.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
MY3f-32.why_new: A 2026 case with what families met at the police; not in the cross-country Cases.

MY3f-33.claim: In the case of Amir Hossain of Naria, Shariatpur, found mentally unwell in a forest in Penang after 27 years out of contact, the Bangladesh mission in Malaysia sent his photo and the information he gave to the Naria UNO, who verified it with the family; Chamta Union Parishad, with the upazila administration's help, issued him a birth registration; that and family members' documents were sent to the mission, which issued a travel pass, and he reached Dhaka in the night after 21 April 2026, about six months after he was found.
MY3f-33.placement: Step 1: Get a passport or Travel Permit (case answering the UNO Need to know)
MY3f-33.why_new: Shows in practice how identity is proved when a worker has no passport or NID (mission to UNO to union parishad birth registration to travel pass), which the guide lists as Need to know (how a worker gets the UNO certificate, how long it takes).

MY3f-34.claim: Amir Hossain was received at Dhaka airport on the night of 21-22 April 2026 by BRAC's Migration Programme and his family, with the help of Civil Aviation Security (AVSEC) and the Probashi Kallyan desk.
MY3f-34.why_new: An example of BRAC's airport reception that the guide lists without a case.

MY3f-35.claim: Amir Hossain, who went to Malaysia through a broker in 1996 after selling inherited farmland and worked as a painter, was traced after two Bangladeshis in Malaysia, an expatriate named Dipu and expatriate journalist Bappi Kumar Das, found him in a tin hut in a Penang forest, rescued him and posted video on social media, from which his wife recognised him.
MY3f-35.why_new: Shows how a missing worker was found (through other expatriates, not an official channel); low priority.

MY3f-36.claim: At a community event in Putrajaya on 1 June 2026, Md Siddiqur Rahman, Minister (Labour) at the Bangladesh High Commission in Kuala Lumpur, said any Bangladeshi in trouble anywhere in Malaysia should tell the High Commission by writing on its Facebook page, by email or by phone, and it would try to solve the problem.
MY3f-36.placement: Where to complain, in Malaysia and from Bangladesh
MY3f-36.why_new: The guide gives his email and phone but not the Facebook page as a channel the labour wing says it takes; no page address is printed, so a reviewer may need to add it.

MY3f-37.claim: On the evening of 5 June 2026 the Coast Guard chased and seized a fishing trawler off Baharchhara on the Teknaf coast that was taking people to Malaysia by sea, rescued 50 people including women and children (39 Bangladeshis and 11 Rohingya) and arrested nine traffickers, who were handed to Teknaf Model Police Station with a case filed, station in-charge Lt Cdr Md Muttakin Siddiqui said.
MY3f-37.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
MY3f-37.why_new: A June 2026 case with a majority of Bangladeshi passengers; not in Cases.

MY3f-38.claim: Organised rings bring Bangladeshis and Rohingya to the Teknaf coast with promises of high-paid jobs abroad and a better life, then lock them in secret hideouts and extract ransom through torture, the Coast Guard's Teknaf station in-charge said on 6 June 2026.
MY3f-38.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
MY3f-38.why_new: Confirms the ransom-before-departure pattern in 2026 (the section's examples are 2024-25).

MY3f-39.claim: In June 2026 all workers at Aerofoam Manufacturing (1969) Sdn Bhd, a Malaysian maker of bedding products employing Bangladeshis, had gone three months without wages, according to documents of the Migrant Welfare Network (MWN), a rights platform for Bangladeshi migrants; they could not meet daily costs or send money home, and many who had borrowed at high interest to migrate could not pay their instalments.
MY3f-39.why_new: The guide mentions 'nearly three [months] at Aerofoam' [F0038] only; MWN as a source of help is not in the guide.

MY3f-40.claim: About 35 Aerofoam workers who entered Malaysia legally had no valid work permit (PLKS) in June 2026 because the company did not renew it on time, leaving them in fear of arrest or fines; their written complaint to the Labour Department (Jabatan Tenaga Kerja, JTK) asked that the 35 workers' visas and permits be regularised quickly.
MY3f-40.placement: How long you can stay and renewing (case for the Need to know on unrenewed passes)
MY3f-40.why_new: Partly answers the guide's Need to know 'Does the Labour Department take a complaint about a pass that isn't renewed?': workers did file one with JTK; the outcome is not reported.

MY3f-41.claim: The Aerofoam workers alleged in June 2026 that the company held most of their passports, forced them to work overtime against their will without enough rest, gave no transport to the workplace and had no working grievance mechanism; their complaint to JTK demanded payment of arrears, return of passports, an end to forced overtime, a safe workplace, an investigation of high recruitment fees and no retaliation against them.
MY3f-41.placement: If you are abused, denied food or medical care, or your passport is taken (case)
MY3f-41.why_new: Shows what a collective JTK complaint asked for; outcome not reported.

MY3f-42.claim: Lal Mia, 54, of Chhoto Amian village, Shalikha, Magura, said he paid a broker Tk 2.5 lakh in 2006 and Tk 3 lakh in 2010 to go to Malaysia, never went and never got the money back; across four attempts from 2002 to 2012 (also Saudi Arabia and Dubai) he paid about Tk 10.5 lakh, selling four bighas of farmland and his 12.5-decimal homestead, and in June 2026 lived in a house on someone else's land, selling eggs by bicycle.
MY3f-42.placement: Step 1: Find a real job > If an agency or broker takes your money (case)
MY3f-42.why_new: An older case (2006, 2010) of repeated loss to brokers; the guide's cases are 2022-26. Low priority.

MY3f-43.claim: In parliament on 10 June 2026 the home minister, Salahuddin Ahmed, said the Prime Minister's first visit abroad had been fixed for Malaysia, to open its labour market, and the state minister for expatriates' welfare, Nurul Haque, said the market opens and closes again, was closed then, that MPs wanted no syndicate there, and that the Prime Minister had given strict instructions that the government must not be given a bad name.
MY3f-43.target_section: Is it open now, and who can go?
MY3f-43.why_new: Dated June 2026 status point before the PM's visit.

MY3f-44.claim: The opposition leader, Shafiqur Rahman, told parliament on 10 June 2026 that many expatriates could not get e-passports because their MRP (machine-readable passport) and national ID data did not match, through small spelling differences in vowel signs or names or a mismatch in age, and that many abroad were becoming or risked becoming undocumented as a result.
MY3f-44.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: How do I get a passport, and what does it cost?
MY3f-44.why_new: The cross-country passport answer says to apply exactly as the NID reads but not what happens to workers abroad whose old MRP differs.

MY3f-45.claim: Dr Selim Reza of North South University's Centre for Migration Studies wrote in Prothom Alo on 16 June 2026 that sending workers to Malaysia began in 1978 with a few workers, and that the market closed in 2008, reopened in 2016, closed in 2018, reopened in a new form in 2022 and was suspended again in 2024.
MY3f-45.target_section: Is it open now, and who can go?
MY3f-45.why_new: CONFLICT: the guide (What closed it before) dates the first closure to 2009 (freeze after 2007-08 surge); this column says 2008. The 1978 start is new.

MY3f-46.claim: Selim Reza wrote in June 2026 that most consular services require Bangladeshis to travel to Kuala Lumpur, and that coming from Sabah, Sarawak, Penang or Johor to Kuala Lumpur to renew a passport or get other services is time-consuming and costly.
MY3f-46.placement: other: consular services outside Kuala Lumpur
MY3f-46.why_new: The guide does not say whether the High Commission offers any service outside Kuala Lumpur; suggests a Need to know (are there consular camps in Sabah, Sarawak, Penang or Johor?).

MY3f-47.claim: Selim Reza wrote in June 2026 that most undocumented Bangladeshis in Malaysia are not involved in crime but lost legal status through employer fraud, company closure, visa-renewal complications or administrative weakness.
MY3f-47.target_section: What ties you to the employer
MY3f-47.placement: What running away or an expired pass does to you
MY3f-47.why_new: A columnist's view, consistent with the IOM study the guide cites; adds company closure and renewal complications as causes. Low priority.

MY3f-48.claim: Prothom Alo, drawing on Malaysia's The Edge, reported on 16 June 2026 that Prime Minister Tarique Rahman's first foreign visit was to be two days in Kuala Lumpur on 21 and 22 June 2026, with a bilateral meeting with Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim on the second day; the High Commission opened formal talks on the visit with Malaysia's foreign ministry on 24 May and Anwar confirmed the invitation on 1 June, and reopening the labour market was a key priority.
MY3f-48.target_section: Is it open now, and who can go?
MY3f-48.why_new: The guide's 'June 2026' entry has no dates for the visit.

MY3f-49.claim: According to The Edge, as reported by Prothom Alo on 16 June 2026, 102 Bangladeshi firms were then approved under FWCMS, built by Bestinet, and Bangladesh was considering including 432 recruiting agencies instead; a manpower-sector executive told The Edge that Bangladesh wanted Malaysia to open recruitment to more Bangladeshi companies rather than a few chosen by some influential people.
MY3f-49.target_section: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut
MY3f-49.placement: The processing agency: the toll gate (conflict on number of approved firms)
MY3f-49.why_new: CONFLICT: the guide says the 2022 list grew to 100 and in 2026 Malaysia chose 25 (from a final Bangladeshi list of 423); this June 2026 report says 102 approved firms and 432 under consideration.
