MY3f-50.claim: Malaysia's Human Resources Minister Ramanan Ramakrishnan proposed a new system called 'Turap' to stop the exploitation of Bangladeshi workers at village level; Turap is also built by Bestinet, and some stakeholders in Bangladesh and Malaysia suspect it is another way to keep recruitment concentrated in a few firms, Prothom Alo reported from The Edge on 16 June 2026.
MY3f-50.why_new: The guide says only that TURAP was approved by Malaysia's Cabinet in April 2026 and has not launched; that Bestinet built it and the concentration concern are new.

MY3f-51.claim: Bangladesh sought the extradition of Bestinet's founder Aminul Islam Abdul Nor and his associate Ruhul Amin in 2024, after the fall of the Sheikh Hasina government, and in June 2026 the matter was still under discussion between the two governments, according to The Edge as reported by Prothom Alo.
MY3f-51.target_section: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut
MY3f-51.why_new: Updates the extradition request's status to June 2026.

MY3f-52.claim: According to The Edge as reported by Prothom Alo in June 2026, the problem peaked in 2023, when many workers spent up to USD 6,600 each (about Tk 8 lakh, as printed) to reach Malaysia and then found that the jobs promised did not exist.
MY3f-52.target_section: What you pay, and what you earn and keep
MY3f-52.why_new: CONFLICT: the guide gives up to USD 5,000 (What closed it before) and a 2022-24 average of Tk 5.44 lakh; this gives an upper figure of USD 6,600.

MY3f-53.claim: When Malaysia stopped workers entering in early 2024, about 18,000 workers who had already paid agents in Bangladesh could not enter, and many of those agents went into hiding in the crackdown under Bangladesh's new government, The Edge reported (Prothom Alo, 16 June 2026).
MY3f-53.target_section: Is it open now, and who can go?
MY3f-53.why_new: Another stranded-worker count (about 18,000) to add to the guide's Need to know list of counts (16,970, 17,777, 31,304, about 40,000, about 11,000).

MY3f-54.claim: Malaysia officially follows an 'employer pays' policy for recruitment costs, but under the current system it is still hard to implement, and the money changing hands in the Bangladeshi recruitment market runs to several hundred crore ringgit while the real cost of recruitment is far lower, The Edge reported (Prothom Alo, 16 June 2026).
MY3f-54.target_section: What you pay, and what you earn and keep
MY3f-54.why_new: Supports the guide's opening line on the gap between the employer-pays rule and what is paid; low priority.

MY3f-55.claim: More than 10,000 Bangladeshi students were studying at Malaysian universities in June 2026, Prothom Alo reported.
MY3f-55.why_new: The student section gives no number of Bangladeshi students.

MY3g-1.claim: In June 2026 the civil aviation minister, Afroza Khanom, told parliament that Biman Bangladesh Airlines had introduced a low-fare 'T-class' ticket for migrant workers, bringing the Dhaka-Kuala Lumpur fare down from Tk 28,000 to Tk 21,000.
MY3g-1.target_section: Going home on leave and coming back
MY3g-1.why_new: The guide gives no fare for Dhaka-Kuala Lumpur and has a Need to know on the usual fare (Going home without valid papers, Step 2: Buy a ticket home). The article gives the Dhaka-KL route only and does not say one-way or return, or whether it applies from KL.

MY3g-2.claim: On 21 June 2026 a Dhaka special judge, Md Sabbir Foyez, granted four days' remand of Masud Uddin Chowdhury (seven were sought) in the ACC case alleging that he and others, abusing government power, got themselves appointed as agents for sending workers to Malaysia and illegally collected Tk 119 crore 32 lakh 70 thousand from workers against the government-fixed fee of Tk 78,990, and laundered it.
MY3g-2.why_new: The guide's March 2026 bullet ends with the ACC applying to show him arrested in its Tk 119 crore case, order due 9 April 2026; this adds that he was remanded in that ACC case on 21 June 2026.

MY3g-3.claim: Prothom Alo reported on 21 June 2026 that Masud Uddin Chowdhury, arrested in Baridhara, Dhaka, on 23 March 2026, had been remanded several times in various cases and has been in jail since.
MY3g-3.why_new: Gives the arrest date (23 March) and that he remains in jail; the guide says he was arrested 'at midnight on a Monday' per a 24 March report.

MY3g-4.claim: Before the June 2026 visit, Bangladesh's High Commissioner to Malaysia, Manjurul Karim Khan Chowdhury, told Prothom Alo that Malaysia's new industrial policy is changing its traditional pattern of hiring, that the market for the kind of workers Bangladesh sends is shrinking, and that Bangladesh had therefore started contacts on recruitment of skilled and semi-skilled workers.
MY3g-4.why_new: New: the High Commissioner's view that demand for the low-skilled workers Bangladesh sends is shrinking. The article ties this to Malaysia's New Industrial Master Plan (NIMP) 2030, aimed at advanced-technology production.

MY3g-5.claim: Several Bangladeshis who do or did specialised work in Malaysia told Prothom Alo in June 2026 that about 10 lakh Bangladeshi workers, legal and illegal combined, were working in Malaysia.
MY3g-5.why_new: The guide gives about 8 lakh work-pass holders at end-2025 [U0057]; this is an informal estimate that includes undocumented workers.

MY3g-6.claim: Prothom Alo wrote in June 2026 that for a decade Malaysia has been regarded as the second main destination for new recruitment of Bangladeshi workers, after Saudi Arabia.
MY3g-6.why_new: Size section has no comparison with other destinations.

MY3g-7.claim: Bangladeshi diplomats told Prothom Alo in June 2026 that at least 11,000 Bangladeshi students were studying in Malaysia, the second-largest group of foreign students after the Chinese (about 62,000).
MY3g-7.why_new: The guide's Student visa section gives no count of Bangladeshi students.

MY3g-8.claim: At the prime ministers' talks in Putrajaya on 22 June 2026, reopening the labour market for Bangladeshi workers, regularising Bangladeshis who had become irregular and renewing work permits were among the issues discussed; the only documents signed or exchanged were a culture MoU and documents on counter-terrorism research and on investment.
MY3g-8.why_new: The guide's June 2026 bullet does not give the date or say that no labour agreement was signed.

MY3g-9.claim: At a joint press conference in Putrajaya on 22 June 2026, Prime Minister Tarique Rahman said he had asked Anwar Ibrahim to consider hiring more Bangladeshi workers and opening the labour market quickly, had raised legalising irregular workers and the possible repatriation of detained Bangladeshis, and that the two agreed recruitment must be transparent, fair and affordable so that the role of middlemen shrinks and workers' costs fall.
MY3g-9.why_new: Shows the visit produced a request and a principle, not a reopening; the guide's June bullet relies only on a 22 July editorial saying the market was reopening.

MY3g-10.claim: At the 22 June 2026 talks, according to the Prime Minister's spokesperson Mahdi Amin, the two sides discussed humanely giving legal status to Bangladeshis in irregular status or in prison in Malaysia, or returning them safely home; no programme was announced.
MY3g-10.target_section: What running away or an expired pass does to you
MY3g-10.placement: other: 'Buying your way back to legal' bullet
MY3g-10.why_new: The guide says no legalisation programme is open (last RTK ended 31 Dec 2023); this records that regularisation was raised at prime-minister level in June 2026, discussion only.

MY3g-11.claim: Mahdi Amin said on 22 June 2026 that Tarique Rahman had asked Malaysia for employment for more Bangladeshi workers at low cost through a transparent process, and that a 33-point joint statement on nine areas of cooperation was issued after the 18-hour visit.
MY3g-11.why_new: Adds the joint statement's existence and scope to the June 2026 Status line.

MY3g-12.claim: At their 22 June 2026 meeting, Anwar Ibrahim and Tarique Rahman agreed to form a joint working group (JWG) that will review the existing labour MoU and serve as the basis for drafting a new MoU in line with both countries' current needs.
MY3g-12.why_new: The guide mentions a new MoU to be signed 31 December 2026 (minister, 5 November) but not its origin in the June 2026 JWG decision.

MY3g-13.claim: Malaysia's Human Resources Minister, R Ramanan, said in a Facebook statement on 22 June 2026 that his ministry would keep strengthening governance so that recruitment of Bangladeshi workers is transparent, fair and ethical and free of exploitation, discrimination and unethical practices.
MY3g-13.why_new: Malaysia's own ministerial position after the visit; not in the guide.

MY3g-14.claim: The joint statement after the 22 June 2026 meeting says a JWG meeting would be called to ensure continued, safe and mutually beneficial migration of Bangladeshi workers to Malaysia, so that a new MoU on worker recruitment can be drafted from that meeting's discussion.
MY3g-14.why_new: The joint statement's own wording on the new MoU; the guide does not have it.

MY3g-15.claim: Malaysia's Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim, referring on 22 June 2026 to allegations of exploitation and abuse of Bangladeshi workers in Malaysia, said exploiting workers, treating them badly and using them only for self-interest could not be accepted, and that both countries must lead in making recruitment transparent.
MY3g-15.target_section: What goes wrong most, and what people wrongly believe
MY3g-15.why_new: A Malaysian head of government publicly acknowledging the exploitation allegations; not in the guide.

MY3g-16.claim: On 23 June 2026 the expatriates' welfare minister, Ariful Haque Chowdhury, told parliament that the government was working to open Malaysia's labour market and hoped the way to send workers would be cleared very soon, and that it was making efforts to legalise Bangladeshi workers staying in Malaysia irregularly or in difficulty.
MY3g-16.why_new: Confirms the market was still not open on 23 June 2026.

MY3g-17.claim: The minister told parliament on 23 June 2026 that no workers are sent to Malaysia, the second-largest labour market for Bangladeshi workers, by the government itself, and that workers can go there through government-approved recruiting agencies.
MY3g-17.why_new: Conflict: the guide lists BOESL (government-owned) as a channel that sent workers in 2022-24 and stranded workers from November 2025, and the same minister later said zero-cost workers would go through BOESL (Status).

MY3g-18.claim: On 24 June 2026 the minister, Ariful Haque Chowdhury, said at Osmani International Airport, Sylhet, that good news on the Malaysian labour market could come within July and that Malaysia's human resources minister and home minister would visit Bangladesh within July.
MY3g-18.why_new: Part of the timeline of promised dates; the guide has none between June and August 2026.

MY3g-19.claim: Dr Selim Reza of North South University's Centre for Migration Studies wrote in Prothom Alo on 30 June 2026 that before the June visit much of the media and some government officials gave the impression that reopening was decided and only a formal announcement remained, but that the visit's main result was agreement in principle on transparent, fair, lower-cost recruitment, not an immediate opening.
MY3g-19.target_section: What people believe, and the facts
MY3g-19.why_new: A documented case of 'the market is opening' claims running ahead of fact; supports a belief/fact bullet. Conflicts with the 22 July editorial cited in the guide's June bullet [MB0017].

MY3g-20.claim: Selim Reza wrote on 30 June 2026 that the most significant outcome of the prime ministers' meeting was the decision to hold a JWG meeting and draft a new MoU for safe and regular migration of Bangladeshi workers.
MY3g-20.why_new: Independent confirmation of the JWG/new-MoU outcome (see MY3g-12, MY3g-14).

MY3g-21.claim: The Prime Minister's deputy press secretary, Shahadat Swadhin, wrote on 1 July 2026 that at the 22 June meeting Tarique Rahman asked Anwar Ibrahim to consider regularising Bangladeshis who had become irregular and renewing their work permits, and asked Malaysia to recruit skilled workers from Bangladesh.
MY3g-21.why_new: Adds the explicit request for skilled-worker recruitment and work-permit renewal.

MY3g-22.claim: On 7 July 2026 the minister, Ariful Haque Chowdhury, told journalists at Sylhet Circuit House that Malaysia's labour market had reopened for Bangladesh from Monday 6 July 2026 as a result of the prime minister's visit; he gave no terms, quota or costs.
MY3g-22.why_new: Conflict: the guide says the corridor stayed closed and the restart was only announced on 15 October 2026 [Z0151]; two days later (9 July) the same minister told parliament he hoped the way would open soon (MY3g-23). Useful as a 'premature reopening announcement' case.

MY3g-23.claim: On 9 July 2026 the minister told parliament that bilateral talks with a high-level Malaysian representative had been held in April 2026, that the prime minister had recently visited, that a Malaysian delegation would visit Bangladesh in July, and that he hoped the way to send workers would open very soon.
MY3g-23.why_new: Contradicts his 7 July statement that the market had reopened on 6 July; adds April 2026 talks not in the guide.

MY3g-24.claim: UNHCR and IOM said in a joint statement on 16 July 2026 that about 300 Rohingya refugees and Bangladeshi nationals had been reported dead or missing in the Andaman Sea and Bay of Bengal so far in 2026, on a route to Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand that has become the world's deadliest sea route for refugees and migrants.
MY3g-24.target_section: Irregular routes, and where an irregular stay ends
MY3g-24.why_new: The guide's irregular routes cover overland via Thailand and airport entry, not the sea route; this shows Bangladeshi nationals among the dead/missing on it.

MY3g-25.claim: According to UNHCR and IOM, two boats carrying more than 500 people, mostly Rohingya including some from camps in Bangladesh, left Rakhine in late June 2026 and are feared lost; about 900 Rohingya died or went missing on the Andaman Sea and Bay of Bengal route in 2025, and in November 2025 a boat capsized off Langkawi near the Thailand-Malaysia border with about 12 rescued alive.
MY3g-25.target_section: Irregular routes, and where an irregular stay ends
MY3g-25.why_new: Cases for the sea-route bullet; mainly Rohingya, so a reviewer may keep only the Bangladeshi-relevant figure in MY3g-24.

MY3h-1.claim: On 30 July 2026, at a press conference at the Bangladesh High Commission in Kuala Lumpur, the Prime Minister's adviser and spokesperson Mahdi Amin said Bangladesh and Malaysia had agreed in principle to reopen the labour market at once, with work open to Bangladeshi workers in all sectors, and had set a target for workers to start arriving from the last week of August 2026.
MY3h-1.why_new: The Status timeline has no entry between June 2026 and 21 August 2026; this dates the in-principle agreement and the missed late-August target.

MY3h-2.claim: Mahdi Amin said on 30 July 2026 that Bangladesh had asked Malaysia to run the first phase of recruitment through BOESL, and that under the MoU valid until December 2026 Malaysia would set the final number of Bangladeshi agencies on its own vetting, from the list of 423 sent during the interim government.
MY3h-2.why_new: Adds the Bangladesh government's own request that BOESL run the first phase, and its statement before the list of 25 that Malaysia alone would fix the number.

MY3h-3.claim: Mahdi Amin said on 30 July 2026 that Bangladesh had told Malaysia that nobody involved in corruption as part of the syndicate would be on the new agency list, and that the Malaysian authorities would confirm this shortly.
MY3h-3.why_new: The guide records later allegations that the old ringleaders are behind the 25 but not this prior government assurance.

MY3h-4.claim: On Monday 3 August 2026 three Bangladeshi men were killed in a fight among Bangladeshi plantation workers who all lived in the same house in Taman Linggi, Port Dickson, Negeri Sembilan, and police arrested a 40-year-old Bangladeshi with no previous record and filed a murder case under section 302 of the Penal Code, the Negeri Sembilan police chief, DCP Aljafni Ahmed, said.
MY3h-4.why_new: No case of workers killed in fights among themselves is in the guide.
MY3h-4.h2: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job

MY3h-5.claim: The Prime Minister's deputy press secretary, Shahadat Swadhin, wrote in Prothom Alo on 19 August 2026 that a special "Probashi card" was to start on a pilot basis from August 2026, under the Prime Minister's direct planning, to improve migrants' social standing, legal protection and living standards.
MY3h-5.placement: after the May 2026 Probashi card line
MY3h-5.why_new: The cross-country doc has the April and May 2026 plans for a Probashi card but no start date.

MY3h-6.claim: On 18 August 2026 in Putrajaya, Malaysia's deputy tourism, arts and culture minister Chiew Choon Man and Bangladesh's state minister for civil aviation and tourism M Rashiduzzaman Millat discussed how to increase the recruitment of qualified Bangladeshi workers in Malaysia's tourism and hospitality sector, which needs skilled and trained staff, as well as easier visa processing and pre-verification, according to the Bangladesh ministry's press release; no decision was reported.
MY3h-6.why_new: Adds the tourism and hospitality sector as a discussed opening; the guide mentions tourism only for stranded 2024 workers.

MY3h-7.claim: The Ministry said on 28 August 2026 that Bangladesh had asked to change the approved medical centres, that a joint delegation of Malaysia's health, human resources and home ministries had inspected every centre in Bangladesh, and that Malaysia had decided to start with the remaining 16 centres on its existing list after dropping, at Bangladesh's request, controversial centres linked to the previous government.
MY3h-7.target_section: Step 2: Medical check in Bangladesh (Bio-Medical), once your VDR is approved
MY3h-7.why_new: The guide gives 46 centres sent for vetting (4 November) and no approved centre; this gives an earlier figure of 16 and conflicts with the 51 approved reported on 19 November.

MY3h-8.claim: The Ministry said on 28 August 2026 that because the MoU signed in 2022 gives the Malaysian government alone the job of choosing Bangladeshi agencies and runs until 31 December 2026, it is not easy for Bangladesh to change Malaysia's conditions, and it hopes a new MoU after that date will protect Bangladesh's interest in approving agencies.
MY3h-8.why_new: The guide says the Ministry had no involvement in vetting, but not that it says the MoU stops it changing Malaysia's conditions until 31 December.

MY3h-9.claim: On 30 August 2026, after Malaysia's High Commissioner in Dhaka, Mohammad Suhadha bin Osman, called on the local government minister, State Minister for Local Government Mir Shahe Alam told reporters that Malaysia would start taking two lakh workers from Bangladesh towards the end of the next month through listed companies, plus another 10,000 entirely free of cost, and that the process would be completed within six months.
MY3h-9.why_new: A dated government claim of two lakh workers from late September 2026 that did not happen; the guide has two lakh only as a figure in 'various statements' (Selim Reza).

MY3h-10.claim: The expatriates' welfare minister, Ariful Haque Chowdhury, told parliament in a written answer on 3 September 2026 that 9,85,120 Bangladeshis went abroad for work in the last fiscal year, including 6,46,062 to Saudi Arabia, 89,023 to Qatar, 75,041 to Singapore, 42,130 to the Maldives and 39,875 to Kuwait.
MY3h-10.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Which countries can I go to for work right now?
MY3h-10.why_new: Official departure totals by country for the last fiscal year; not in the cross-country doc.

MY3h-11.claim: The minister told parliament on 3 September 2026 that after the Prime Minister's recent visit to Malaysia and a visit by the Ministry's adviser and minister in late July, the way to send Bangladeshi workers to Malaysia was expected to open very soon.
MY3h-11.why_new: Shows that as of 3 September 2026 the government still described sending as not yet started, against the late-August target.

MY3h-12.claim: On 16 September 2026 the expatriates' welfare secretary, Md Mokhtar Ahmed, said the process to reopen Malaysia's closed market was still under way, that the administrative work on which process would be used to send workers was pending, and that it would be announced formally once confirmed.
MY3h-12.why_new: Dates that the method of sending was still undecided in mid-September 2026.

MY3h-13.claim: In a memorandum to the expatriates' welfare secretary on 16 September 2026, BAIRA members demanded equal opportunity for all valid and eligible agencies including the 312 listed ones, an end to the syndicate and monopoly, a significant cut in migration cost, full transparency in recruitment, opening up all eligible medical centres, and a one-stop service through BOESL.
MY3h-13.why_new: Adds BAIRA's September 2026 demands, including opening all medical centres, which the guide does not have.

MY3h-14.claim: The expatriates' welfare secretary said on 16 September 2026 that a mobile court had sealed the office of Triple A Overseas, fined it and seized three boxes of passports.
MY3h-14.why_new: Adds the scale (three boxes of passports) to the guide's 10 September Triple A raid [A0043].

MY3h-15.claim: At a Jamaat-e-Islami seminar on 17 September 2026, the opposition leader and Jamaat Ameer, Shafiqur Rahman, said the 25 agencies appeared to be "master agencies" with associates under them, demanded the government explain the criteria for choosing them when some had no previous experience, and said "we are hearing" that Tk 15 to 22 crore was being invested to get in, which he said could not happen without the government's involvement.
MY3h-15.why_new: A new alleged price for a place on the 2026 list (Tk 15 to 22 crore), against the Tk 5 crore (2022) and Tk 14 crore (2025) alleged in the guide.

MY3h-16.claim: Shafiqur Rahman alleged on 17 September 2026 that the syndicate built in Malaysia under the previous government by a man he called Dato Sri Amin was still operating, and that some leaders still met him secretly.
MY3h-16.why_new: Adds the opposition leader's September 2026 allegation that Amin's syndicate is still active.

MY3h-17.claim: On 11 September 2026 traffickers took five teenagers and young men (two aged 16, two 18 and one 20) from Mithachhari, Ramu, by CNG auto-rickshaw on the pretext of visiting Teknaf's Marine Drive, blindfolded and held them, beat them and collected ransom from their families in instalments while planning to send them by sea to Indonesia and Malaysia; SRB-15 (Special Response Battalion 15) rescued them on 20 September at Khonkarpara ghat near Sabrang Zero Point, Teknaf, and arrested Md Anas alias Munna (21).
MY3h-17.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
MY3h-17.why_new: New 2026 case; adds a tourist-trip lure aimed at Bangladeshi teenagers, not Rohingya.

MY3h-18.claim: A boat of irregular migrants from Myanmar's Rakhine state capsized off the Baharchhara coast of Teknaf at dawn on 22 September 2026, killing a Rohingya woman, Chhura Khatun (28), and her 9-year-old son; of the 16 rescued, eight were Bangladeshis who told police they had been taken to Myanmar about a year earlier on the promise of Malaysia, kept in various parts of Myanmar for a year, and put on the boat for Malaysia the night before.
MY3h-18.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
MY3h-18.why_new: New 2026 case of Bangladeshis held a year in Myanmar on a Malaysia promise; fits the guide's 'journeys sold as going through Malaysia end in Myanmar'.

MY3h-19.claim: On the night of 1 October 2026 the navy ship BNS Khalid Bin Walid, alerted by fishermen, rescued 76 people from a wooden boat whose engine had failed and which was sinking about 81 km west of the St Martin's Island lighthouse; the navy said 65 men, women and children aboard, some lured with good jobs and some kidnapped and held in remote parts of Teknaf, were being trafficked to Malaysia by way of the Myanmar and Thai coasts, and it detained 11 alleged traffickers.
MY3h-19.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Malaysia: boats and land crossings

MY3h-21.claim: The Ministry's press release of 15 October 2026 dates the Bangladesh-Malaysia MoU to 18 December 2022 and says that under it choosing and listing the recruiting agencies is the job of Malaysia's human resources ministry.
MY3h-21.why_new: The guide gives the MoU's end date (31 December 2026) but not its signing date; elsewhere the guide calls it the 2021 MoU (What closed it before), which this contradicts.

MY3h-22.claim: The Ministry said on 15 October 2026 that the medical checks would start through the centres listed on Malaysia's website, that Bangladesh had asked for the existing centres to be changed and a joint Malaysian delegation would give final approval after inspecting each centre, and that any new centre added would be published on that website.
MY3h-22.target_section: Step 2: Medical check in Bangladesh (Bio-Medical), once your VDR is approved
MY3h-22.why_new: Adds the 15 October position (start with centres on Malaysia's website), between the 28 August '16 centres' and the 4 November '46 sent for vetting'.

MY3h-23.claim: Prothom Alo's 15 October 2026 summary of the Ministry's announcement says Malaysia allowed 337 agencies to work, including BOESL and the 25 processing agencies.
MY3h-23.target_section: The processing agency: the toll gate
MY3h-23.why_new: Conflict: the guide counts 338 (BOESL, 25 processing agencies and 312 associates) [Z0144]; 1 + 25 + 312 = 338, so 337 is likely the 25 plus 312 without BOESL.

MY3h-24.claim: The Ministry's instructions of 28 October 2026 say a medical centre or recruiting agency that disobeys them may have its operations shut (centre) or its overseas recruitment suspended and Ministry approval cancelled (agency).
MY3h-24.target_section: Step 2: Medical check in Bangladesh (Bio-Medical), once your VDR is approved
MY3h-24.placement: Scams / penalties for centres and agencies
MY3h-24.why_new: The guide says a centre is removed from the list [Z0160] but not the penalty on agencies.

MY3h-25.claim: BOESL's DHL Supply Chain (Malaysia) circular of November 2026 had two posts: Operations Assistant, needing at least SSC, English reading, writing and communication, physical fitness for warehouse work and one to two years' experience, with forklift, power pallet truck or reach truck skills a plus; and Technical Skill Workers, needing at least HSC and good knowledge of warehouse network cabling, racking and IT equipment, with electrical vocational, polytechnic or degree holders preferred.
MY3h-25.why_new: The guide gives the age limit and SSC/HSC but not the posts or their skill requirements.

MY3h-26.claim: The DHL circular offered a three-year renewable contract at RM1,700 (about Tk 52,000) a month, eight hours a day, six days a week, with overtime as the company needs and Malaysian labour law allows, and said the employer would provide housing, first aid and transport.
MY3h-26.why_new: Contract length, hours and what the employer provides are not in the guide's DHL example.

MY3h-27.claim: Under the DHL circular, a software lottery first picks 300 applicants, whose list BOESL posts on its website, and the employer's representatives then choose the final 112 by technical and oral tests.
MY3h-27.why_new: Adds the shortlist size (300 for 112 places).

MY3h-28.claim: On 5 November 2026 a joint army, BGB and police operation freed 57 people from a traffickers' den in the deep hills of Rangikhali, Teknaf, where they were being tortured for ransom and were to be put on a trawler to Malaysia that night; a soldier, Md Titas Sheikh (27), was shot dead in a gunfight, five ring members were detained, and police said one of the 57 was identified as a trafficker.
MY3h-28.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Malaysia: boats and land crossings

MY3h-29.claim: Nur Kamal (21) of Daganbhuiyan, Feni, told Prothom Alo in November 2026 that someone added him to a WhatsApp group offering to take him to Malaysia free of cost, with payment due only after arrival; he left home on 2 November and on reaching Cox's Bazar was taken to a hut in the Teknaf hills, held under 10 to 12 armed guards and beaten.
MY3h-29.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
MY3h-29.placement: How it is sold / Other lures
MY3h-29.why_new: New lure: 'free now, pay on arrival' through WhatsApp groups, in the month the government was advertising zero-cost Malaysia jobs.

MY3h-30.claim: In November 2026 a young man from Feni was added to a WhatsApp group offering to take him to Malaysia free of cost, paying only after arrival, and ended up held by traffickers in the Teknaf hills awaiting a boat, he told Prothom Alo.
MY3h-30.why_new: The Malaysia guide's scam list covers fake zero-cost BOESL places but not a 'free Malaysia' offer that leads to the sea route.

MY3h-31.claim: Victims freed on 5 November 2026 said people were handed to the traffickers for money: S M Asaduzzaman (50) of Saltha, Faridpur, said a man he met in Kutupalong camp lured him with work and handed him over for Tk 10,000, then he agreed a Tk 2 lakh release deal; Md Saiful Islam of Ukhiya said a broker named Nur Ali handed him over and the traffickers said they had bought him and another man for Tk 1 lakh, and that captives who tried to flee were beaten and chained.
MY3h-31.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Malaysia: boats and land crossings
MY3h-31.why_new: Adds the price at which people are sold into the dens (Tk 10,000 a head; Tk 1 lakh for two), which the cross-country doc lacks.

MY3h-32.claim: On the evening of 7 November 2026 BGB rescued nine people, including two aged 16 and 17, gathered at South Lombori ghat, Teknaf Sadar union, to be taken to Malaysia by sea, while 10 to 15 ring members fled by boat; the rescued said men were lured with good jobs and women with marriage to suitable grooms in Malaysia, the Teknaf BGB battalion commander said.
MY3h-32.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Malaysia: boats and land crossings

MY3h-33.claim: BOESL held the DHL lottery electronically on 8 November 2026 at the Probashi Kallyan Bhaban auditorium, with Ministry representatives, BOESL officials and journalists present, picking 300 of 4,029 applicants (200 for Operations Assistant, 100 for Technical Skill Workers) for practical and oral tests before DHL's representatives.
MY3h-33.why_new: Gives the odds (about 1 in 36 applicants reached the final 112) and how the lottery was run.

MY3h-34.claim: BOESL's managing director, Mohammad Rashedul Haque, said on 8 November 2026 that this was the first time a lottery had been used to choose workers for government-channel sending to Malaysia, and that flights for the selected DHL workers would start from the first week of December.
MY3h-34.why_new: A dated first-flight target for BOESL's DHL workers; the guide has only the minister's hope of December flights [YD0005].

MY3h-35.claim: BOESL's managing director said on 8 November 2026 that BOESL had received demand letters for 558 more workers in Malaysia's tourism, manufacturing and caregiving sectors, with the employers bearing all costs including the medical and airfare, so these workers too would go with no migration cost.
MY3h-35.why_new: New: further BOESL demand (558) beyond DHL, including caregiving; bears on the guide's Need-to-know whether zero-cost workers pay the medical and airfare (here the employer pays both).

MY3h-36.claim: The Ministry said on 12 November 2026 that a nine-member delegation from Malaysia would hold practical tests and interviews of the 300 shortlisted DHL candidates from 12 to 15 November, that BOESL would not interfere in the selection, and that the candidates the employer picks are final.
MY3h-36.why_new: Adds who runs the selection test and that BOESL has no say, which matters for anyone offered a 'BOESL place' for money.

MY3h-37.claim: BOESL's managing director said on 12 November 2026 that if any broker, middleman or unauthorised person tries to take money at any stage of the recruitment, or any candidate takes part in an unethical transaction, strict legal action will be taken against both on proof.
MY3h-37.why_new: New: the candidate who pays is also liable, not only the broker.

MY3h-38.claim: BOESL's managing director called Malaysia Bangladesh's second-largest labour market on 12 November 2026.
MY3h-38.why_new: A ranking the Size section lacks; low priority.

MY3h-39.claim: The expatriates' welfare minister, Ariful Haque Chowdhury, told parliament on 15 November 2026 that the cost of sending a worker to Malaysia had been cut and fixed at Tk 1,54,000, and that strict action would be taken against anyone who collects more or breaks the government's arrangements.

SA3g-1.claim: According to Gulf News as reported by Prothom Alo (16 October 2026), the court sentenced the two Bangladeshis executed in Makkah on 14 October 2026 to death under 'taazir', the judge's discretionary punishment under Shariah law, a higher judicial authority upheld the verdict and a royal order directed that it be carried out.

SA3g-7.claim: According to Wage Earners' Welfare Board data cited by The Daily Star and a Prothom Alo column (17 October 2026), the bodies of 799 women migrant workers came home to Bangladesh in eight years, most from Saudi Arabia, and many death certificates gave suicide as the cause.

SA3h-2.target_section: If you or a relative is arrested
SA3h-2.why_new: New: shows how the mission handles Saudi prisoner lists and why the death sentence was missed.

SA3h-3.claim: On 25 October 2026 the parliamentary committee, chaired by Zahurat Adib Chowdhury, asked the foreign ministry to report whether the Jeddah consulate was weak or negligent over the two executions, what action was taken and what is being done to stop a repeat; the ministry has asked Saudi Arabia questions about the case.
SA3h-3.target_section: If you or a relative is arrested
SA3h-3.why_new: New: possible Need to know: what has the mission changed in how it tracks Bangladeshi prisoners after the October 2026 executions?

SA3h-4.claim: According to Bangladesh's foreign ministry in October 2026, about 1 lakh 69 thousand (169,000) Bangladeshi women workers are now in Saudi Arabia.
SA3h-4.why_new: New: the guide has departure numbers but no stock of women workers.

SA3h-5.claim: Bangladesh's foreign ministry told the parliamentary committee in October 2026 that 1-2 percent of Bangladeshi women workers in Saudi Arabia are abused, a figure it gets by asking women when they come for passport services and from a third-party survey.
SA3h-5.target_section: Work visa: domestic worker > If something goes wrong
SA3h-5.why_new: New: the guide gives no official abuse rate for women domestic workers.

SA3h-6.claim: The foreign ministry reported in October 2026 that 1,364 Bangladeshi women domestic workers had been rescued from Saudi Arabia and safely repatriated (period not stated); the committee chair called the number unacceptable and the committee directed the ministry to bring abuse to zero.
SA3h-6.target_section: Work visa: domestic worker > If something goes wrong
SA3h-6.why_new: New: rescue/repatriation count for women domestic workers; evidence that the mission does bring women home.

SA3h-7.claim: In October 2026 the Bangladesh Hajj Office in Jeddah (under Bangladesh's Ministry of Religious Affairs) advertised posts open to Bangladeshis living in Saudi Arabia with a valid iqama and passport, and to Saudis: protocol assistant and computer operator cum interpreter at SR 4,425-6,875, caretaker cum night guard at SR 2,815-5,090 and two drivers at SR 3,250-5,525 a month, age limit 32, deadline 4 pm on 12 November 2026.
SA3h-7.target_section: NEW: Jobs at Bangladesh government offices in Saudi Arabia (after If you want to change employer)
SA3h-7.why_new: New: the guide does not mention Bangladesh mission jobs open to iqama holders; deadline has passed, so useful only as an example that such posts are advertised. Reviewer may drop.

SA3h-8.claim: Applications to the Bangladesh Hajj Office in Jeddah go by hand or by email to missionhajj@gmail.com, with a handwritten application and CV, 2 passport photos, copies of the iqama and passport and attested copies of certificates (October 2026 notice).
SA3h-8.why_new: New: the guide lists no contact for the Bangladesh Hajj Office in Jeddah.

SA3h-9.claim: On 26 October 2026 Expatriates' Welfare Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury said Saudi-based workers stranded in Bangladesh by the flight disruption whose iqama has expired will be allowed to enter Saudi Arabia: when they can travel, they will be included automatically in the Saudi system and given permission to enter.
SA3h-9.why_new: New: partly answers the guide's Need to know on stranded workers (guide only says Bangladesh was discussing an extension, SG0036); concerns iqama holders on leave, not new entry visas. Also relevant to Going home on leave and coming back.

SA3h-10.claim: According to the expatriates' ministry on 26 October 2026, Houthi attacks on Saudi airports had so far disrupted 144 flights on direct and transit routes between Bangladesh and Saudi Arabia, so many workers could not get back after leave on time and their iqamas could expire.
SA3h-10.why_new: Different figure: the guide says over 1,000 flights cancelled since February (E0130), likely all routes; this is Bangladesh routes only. Adds that workers on leave risk iqama expiry.

SA3h-11.claim: At a 26 October 2026 meeting the expatriates' welfare minister said that where it is possible to go for Tk 3 lakh, taking Tk 7-8 lakh is improper, and urged agencies to stop collecting extra money from workers.
SA3h-11.target_section: The legal maximum and what people really pay
SA3h-11.why_new: New: a minister's own statement that Tk 7-8 lakh is being taken; the guide has Tk 3.5-5 lakh typical, up to Tk 9 lakh.

SA3h-12.claim: On 26 October 2026 State Minister Md Nurul Haque asked the Saudi government to include imprisoned Bangladeshis in a special pardon next Ramadan; this was a request, not a decision.
SA3h-12.target_section: If you or a relative is arrested
SA3h-12.placement: other: If a relative or friend is arrested
SA3h-12.why_new: New: the guide does not mention Ramadan pardons; possible Need to know: did Saudi Arabia include Bangladeshi prisoners in a Ramadan 2027 pardon?

SA3h-13.claim: Saudi ambassador Abdullah Zafer H bin Abiyah said on 26 October 2026 that, after Saudi citizens, Bangladeshi workers are the largest group living in Saudi Arabia.
SA3h-13.why_new: New: Saudi official statement on the size of the Bangladeshi community; the guide has flows but no stock.

SA3h-14.claim: At the 26 October 2026 meeting with the expatriates' ministry, recruiting agency representatives demanded a simpler Takamol test process and lower fees.
SA3h-14.why_new: New but minor: shows the skill test and its USD 85 fee remain a sticking point in late 2026.

SA3h-15.claim: The expatriates' welfare minister said on 26 October 2026 that work is under way on technology at BMET to check visa validity quickly, and that an open email service to settle any complaint is being launched and publicised.
SA3h-15.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Where to complain and get help
SA3h-15.why_new: New: announced (not yet live) complaint email and visa-check tool; not Saudi-specific. Need to know: what is the address and is it live?
SA3h-15.h2: Dalal scams: the usual tricks and how to spot them

SA3h-16.claim: According to the Berlin-based rights group ESOHR (European Saudi Organisation for Human Rights), Saudi Arabia executed 108 people in January-June 2026, 59 (about 54 percent) of them foreigners, and 49 of the 71 executed for drug offences in that period were foreigners.
SA3h-16.target_section: What can get you jailed or deported
SA3h-16.why_new: New: scale behind the guide's line that Saudi Arabia executes foreigners for drug smuggling (C0107).

SA3h-17.claim: ESOHR's list of the 108 people executed in Saudi Arabia in January-June 2026 includes Bangladeshis, but how many is not known; the two Bangladeshis executed for an 'immoral act' in a Makkah mosque are outside that count.
SA3h-17.target_section: What can get you jailed or deported
SA3h-17.why_new: New: Bangladeshis other than the two mosque cases were executed in 2026. Possible Need to know: how many Bangladeshis were executed in 2026 and for what?

SA3h-18.claim: According to Amnesty International, Saudi Arabia executed 597 people for drug offences alone from January 2014 to June 2025, about 75 percent of them foreigners.
SA3h-18.target_section: What can get you jailed or deported
SA3h-18.why_new: New: long-run figure on drug executions of foreigners.

SA3h-19.claim: In two of the drug cases Amnesty International documented (published July 2025), the accused said they had been forced to carry the banned drugs, but the Saudi court neither examined nor accepted this.
SA3h-19.target_section: What can get you jailed or deported
SA3h-19.placement: other: Never carry a parcel line
SA3h-19.why_new: New: evidence that being forced or tricked into carrying drugs is not accepted as a defence.

SA3h-20.claim: Prothom Alo reported in October 2026 that Bangladeshis are the largest group of foreign workers in Saudi Arabia, at least 25 lakh (2.5 million), followed by Indians, Pakistanis, Yemenis and Egyptians, and that migrant workers are about 77 percent of Saudi Arabia's workforce.
SA3h-20.why_new: New: stock of Bangladeshi workers; the guide gives only yearly departures. No primary source named for the 25 lakh.

SA3h-21.claim: Saudi Arabia's Law of Criminal Procedure (Royal Decree M/39 of 2001; the article text calls it the 2013 code) gives defendants the right to legal assistance at both investigation and trial and prohibits torture, according to Prothom Alo's October 2026 report.
SA3h-21.target_section: If you or a relative is arrested
SA3h-21.why_new: Partly answers the guide's Need to know 'does Saudi law give them a lawyer?': the law grants a right to legal assistance (not necessarily a free lawyer). Date conflict inside the article (2013 in text, 2001 decree in references).

SA3h-22.claim: ESOHR documented that death-row prisoners in Khamis Mushait, Najran and Tabuk prisons had no professional interpreter and no legal aid, did not understand the proceedings and often did not know when their sentence was upheld or their pardon plea rejected.
SA3h-22.target_section: If you or a relative is arrested
SA3h-22.why_new: Conflict: the guide says the court provides an interpreter (G0004); ESOHR found no professional interpreter in these death-row cases.

SA3h-23.claim: Amnesty International found (July 2025 report) that many of 25 foreigners convicted of drug offences in Saudi Arabia went through the system alone, did not understand or did not receive the court papers and charges, got no consular help, and gave confessions without adequate interpreters or lawyers.
SA3h-23.target_section: If you or a relative is arrested
SA3h-23.why_new: New: what happens in practice after arrest; supports a line not to sign or confess to anything not understood (reviewer to decide wording).

SA3h-24.claim: According to Amnesty International, Saudi law has no clear rule on advance notice of an execution to the prisoner or family: families said at most the prisoner can phone 24 hours before, and many learned of the execution from other prisoners' calls or from the media after the interior ministry announced it.
SA3h-24.target_section: If you or a relative is arrested
SA3h-24.placement: other: If a relative or friend is arrested
SA3h-24.why_new: New: what families can expect; the guide does not cover notice of execution.

SA3h-25.claim: Saudi law does not guarantee that the body of an executed person is handed over: in all three executions of January-June 2025 among the cases Amnesty International documented, Saudi Arabia neither returned the body to the family nor told them where the grave is.
SA3h-25.target_section: If a worker dies in Saudi Arabia
SA3h-25.why_new: New: the repatriation steps in the guide do not apply to executed workers.
SA3h-25.h2: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job

SA3h-26.claim: ESOHR said it could learn nothing about 91 of the 108 cases (84.2 percent) before the executions of January-June 2026, and Prothom Alo found no answer on how many Bangladeshis are held, on what charges, or whether they get lawyers, interpreters or consular help.
SA3h-26.target_section: If you or a relative is arrested
SA3h-26.why_new: Supports a Need to know: how many Bangladeshis are in Saudi prisons or on death row, and on what charges?

SA3h-27.claim: In December 2024 the UN Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination said migrant workers and domestic workers, including women, face arbitrary detention, torture and ill-treatment in Saudi Arabia's criminal justice system.
SA3h-27.target_section: What goes wrong most, and what people wrongly believe
SA3h-27.why_new: New, but general; reviewer may drop under the actionable rule.

SA3h-28.claim: In an October 2026 Prothom Alo column, Professor A K M Ahsan Ullah (Universiti Brunei Darussalam) wrote that if the Houthi-Saudi conflict is prolonged, new hiring may fall, construction projects may slow and wages and overtime may become uncertain, while demand may hold in repair, health care, transport and emergency supply.
SA3h-28.why_new: Forecast by a columnist, not a fact; the guide has no outlook line. Reviewer may drop under the no-opinion rule.

SA3h-29.claim: An Indian worker, Sheikh Sahabuddin, a cleaner at the Makkah mosque, was arrested in 2023 and jailed by a Saudi court after posting on social media a video of the two Bangladeshis later executed; Saudi authorities treated the post as a serious offence against the dignity of a holy place.
SA3h-29.target_section: What can get you jailed or deported
SA3h-29.why_new: New: a concrete case for the guide's Need to know on which online acts are crimes (posting a video of others).

SA3h-30.claim: The Saudi interior ministry announced in mid-October 2026 that the two Bangladeshis, Nazrul Islam Abdul Basir and Sweety Akter, had been executed under 'tazir' (punishment at a judge's discretion), three years after the 2023 incident in the Makkah mosque.
SA3h-30.target_section: What can get you jailed or deported
SA3h-30.why_new: New detail: tazir basis and the 3-year gap; the guide already records the execution (G0007, G0001). The gloss of tazir is ours; the article does not define it.

SA3h-31.claim: Sixteen Bangladeshi workers died in a fire at a sofa factory in Riyadh on 9 August 2026; nine bodies were sent home on 27 August, and the other seven, identified by DNA tests, were due in Dhaka on 31 October, nearly three months later.
SA3h-31.target_section: If a worker dies in Saudi Arabia
SA3h-31.why_new: New: the guide has no case of this fire or of DNA identification delaying a body by months.
SA3h-31.h2: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job

SA3h-32.claim: The seven bodies from the 9 August 2026 Riyadh sofa-factory fire were burned beyond recognition, identified by DNA tests and reached Dhaka on 31 October 2026, 2 months 22 days after the deaths.
SA3h-32.target_section: If a worker dies in Saudi Arabia
SA3h-32.why_new: New: confirms arrival and the timeline for DNA cases. Possible Need to know: how does a family give a DNA sample from Bangladesh?
SA3h-32.h2: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job

SA3h-33.claim: According to a letter signed by labour counsellor Muhammad Rezaye Rabbi, all flights from Riyadh have been suspended since 10 October 2026, so the bodies of the fire victims were taken by road to King Abdulaziz International Airport in Jeddah and flown to Dhaka on Biman.
SA3h-33.why_new: New: start date (10 October) of the Riyadh flight suspension; the guide says Dhaka-Riyadh is suspended without a date. Also relevant to If a worker dies in Saudi Arabia, item 2 (bodies from Riyadh go via Jeddah).

SA3h-34.claim: For the bodies flown home on 31 October 2026, the expatriates' ministry sent its letter with the flight time to the district deputy commissioners, upazila nirbahi officers and expatriate-welfare offices concerned, and the Atrai UNO confirmed the families had been told.
SA3h-34.target_section: If a worker dies in Saudi Arabia
SA3h-34.why_new: New: how a family learns when a body will arrive (via the DC/UNO offices).
SA3h-34.h2: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job

SA3h-35.claim: On 31 October 2026 the Biman flight with the seven bodies landed in Dhaka at about 8:30 am; after airport formalities expatriates' ministry officials handed the bodies to relatives, who took them home to Naogaon and Natore, where they were buried that afternoon and evening.
SA3h-35.target_section: If a worker dies in Saudi Arabia
SA3h-35.why_new: Consistent with the guide's airport handover step; adds a real same-day timeline. Low priority.
SA3h-35.h2: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job

SA3h-36.claim: The Atrai upazila nirbahi officer said in October 2026 that each family of the Riyadh fire victims would get Tk 35,000 now for burial and a Tk 3 lakh grant after three months.
SA3h-36.why_new: Consistent with the guide (Tk 35,000 at the airport, Tk 3 lakh grant); timing 'after three months' vs the guide's 'within 60 working days of complete papers'.
SA3h-36.h2: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job

SA3h-37.claim: Md Shahin of Par Naogaon went to Saudi Arabia in April 2026 on a Tk 5 lakh 70 thousand loan from a samity (a lending society), found work, and died in the Riyadh factory fire three months after arriving, according to his mother.
SA3h-37.target_section: What reaches home, and how long the debt takes
SA3h-37.why_new: New: real 2026 cost and source of the loan (samity).

SA3h-38.claim: Akkas Pramanik of Atrai, Naogaon, said he sent his son Minhaz to Saudi Arabia in 2025 on a Tk 7 lakh loan through a broker ring; Minhaz got no iqama for a year, found work at a Riyadh sofa factory four months before he died in the August 2026 fire, and the family is left with the debt.
SA3h-38.target_section: What goes wrong most, and what people wrongly believe
SA3h-38.why_new: New case of the guide's top complaint (no iqama) with a real cost of Tk 7 lakh; 'in 2025' is derived from 'a year ago' in an October 2026 article. Raises a Need to know: can a family claim the Tk 3 lakh grant/insurance for a worker who had no iqama?

SA3h-39.claim: According to a protest letter Bangladeshis in Berlin handed to the Saudi embassy on 30 October 2026, the two Bangladeshi migrant workers were executed on 14 October 2026; the organisers said Bangladesh's authorities said they knew nothing until the media reported it.
SA3h-39.target_section: What can get you jailed or deported
SA3h-39.why_new: Adds the exact date (14 October 2026; guide says October 2026). The 'knew nothing' claim conflicts with the foreign ministry's account of a prisoner list sent 14 days earlier (article 1449ee21).

SA3d-33.claim: Expatriates' Welfare Secretary Neyamat Ullah Bhuiyan said in October 2025 that the government is pushing, through bilateral agreements, for workers to be sent at the employer's cost.
SA3d-33.why_new: Government stance on employer-pays not in guide.

MY3h-20.claim: In the A-to-B raid of 8 October 2026, Immigration's Director General, Datuk Zakaria Shaban, said the team seized 265 Bangladeshi passports (with 63 Indonesian, 12 Pakistani and 1 Indian) and RM6,700 believed paid by customers, detained 9 Bangladeshi men among 12 foreign "customers", and found that the workers brought in did not work for the companies that applied for the quota but worked independently for other companies.
MY3h-20.placement: after the October 2026 A-to-B ring sentence
MY3h-20.why_new: The guide has the ring and its RM3,800 to 5,000 profit [YE0007-9]; this adds that Bangladeshi workers who used it were themselves detained and 265 passports seized.

MY3d-1.claim: Teenagers and young men from Teknaf and Ukhiya in Cox's Bazar, some aged 16 and some nearly 18, lured by brokers with promises of well-paid jobs in Malaysia, set off by the illegal sea route without telling their families, were detained in Myanmar in June 2023 for illegal entry and served 22 months in prison, Prothom Alo reported on 15 April 2025.
MY3d-1.target_section: Irregular routes, and where an irregular stay ends
MY3d-1.placement: other: new bullet, sea route via Myanmar
MY3d-1.why_new: The guide's irregular routes cover Thailand overland, airport and overstaying; the Bay of Bengal sea route from Teknaf via Myanmar is absent.

MY3d-2.claim: The 20 Bangladeshis detained in Myanmar were brought back after the government verified their citizenship and negotiated with Myanmar, and the Bangladesh embassy arranged their repatriation on the navy ship BNS Samudra Avijan from Yangon, arriving at Chattogram on 15 April 2025; families had learned of the arrest only about a month after it and had submitted papers to the government a year before the return.
MY3d-2.target_section: Irregular routes, and where an irregular stay ends
MY3d-2.placement: other: new bullet, sea route via Myanmar
MY3d-2.why_new: How a sea-route detainee in Myanmar gets home, and how long it took; not in the guide.

MY3d-3.claim: In April 2025 recruiting agency owners told Prothom Alo that the old Malaysia syndicate led by Ruhul Amin (Swapan) and Aminul Islam (Amin Nur) was trying to re-form, dropping agencies owned by Awami League leaders and bringing in people from other political parties, and that at least two lists of agencies to be in the new syndicate had been found; Ruhul Amin said the allegation was a rumour created by one group, and Aminul Islam could not be reached.
MY3d-3.placement: other: Objections and allegations, new dated bullet (April 2025)
MY3d-3.why_new: Adds the April 2025 re-forming allegation and Swapan's denial; the guide has the May 2025 memorandum but not this.

MY3d-4.claim: BAIRA members alleged in April 2025 that last time the syndicate's ringleaders took Tk 5 crore each in advance as a security deposit from member agencies, and that this time they would take RM50 lakh (Tk 12.5 crore) each, to be adjusted once worker sending starts.
MY3d-4.placement: other: Objections and allegations, new dated bullet (April 2025)
MY3d-4.why_new: The guide gives Tk 5 crore (2022) and Tk 14 crore (May 2025 memorandum) per agency; this April 2025 figure is RM50 lakh (Tk 12.5 crore), and adds that the deposit was to be adjusted against workers sent. Conflicts with the Tk 14 crore figure.

MY3d-5.claim: A BAIRA members' memorandum to the Ministry of 5 February 2025 said the syndicate built by Ruhul Amin and Aminul Islam had extorted Tk 1,07,000 a person for sending workers to Malaysia last time, and demanded legal action against both and that sending be opened to all agencies.
MY3d-5.target_section: The processing agency: the toll gate
MY3d-5.placement: other: How the toll worked in 2022-24
MY3d-5.why_new: The guide's toll range is Tk 1.07 to 1.52 lakh without saying who gave 1.07; this attributes it to a dated BAIRA memorandum.

MY3d-6.claim: Prothom Alo reported in April 2025 that Bestinet, Aminul Islam's company that owns the Migram software running FWCMS, is supposed to receive RM100 (Tk 2,500) per worker, but is alleged to have done illegal business by controlling the whole process in the name of selecting agencies.
MY3d-6.why_new: Guide has RM100 per worker from the Auditor-General; this adds the allegation that agency selection was the illegal business. Minor addition.

MY3d-7.claim: Prothom Alo reported in April 2025 that 17,000 workers who had completed every procedure could not go by the 31 May 2024 deadline, while BAIRA members said about 50,000 workers who had paid money and were in process were harmed.
MY3d-7.why_new: Adds BAIRA's count of about 50,000 who paid and were in process; the guide's counts run to about 40,000.

MY3d-8.claim: Prothom Alo reported in April 2025 that the existing Bangladesh-Malaysia MoU was valid until August 2026, that agency selection would stay in Malaysia's hands if sending started within that period, and that the clause could be amended by agreement at renewal.
MY3d-8.why_new: Conflict: the guide says the MoU runs to 31 December 2026 [Z0156]; this April 2025 article says August 2026 (and a May 2025 article says December).

MY3d-9.claim: In April 2025 the Ministry's joint secretary (employment wing), A Z M Nurul Haque, said there was no scope for a syndicate over the Malaysian market, that the Ministry wanted all agencies to take part, and that amending parts of the MoU would be discussed with Malaysia; Andy Hall, a UK migration and human-rights campaigner, said in a statement of 7 April 2025 that moves to form a syndicate were again under way and the clauses handing control to it must be amended.
MY3d-9.placement: other: Objections and allegations, new dated bullet (April 2025)
MY3d-9.why_new: Official position and Andy Hall's statement in 2025 not in guide.

MY3d-10.claim: Prothom Alo reported in April 2025 that after the change of government the ACC had begun investigating four former MPs in the syndicate, A H M Mustafa Kamal, Nizam Uddin Hazari, Masud Uddin Chowdhury and Benzir Ahmed, but that no action had yet been taken against the syndicate's main figures, Ruhul Amin (Swapan) and Aminul Islam (Amin Nur).
MY3d-10.why_new: Names the four MPs under ACC investigation as of April 2025 and notes no action against the two ringleaders then; guide's 2024-25 bullet mentions four MPs only via RMMRU.

MY3d-11.claim: BAIRA members, who on 21 April 2025 submitted to the Ministry a memorandum signed by owners of 453 recruiting agencies, alleged that the syndicate took Tk 1,52,000 a worker last time, of which RM5,000 (Tk 1,25,000) went to Bestinet, the online software company owned by Amin Nur, with the money collected in Bangladesh by his local representative Ruhul Amin, and that workers' cost of going to Malaysia came to Tk 4 to 5 lakh.
MY3d-11.target_section: The processing agency: the toll gate
MY3d-11.placement: other: How the toll worked in 2022-24
MY3d-11.why_new: Splits the Tk 1.52 lakh toll: RM5,000 (Tk 1.25 lakh) to Bestinet, collected by Swapan. The guide has the total but not this split.

MY3d-12.claim: The 21 April 2025 memorandum said that although Malaysia takes workers from 14 countries it selects specific agencies for none of them, so all agencies in those countries can send workers, and that the syndicate's seed was sown in the MoU that gave Malaysia's government the job of selecting Bangladesh's agencies; it also said the ringleaders were telling the government that Malaysia would not take workers without a syndicate, which it called untrue.
MY3d-12.why_new: Guide mentions the 21 April memorandum only via MA0096 (same demand); adds the 'no syndicate, no workers' claim and the 14-country comparison.

MY3d-13.claim: After the memorandum was handed in on 21 April 2025, former BAIRA joint secretary general Mohammad Fakhrul Islam said the Ministry's senior secretary had told them the government did not want a syndicate and had promised to work on amending the MoU; BNP Dhaka district president and BAIRA member Khandaker Abu Ashfaq said some were trying to add new people to the old syndicate and that no one in the BNP believed in a syndicate.
MY3d-13.why_new: Official response to the 21 April memorandum; not in guide.

MY3d-14.claim: At a human chain outside Probashi Kallyan Bhaban, Eskaton, Dhaka, on 24 April 2025, BAIRA's general members said 13 countries had accepted Malaysia's conditions and kept sending workers while Bangladesh lagged behind, and estimated that a reopened Malaysia could take at least 2 lakh Bangladeshi workers a year, 10 lakh in five years, bringing at least USD 500 crore a year in remittances.
MY3d-14.why_new: Agency owners' projection of the corridor's size; not in guide. Low priority.

MY3d-15.claim: At a human chain held under the banner of BAIRA's general members outside Probashi Kallyan Bhaban in Eskaton, Dhaka, on 24 April 2025, BAIRA members said a vested-interest group was obstructing the reopening of Malaysia's labour market by raising false allegations of human trafficking and money laundering in Malaysia, calling into question the MoU signed by the two countries and the joint working committee's decisions.
MY3d-15.why_new: Shows BAIRA was split: a faction defending the MoU arrangement. Not in guide.

MY3d-16.claim: A six-member Ministry committee formed on 2 June 2024 found that the failure to send 17,777 workers who had BMET clearance cards lay entirely with the recruiting agencies concerned; its report was filed in the High Court in a writ by Supreme Court lawyer Tanvir Ahmed, and on 27 April 2025 a High Court bench of Justices Fahmida Quader and Mubina Asaf ordered a progress report on the action taken by 27 August 2025.
MY3d-16.why_new: Guide has the 17,777 count but not the committee's finding that agencies were wholly to blame, nor the High Court case.

MY3d-17.claim: The Ministry committee's report says Malaysia allocated Bangladesh a quota of 5,32,162 workers, sending ran from August 2022 to 31 May 2024, the Ministry gave recruitment permission for 5,27,999 workers, agencies took BMET smart cards for 4,93,729, and 17,777 with clearance cards (3.66%) could not go.
MY3d-17.why_new: Exact official quota and clearance figures for 2022-24; the guide says 'about 4.5 lakh'.

MY3d-18.claim: The committee found that some agencies took Ministry recruitment permission but never applied for BMET smart cards for 34,270 workers, which it called clear negligence, and recommended legal action against the agencies, an order to refund at once the money taken from workers who could not go, and settlement under the law of complaints that agencies took more than the Tk 78,990 cap.
MY3d-18.why_new: Committee's refund recommendation and the 34,270 figure not in guide; relevant to stranded workers seeking refunds.

MY3d-19.claim: According to the writ petitioner's lawyer Tanvir Ahmed, at the 27 April 2025 High Court hearing the government side said workers who could not go would be taken to Malaysia on a priority basis, and the court asked to be told what had been done to refund in full those charged more than the fixed Tk 78,990.
MY3d-19.why_new: Court-ordered refund question; not in guide.

MY3d-20.claim: On the night of 10 May 2025 BGB (Border Guard Bangladesh) rescued 14 teenagers and young men from a house in Uttar Lambori, Teknaf Sadar union, Cox's Bazar; BGB said they had been locked in a room there to be trafficked to Malaysia by sea and held hostage to extort money from their families, and no one was arrested.
MY3d-20.target_section: Irregular routes, and where an irregular stay ends
MY3d-20.placement: other: new bullet, sea route via Myanmar
MY3d-20.why_new: Sea-route trafficking hostage houses in Teknaf; not in guide.

MY3d-21.claim: Two of those rescued, Mohammad Kasem and Mohin Uddin of Cox's Bazar town, told Prothom Alo that a CNG auto-rickshaw driver tricked them into the house while they were visiting Inani; they were beaten, Tk 1 lakh each was extorted from their families, and they were still held for 18 days while the captors tried to sell them to brokers for the sea route to Malaysia.
MY3d-21.target_section: Irregular routes, and where an irregular stay ends
MY3d-21.placement: other: new bullet, sea route via Myanmar
MY3d-21.why_new: How the sea-route traffickers capture people (not only volunteers); not in guide.

MY3d-22.claim: Bangladesh Civil Society for Migrants (BCSM), a coalition of 23 organisations including RMMRU and BRAC, said in a statement of 14 May 2025 that the 2021 MoU gave Malaysia the job of selecting agencies, which let a Malaysian company and some Bangladeshi agencies form a syndicate that pushed the cost of sending a worker to Tk 5.5 lakh.
MY3d-22.placement: other: How the 2022-24 syndicate was formed
MY3d-22.why_new: BCSM's 2025 statement; guide cites BCSM only for March 2024.

MY3d-23.claim: BCSM said in May 2025 that before the syndicate some Malaysian companies took workers from Bangladesh at the employer's cost, but could no longer do so, and that some who went earlier found no job and lived half-starved abroad or on money sent from home.
MY3d-23.why_new: Claim that employer-pays recruitment was crowded out by the syndicate; complements BOESL officials' account in the guide.

MY3d-24.claim: BCSM's recommendations of May 2025 to the delegation in Malaysia led by the expatriates' welfare adviser, Asif Nazrul, were that Malaysia be persuaded to take Bangladeshi workers by the same process as from its 14 other source countries, that cost be cut and a job on arrival guaranteed, and that a letter be sent to Malaysia's Prime Minister to drop one clause of the MoU.
MY3d-24.why_new: Civil-society position in 2025 negotiations; low priority context.

MY3d-25.claim: A three-member delegation led by the expatriates' welfare adviser, Asif Nazrul, with senior secretary Neyamat Ullah Bhuiyan and deputy secretary Md Sarwar Alam, went to Malaysia on 13 May 2025 to meet Malaysia's human resources and home ministers about reopening; Ministry officials said Bangladesh would propose at the joint technical committee that all legal agencies be allowed to send workers, and that since the MoU ran to December there was no scope for a new agreement, only for amending the existing one.
MY3d-25.why_new: 2025 negotiation timeline absent from Status (which jumps from May 2024 to June 2026). MoU 'to December' conflicts with the April 2025 article's 'August 2026' and agrees with guide's 31 December 2026.

MY3d-26.claim: Prothom Alo reported in May 2025 that more than 4 lakh workers went in 2007-08 before the first closure, about 3 lakh in 2017-18 before the second, and about 5 lakh from August 2022 to May 2024; about 13 lakh Bangladeshi workers went to Malaysia from 2004 to May 2024, the most in a single year in 2023, more than 3.5 lakh.
MY3d-26.why_new: Adds the 2017-18 surge (about 3 lakh) before the 2018 closure; the guide says about 2 lakh went through the 10 agencies. 2022-24: about 5 lakh here vs 4.5 lakh in guide.

MY3d-27.claim: Prothom Alo reported in May 2025 that Malaysia had taken workers from 14 countries but closed its labour market to all of them, Bangladesh included, at the start of 2024, amid allegations of a syndicate in sending workers.
MY3d-27.why_new: Minor: confirms closure applied to all source countries; guide has this via MA0003. Low priority.

MY3d-28.claim: After meeting Malaysia's home, human resources and trade ministers on 15 May 2025, the adviser Asif Nazrul said in a Facebook video that Malaysia might take 1 to 1.5 lakh foreign workers in the coming months, that human resources minister Steven Sim Chee Keong had assured Bangladesh top priority, and that Bangladesh had asked that all its recruiting agencies be allowed to send workers, which Malaysia said it would consider.
MY3d-28.why_new: 2025 negotiation step not in guide's Status.

MY3d-29.claim: Asif Nazrul said on 15 May 2025 that Malaysia had confirmed the first batch of 7,926 workers who could not go would be taken and that the process had begun; the Malaysian Prime Minister had promised during his 2024 visit to Bangladesh to let those workers go.
MY3d-29.why_new: Conflict: guide says Malaysia cleared 7,873 [YI0011]; this says 7,926 in the first batch (May 2025).

MY3d-30.claim: On 15 May 2025 Bangladesh proposed that Malaysia take skilled workers including security guards, nurses and caregivers, Asif Nazrul said.
MY3d-30.target_section: Skill tests and narrower job orders
MY3d-30.why_new: Proposal only; guide has nothing on these job types. Low priority.

MY3d-31.claim: On 15 May 2025 Asif Nazrul said Bangladeshi workers got single-entry visas and that he had asked Malaysia's home minister to give them multiple-entry visas like other countries' workers, and the minister told his officials to act quickly.
MY3d-31.target_section: Going home on leave and coming back
MY3d-31.placement: other: history of the multiple-entry visa
MY3d-31.why_new: Background to the multiple-entry visa the guide says is now included with renewal [H0027]; shows it is new since 2025.

MY3d-32.claim: Asked on 15 May 2025 to legalise undocumented Bangladeshi workers, Malaysia replied that it does so from time to time, last in the previous year, but cannot for those whose visas have expired; Bangladesh asked it to consider them too, since workers often cannot renew because of the employer, and Malaysia said it would consider it.
MY3d-32.target_section: What running away or an expired pass does to you
MY3d-32.placement: other: Buying your way back to legal
MY3d-32.why_new: Possible conflict: guide says the last legalisation (RTK) ended 31 December 2023; Malaysia here said 'last year' (2024). Also: expired-visa holders excluded.

MY3d-33.claim: On 19 May 2025 a press conference called by a BAIRA faction at the Dhaka Reporters Unity was preceded by fighting in which former BAIRA joint secretary general Mohammad Fakhrul Islam and others were injured; Fakhrul Islam alleged the attackers were linked to the old syndicate and came on the orders of Ruhul Amin Swapan and Kazi Rafiq, and the accused BAIRA members held a rival press conference.
MY3d-33.placement: other: Objections and allegations, new dated bullet (19 May 2025)
MY3d-33.why_new: Shows the violence around the syndicate dispute and names Kazi Rafiq; not in guide.

MY3d-34.claim: The Fakhrul Islam faction demanded on 19 May 2025 that two clauses of the MoU be scrapped or amended at the joint technical committee so that Malaysian employers, rather than Malaysia's government, could choose Bangladeshi recruiting agencies; at the rival press conference Mezbah Uddin Sayeed, a director of Instance International Limited, said there had been no syndicate and that the name was hype, and Al Akaba Associates' proprietor Atikur Rahman Atik called the other faction Awami League collaborators trying to close the market.
MY3d-34.placement: other: Objections and allegations, new dated bullet (19 May 2025)
MY3d-34.why_new: Specific MoU change demanded (employer chooses agency) and the counter-claim; not in guide.

MY3d-35.claim: At the opening of the two countries' joint working group meeting at the InterContinental hotel, Dhaka, on 21 May 2025, the Chief Adviser's special envoy Lutfey Siddiqi said Malaysia wanted to take workers through a limited number of agencies because Bangladesh has so many, that amending the MoU would be discussed if needed for transparency, and that Malaysia had set no conditions, including withdrawal of the cases against those who formed the syndicate.
MY3d-35.why_new: Malaysia's stated reason for limiting agencies (the root of the 25-agency list) and the denial of conditions; not in guide.

MY3d-36.claim: Lutfey Siddiqi said on 21 May 2025 that about 8,000 workers who had completed every procedure but could not go when the market closed would go first, sent quickly through BOESL under government management.
MY3d-36.why_new: Dates the decision to route the stranded workers through BOESL to May 2025; guide has the August 2025 notice and the 7,873 figure.

MY3d-37.claim: In a 13-point proposal handed to the foreign adviser on 21 May 2025, the AB Party (Amar Bangladesh Party) demanded that passport renewal be completed within seven days with courier delivery, and that the corruption and syndicate 'in the name of business' at ESKL in Malaysia be stopped and the service decentralised under the High Commission's control.
MY3d-37.target_section: How long you can stay and renewing
MY3d-37.why_new: Guide mentions ESKL's RM32 charge [Z0020] but not complaints about it. A political party's allegation only.

MY3d-38.claim: On 25 May 2025 Dhaka senior special judge Md Zakir Hossain barred from leaving the country, at the ACC's request, ten people linked to the Malaysia labour market whom the ACC said were trying to flee abroad while it investigated overcharging and money laundering: Nizam Hazari and his wife Nurjahan Begum, Snigdha Overseas owners Sheikh Abdullah and M Amirul Islam, Catharsis International's managing director Mohammad Ruhul Amin, Unique Eastern's managing director Noor Ali, Nasir Uddin Ahmed and Khondoker Shawkat Hossain, BM Travels' chairman Shafiqul Islam, and BNS Overseas' managing director Ishtiaque Ahmed.
MY3d-38.why_new: Travel ban of May 2025 not in the guide's case timeline.

MY3d-39.claim: In a rejoinder to Prothom Alo on 24 June 2025 the Ministry said Malaysia's market had been closed since June 2024, that several joint working group and high-level meetings had been held, that it hoped the market would reopen soon by a transparent, broker-free method, and that a proposal for a joint, technology-based recruitment process was at its final stage.
MY3d-39.why_new: Ministry's June 2025 position; not in guide. Low priority.

MY3d-40.claim: In its rejoinder of 24 June 2025 the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare said the government was continuing a 2% cash incentive for money sent through banking channels and had stepped up surveillance of hundi.
MY3d-40.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: How do I send money home safely?
MY3d-40.why_new: Conflict: the cross-country guide (and the Malaysia guide) give a 2.5% government incentive; the Ministry said 2% in June 2025.

MY3d-41.claim: Malaysia's home minister, Saifuddin Nasution Ismail, said on 27 June 2025 that police had arrested 36 Bangladeshis on allegations of direct involvement in a 'radical militant movement', in three phases of operations in Selangor and Johor from 24 April 2025; five were charged under 6A of Malaysia's Penal Code, which applies to terrorism-related offences, at the Shah Alam and Johor Bahru sessions courts, removal orders were issued for 15, and 16 were still under investigation.
MY3d-41.target_section: NEW: Militancy and terrorism charges (after What can get you jailed or deported > Drugs)
MY3d-41.placement: other: new H4 under What can get you jailed or deported
MY3d-41.why_new: Guide has nothing on terrorism/militancy arrests of Bangladeshi workers.

MY3d-42.claim: The home minister said police found the group, inspired by Islamic State ideology, had formed a cell to spread extremism within its own community, radicalise people, raise money for terrorist activities and work to overthrow the legitimate government of its home country.
MY3d-42.target_section: NEW: Militancy and terrorism charges (after What can get you jailed or deported > Drugs)
MY3d-42.why_new: What the cell was accused of; not in guide.

MY3d-43.claim: Malaysia's police chief, Khalid Ismail, told a press conference in Kuala Lumpur on 4 July 2025, as reported by Reuters and citing intelligence, that the ring targeted other Bangladeshi workers to recruit members and spread extremist ideology through social media and online messaging platforms, that those detained sent money to Islamic State in Syria and Bangladesh, and that 100 to 150 people might be involved; those less involved would be sent home and those deeply involved dealt with under Malaysian law.
MY3d-43.target_section: NEW: Militancy and terrorism charges (after What can get you jailed or deported > Drugs)
MY3d-43.why_new: How recruitment of workers into the cell worked, per police; not in guide.

MY3d-44.claim: The expatriates' welfare adviser, Asif Nazrul, told Prothom Alo on the night of 4 July 2025 that three of the arrested workers had already returned to Bangladesh and were being questioned, that everyone returned on this allegation would be questioned, and that those against whom proof of involvement was found would be put on trial.
MY3d-44.target_section: NEW: Militancy and terrorism charges (after What can get you jailed or deported > Drugs)
MY3d-44.why_new: What happens on return to Bangladesh after deportation on such charges; not in guide.

MY3d-45.claim: Bangladesh's foreign ministry said on 5 July 2025 that the High Commission in Kuala Lumpur contacted Malaysian authorities right after the arrests, that Bangladesh had formally asked for the identities of those held and the charges against them, that it would cooperate fully with Malaysia's investigation, and that the High Commission would give Bangladeshis the help they needed.
MY3d-45.target_section: NEW: Militancy and terrorism charges (after What can get you jailed or deported > Drugs)

MY3d-46.claim: Malaysia's police chief said all those detained had been working in factories, construction and services in Malaysia.
MY3d-46.target_section: NEW: Militancy and terrorism charges (after What can get you jailed or deported > Drugs)
MY3d-46.why_new: Confirms those arrested were ordinary workers; not in guide.

MY3d-47.claim: Bangladesh High Commission sources in Kuala Lumpur said in July 2025 that the Royal Malaysia Police counter-terrorism division had arrested 35, not 36, Bangladeshis between April and June 2025; 14 of them had overstayed their visas and were handed to immigration, six of whom had been sent back to Bangladesh, five were charged with terrorism offences, and 16 were under further investigation.
MY3d-47.target_section: NEW: Militancy and terrorism charges (after What can get you jailed or deported > Drugs)
MY3d-47.why_new: Conflict between Malaysian (36) and High Commission (35) counts; shows overstayers arrested in such raids are handed to immigration and deported.

MY3d-48.claim: The five charged were held in two prisons, two in Selangor and three in Johor Bahru, and High Commission officials were due to visit them on 9 July 2025 to give consular service after the prison authorities gave permission, to learn whether they needed legal or other basic help.
MY3d-48.target_section: NEW: Militancy and terrorism charges (after What can get you jailed or deported > Drugs)
MY3d-48.why_new: How consular access to a jailed Bangladeshi works in practice; complements 'After arrest'.

MY3d-49.claim: A diplomatic source said in July 2025 that the High Commission had contacted Malaysia's foreign, home and human resources ministries from the start for help over the 35 Bangladeshis arrested in the counter-terrorism raids but had not received the expected response, and had not been told at the time that a counter-terrorism operation was under way.
MY3d-49.placement: other: what consular help reaches people
MY3d-49.why_new: Evidence on the limits of consular help after arrest; guide's After arrest gives only the consular line.

MY3d-50.claim: Farhad Hossain alias Rony, 31, of Baguri village, Kayba union, Sharsha upazila, Jashore, who went to Malaysia in January 2023 at a cost of Tk 5 lakh, which his father borrowed, and worked as a labourer for a construction company in Seremban, was killed on 5 July 2025 when a crane chain snapped and he was crushed under it; his family said Bangladeshi workers there were trying to bring the body home, and his father said the loan had not yet been fully repaid.
