MY3d-50.h2: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job

MY3d-51.claim: The father of Farhad Hossain, killed on a Seremban construction site in July 2025 two and a half years after going to Malaysia on a Tk 5 lakh loan, said the loan had still not been fully repaid.
MY3d-51.why_new: Case evidence that a Tk 5 lakh debt was unpaid after 2.5 years; supports the 21-22 month to 3 year range.

MY3d-52.claim: Asif Nazrul said on 15 July 2025 that a circular signed on behalf of Malaysia's Immigration Director General and issued on 10 July 2025 gave Bangladeshi workers multiple-entry visas: workers already issued a single-entry visa and a PLKS (temporary employment visit pass) before the circular need not apply, the multiple-entry visa is issued automatically when the PLKS is renewed, workers with a single-entry visa and a valid PLKS can travel home and back without a new multiple visa, and instructions were sent to all of Malaysia's international airports and land ports.
MY3d-52.target_section: Going home on leave and coming back
MY3d-52.placement: other: source and how it works
MY3d-52.why_new: Guide states the rule [H0027] but not that a valid PLKS alone suffices before renewal, nor the 10 July 2025 circular date; partly answers the guide's Need to know on checking the visa.

MY3d-53.claim: Asif Nazrul said that of the 15 countries Malaysia takes workers from, only Bangladeshi workers had been given single-entry rather than multiple-entry visas before July 2025, causing them much hardship.
MY3d-53.target_section: Going home on leave and coming back
MY3d-53.why_new: Background; source count 15 countries conflicts with 14 in other articles (minor).

MY3d-54.claim: The adviser Asif Nazrul said on 2 August 2025 that some Bangladeshis in Malaysia had messaged him complaining that undocumented workers there could not become legal while more people were being brought from Bangladesh.
MY3d-54.target_section: What running away or an expired pass does to you
MY3d-54.placement: other: Buying your way back to legal
MY3d-54.why_new: Minor: confirms no regularisation route in mid-2025; consistent with guide.

MY3d-55.claim: Prothom Alo reported on 9 August 2025 that Chief Adviser Muhammad Yunus was to make a three-day visit to Malaysia from 11 August and meet Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim in Putrajaya on Tuesday 12 August, that five MoUs (on defence, energy, BIISS-ISIS, BMCCI-MIMOS and business chambers) and three exchange notes (halal ecosystem, foreign service academies, higher education) might be signed, and that a senior foreign ministry official said removing Bangladeshis' problems in Malaysia's labour market and taking more workers would get priority.
MY3d-55.why_new: The August 2025 summit is absent from the guide's Status timeline. 'None concerned labour' is read from the listed MoUs (defence, energy, BIISS-ISIS, BMCCI-MIMOS, FBCCI).

MY3d-56.claim: At the Chief Adviser's meeting with Bangladeshis in Kuala Lumpur on 12 August 2025, the problems discussed included more staff at the mission, a 'graduate plus' visa for Bangladeshi students, and regularising those who had become irregular.
MY3d-56.why_new: Shows Bangladeshi students lacked a post-study visa in August 2025 and regularisation was unresolved; consistent with guide.

MY3d-57.claim: BCSM said in a statement of 12 August 2025, signed by its chair Tasneem Siddiqui and co-chair Syed Saiful Haque, that news reports said three former MPs linked to the syndicate, including the family of former finance minister A H M Mustafa Kamal (Lotus Kamal), were being freed from the allegations, and that Malaysiakini had reported Bangladesh agreed to Malaysia's request to suspend the investigation into the syndicate; BCSM demanded no impunity, a fresh and judicial investigation, and public reporting of the ACC's progress.
MY3d-57.why_new: Reported move in August 2025 to drop charges and suspend investigation, against the guide's case timeline (which shows cases continuing). Links with the guide's April 2025 Malaysian letter asking Bangladesh to withdraw allegations.

MY3d-58.claim: BCSM said in August 2025 that, according to the government's white paper on the economy, press reports and ACC allegations, each worker sent to Malaysia in 2022, 2023 and 2024 was charged five to six times the government-fixed cost, and that a syndicate of ten operated in 2017 and 2018 without anyone ever being tried.
MY3d-58.why_new: Adds the government white paper as a source for the five-to-six-times overcharge.

SA3e-1.claim: In January 2026 Bangladesh's interim government set a special Biman Bangladesh Airlines fare for migrant workers of at least Tk 20,500 one way on the Madinah-Dhaka and Jeddah-Dhaka routes and Tk 42,000 return on Madinah-Dhaka-Madinah and Jeddah-Dhaka-Jeddah, according to the Chief Adviser's press wing.
SA3e-1.target_section: Going home on leave and coming back
SA3e-1.why_new: Guide has no cheap-fare scheme for workers going home on leave.

SA3e-2.claim: The special fare applied to travel to Bangladesh from 18 April to 25 May 2026 and back to Saudi Arabia from 30 May to 30 June 2026, using flights that the civil aviation adviser said usually return empty during Hajj, with a target of 80,000 tickets sold in Saudi Arabia and Bangladesh combined.
SA3e-2.target_section: Going home on leave and coming back
SA3e-2.why_new: Dates and size of the scheme; a reviewer may want a Need to know on whether it will run again in the 2027 Hajj season.

SA3e-3.claim: Prothom Alo reported in February 2026 that Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Qatar, the UAE and several other Middle Eastern countries do not let foreigners with HIV stay, under their immigration and public health laws or residence regulations.

SA3e-4.claim: According to the same February 2026 report, HIV is usually found in these countries at the compulsory medical check for work-permit renewal or when a sick worker goes to hospital, after which the visa is cancelled and the worker is quickly sent home; in one case a Bangladeshi construction worker in an unnamed Middle Eastern country had his visa cancelled within a few days of testing positive and was quickly sent home, with no chance to discuss a treatment plan or counselling.
SA3e-4.why_new: Guide doesn't say a medical is part of permit renewal or what an HIV finding does.

SA3e-5.claim: Tasneem Siddiqui, acting executive director of RMMRU, a non-governmental organisation working on migration, told Prothom Alo in February 2026 that in these Middle Eastern countries a woman worker who becomes pregnant is also sent back at once.
SA3e-5.target_section: What can get you jailed or deported
SA3e-5.why_new: Guide covers pregnancy outside marriage as a crime risk (domestic worker, If you are sexually abused) but not deportation on pregnancy generally; attributed expert view, not a rule.

SA3e-6.claim: According to Prothom Alo (February 2026), the Bangladesh government supplies antiretroviral (ARV) drugs free, but counselling, mental health support and livelihood rehabilitation for returnees are very limited; Mir of the youth organisation Brave Dimension Global said one deported worker got counselling not from any government agency but from a private organisation.
SA3e-6.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: What help is there when I come back?
SA3e-6.why_new: Cross-country: help for returnees deported with HIV.

SA3e-7.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: What is the pre-departure orientation (PDO)?

SA3e-8.claim: According to the national AIDS/STD control programme of Bangladesh's Directorate General of Health Services, 1,891 people were found infected with HIV in Bangladesh from December 2024 to November 2025, 12% of them people who had come back from abroad.
SA3e-8.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: What help is there when I come back?
SA3e-8.why_new: Statistic; keep only if the HIV item is added.

SA3e-9.claim: For Bangladesh's 12 February 2026 national election, the first in which Bangladeshis abroad could vote (by postal ballot), more than 239,000 Bangladeshis in Saudi Arabia registered, according to Election Commission figures; in the UK, voting required an NID card, biometric registration at the High Commission and then a mobile app.
SA3e-9.target_section: Renewing your passport and getting an NID
SA3e-9.why_new: Guide says nothing about voting from Saudi Arabia; the NID step links it to this section. Low priority.

SA3e-10.claim: On 15 February 2026 five Bangladeshis from Ramganj, Lakshmipur, died when their private car crashed in Abha on the way home after Umrah: Mizanur Rahman (42), who had long run a hotel business in Abha, his wife, two daughters and their driver Mohammad Jilani alias Babor (30); an 11-year-old daughter was seriously injured.
SA3e-10.why_new: Road-death case; guide has crash liability (Driving) but no cases. Low priority.

SA3e-11.claim: Saudi ambassador Abdullah Zafer H. bin Abiyah told Bangladesh's foreign minister on 22 February 2026 that Saudi Arabia issued 750,000 work visas and 1.4 million visas in all to Bangladeshis in 2025, and that ongoing development work there means more jobs for skilled and semi-skilled workers.
SA3e-11.why_new: Saudi-side visa count; guide gives BMET departures (755,194 in 2025, SB0017). Different measure, close figure; no real conflict.

SA3e-12.claim: On 23 February 2026 Mehedi Hasan (25) of Brahmanpara, Cumilla, whose flight to Saudi Arabia was due at 1:20 pm, had to leave for Saudi Arabia without burying his 14-year-old brother, who died that morning in a crash of the microbus taking him to Dhaka airport, because, his uncle said, his visa had no time left.
SA3e-12.target_section: When to pay, when to fly, and Hajj-season pauses
SA3e-12.why_new: Shows the pressure of a visa near expiry at departure. Low priority; reviewer may drop.

SA3e-13.claim: In early March 2026 Lokman Hossain (35) of Madaripur, a super-shop worker who has lived in Riyadh for a decade, told Prothom Alo that panic spread when the US embassy in Saudi Arabia was hit by a drone, and that Bangladeshis were still working but in fear.
SA3e-13.why_new: Guide mentions the Iran war only for flights. Low priority.

SA3e-14.claim: Mofizur Rahman (65) of Patiya, Chattogram, who had worked in Makkah for 12 years at whatever job he found and last came home in 2009, was hit by a car walking home from Tarawih prayers on 9 March 2026 and died in hospital; his kafil confirmed the death to the family and, at his dying request to the kafil, he was to be buried in Makkah.

SA3e-22.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Which countries can I go to for work right now?

SA3e-25.claim: Abdullah Al Mamun's body reached Dhaka on a Saudi Airlines flight on 6 April 2026, and the expatriates' welfare minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury received it at the airport.
SA3e-25.target_section: If a worker dies in Saudi Arabia
SA3e-25.why_new: Timeline for a war death's repatriation.
SA3e-25.h2: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job

SA3e-26.claim: For Abdullah Al Mamun's funeral in April 2026, the Wage Earners' Welfare Board gave his family Tk 35,000 and Tk 50,000 in cash on the spot, with Tk 3 lakh in financial aid to follow.
SA3e-26.placement: other: what was paid in practice
SA3e-26.why_new: Guide has the Tk 35,000 cheque and Tk 3 lakh grant but not an extra Tk 50,000 cash payment, which may be war-specific.
SA3e-26.h2: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job

SA3e-27.claim: Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury said on 6 April 2026 that seven deaths of Bangladeshis from the Middle East war had been reported, four bodies had been received in Bangladesh and one had been buried in Saudi Arabia with the family's consent.
SA3e-27.why_new: Region-wide war death count; RMMRU gave 'at least 9' on 13 May 2026 (A24).

SA3e-28.claim: In the first week of March 2026 the Bangladesh embassy in Riyadh asked Bangladeshis, out of respect for Saudi law, not to upload photos or videos of the war on social media, or to post, share, like or comment on war news.
SA3e-28.target_section: What can get you jailed or deported
SA3e-28.why_new: Gives a concrete online act to avoid; partly answers the guide's Need to know on which online acts count as crimes.

SA3e-29.claim: Two Bangladeshis in Makkah and Jeddah told Prothom Alo in March 2026 that early panic had largely eased and people in Makkah, Madinah and Jeddah were going to work, and, citing acquaintances, that areas in the east, especially on the Gulf coast, were tense and Riyadh was on extra alert.
SA3e-29.why_new: Regional picture during the war. Low priority.

SA3e-30.claim: According to expatriates' welfare ministry statistics reported in March 2026, about 20 lakh (2 million) Bangladeshi workers are in Saudi Arabia.
SA3e-30.why_new: Guide gives departures but no stock of Bangladeshi workers in Saudi Arabia.

SA3e-31.claim: A Bangladesh Bank report showed USD 1.31 billion of remittances came from Saudi Arabia in the October-December second quarter of what the article calls the current 2026-27 fiscal year, the most of the six Gulf countries, ahead of the UAE at USD 1.18 billion.
SA3e-31.why_new: Guide has no quarterly Saudi remittance figure. Article's fiscal-year label looks wrong (published March 2026).

SA3e-32.claim: Prothom Alo reported in March 2026, without naming a source, that 743,000 of the 1,116,000 Bangladeshis who went abroad for work in 2025 went to Saudi Arabia.
SA3e-32.why_new: CONFLICT: guide says 755,194 went to Saudi Arabia in 2025 (SB0017).

SA3e-33.claim: The Bangladesh embassy in Riyadh announced on Monday 23 March 2026 that the fine-free exit until 18 April 2026 covered all kinds of visit visa, Umrah visas, transit visas and final exit visas whose validity had passed 25 February, and warned that anyone not leaving by then could face serious legal trouble and punishment.
SA3e-33.why_new: Guide (E0087) lists visit, Umrah and final exit; adds transit visas. Otherwise duplicate.

SA3e-34.claim: Fahim Ahmed Munna (20) of Dowarabazar, Sunamganj, whose father has worked in Saudi Arabia for 18 years, left home on 16 February 2026, spent two days in Saudi Arabia, was taken to Libya and put on a small rubber boat (a 'game') on 21 March, and died of hunger and thirst at sea, his uncle said; he had been sent through a relative acting as dalal.
SA3e-34.target_section: Irregular routes and how they end
SA3e-34.placement: other: Saudi as a transit to Libya
SA3e-34.why_new: Saudi Arabia used as a stepping stone to Libya; not in guide.

SA3e-35.claim: According to a survivor from Fahim's area, the boat carrying 38 people from Libya lost its way and drifted six days; 18 died for lack of food and clean water, their bodies were kept on the boat two days and then thrown into the sea, and the survivors were taken to a camp after the boat reached the Greek coast on 27 March 2026.
SA3e-35.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Libya to Italy by boat
SA3e-35.why_new: Libya-Greece crossing deaths; the headline says 12 of the dead were from Sunamganj.

SA3e-36.claim: Azgar Bepari (38) of Dohar, Dhaka, who went to Saudi Arabia through a dalal on borrowed money three and a half years earlier and had worked illegally for a year as a welder's helper, fell from a roof in Hara, Riyadh, on 24 March 2026 and died in hospital; his sister-in-law said the family had heard bringing the body home would cost Tk 4 lakh, which they could not pay.
SA3e-36.target_section: If a worker dies in Saudi Arabia
SA3e-36.why_new: Undocumented death case with a cost families hear quoted; guide says only that it takes longer.
SA3e-36.h2: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job

SA3e-37.claim: Azgar Bepari's sister-in-law told Prothom Alo (reported 1 April 2026) that he had paid money for his iqama twice without getting it.
SA3e-37.target_section: Irregular routes and how they end
SA3e-37.why_new: Another case of the guide's 'kafil who keeps the renewal money' (SL0028).

SA3e-38.claim: The Dohar UNO said, in a report published 1 April 2026, that if someone contacts the Bangladesh embassy in Riyadh on the dead worker's behalf, it will arrange to send the body home with government help.
SA3e-38.target_section: If a worker dies in Saudi Arabia
SA3e-38.why_new: Official's statement for an undocumented worker; consistent with guide's Welfare-2 route.
SA3e-38.h2: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job

SA3e-39.claim: Mohammad Jalal Uddin Sikder of North South University wrote in a Prothom Alo opinion piece in April 2026 that during the Iran war many migrant workers were being detained or sent home after being accused of sharing war videos or photos on social media.
SA3e-39.target_section: What can get you jailed or deported
SA3e-39.why_new: Opinion piece, region-wide, not Saudi-specific; supports the embassy warning in A11.

SA3e-40.claim: According to BMET figures cited in Prothom Alo in April 2026, 919,981 (about 82.4%) of the 1,116,399 Bangladeshis who went abroad in 2025 went to the Middle East or GCC countries, and according to Bangladesh Bank about 46% (USD 15.07 billion) of USD 32.8 billion remittances in 2025 came from GCC countries.
SA3e-40.why_new: Regional context; better cross-country. Conflicts with the 1,130,757 total in A8.

SA3e-41.claim: The expatriates' welfare minister told parliament on 5 April 2026 that Bangladesh's agreement with Saudi Arabia secures a woman domestic worker's right to keep a mobile phone, so she can alert her family, the embassy or the ministry at any time.
SA3e-41.why_new: Target is the domestic-worker 'Your rights at work' (under Work visa: domestic worker). Guide says the employer must let her contact family and embassy (D0010) but not that the agreement guarantees a phone.

SA3e-42.claim: The expatriates' welfare minister told parliament on 5 April 2026 that 1,132,519 workers went abroad in 2025, 62,352 of them women, and that more than 1.5 crore (15 million) Bangladeshis work in 176 countries.
SA3e-42.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: How many women work abroad?
SA3e-42.why_new: Cross-country figures; conflict on the 2025 total (1,130,757 in A8, 1,116,399 in A18).

SA3e-43.claim: The Prime Minister's spokesman Mahdi Amin said on 18 April 2026 that the cost of Hajj travel had been cut by Tk 12,000 per ticket.
SA3e-43.why_new: Guide gives 2027 package prices, which may already include this; check.

SA3e-44.claim: The Prime Minister's spokesman said on 18 April 2026 that the government had begun work on a 'Probashi card' for migrants; no details were given.
SA3e-44.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: What help is there when I come back?
SA3e-44.why_new: Announcement only; a reviewer could turn it into a Need to know.

SA3e-45.claim: Murad Sheikh (34) of Goalanda, Rajbari, who went to Saudi Arabia about a year earlier through his brother Atikur working there, died in a road accident; his brother said the company gave no help and the body came home on 9 May 2026, 15 days later, paid for privately by a Goalanda expatriate named Hussain with help from the Bangladesh embassy.
SA3e-45.target_section: If a worker dies in Saudi Arabia
SA3e-45.why_new: Case where the employer did not pay to send the body home, though the guide says Saudi rules make it the employer's cost (E0135).
SA3e-45.h2: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job

SA3e-46.claim: At a press conference on 13 May 2026, RMMRU quoted a packaging worker at the warehouse of an app-based delivery company in Saudi Arabia as saying the warehouse had over 400 workers and now only 65, the rest laid off as sales fell, and said Gulf workers faced heavy wage cuts and higher living costs and airfares.
SA3e-46.why_new: War-time layoffs and wage cuts in Saudi Arabia; not in guide.

SA3e-47.claim: RMMRU said on 13 May 2026 that at least 9 workers had died in the Gulf and Middle East because of the war and that emigration clearances in March 2026 were 50% below March 2025.
SA3e-47.why_new: Region-wide; conflicts with the minister's 7 deaths on 6 April (A20), likely a later count.

SA3e-48.claim: Nure Alam (42) and Yunus Mia (43) of Cumilla, friends who ran a business together in Riyadh, died in a head-on collision at Afif on the Jeddah-Riyadh highway on the night of Friday 15 May 2026 while bringing shop goods from Jeddah, a relative said.

SA3e-49.claim: Ripon Mia (37) of Madan, Netrokona, who went to Saudi Arabia in October 2025 to work for a private company, was killed near Madinah in May 2026 when a lorry hit his taxi; with little work for a few days he had set out to visit an acquaintance, his family said, and the official acting as Kendua upazila's UNO said the papers had been collected and the expatriates' welfare ministry contacted to bring the body home.
SA3e-49.target_section: If a worker dies in Saudi Arabia
SA3e-49.why_new: Case showing the upazila office collecting papers for repatriation. Low priority.
SA3e-49.h2: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job

SA3e-50.claim: Lal Mia (54) of Shalikha, Magura, said he paid a broker Tk 1.3 lakh in 2002 to go to Saudi Arabia but could not go, then paid brokers Tk 2.5 lakh for Malaysia in 2006, Tk 3 lakh for Malaysia in 2010 and Tk 3.6 lakh for Dubai in 2012, about Tk 10.5 lakh over the four attempts, selling four bighas of farmland and 12.5 decimals of homestead, and never went abroad or got the money back.
SA3e-50.why_new: Old case (2002), mainly cross-country (repeat victims). Low priority.

SA3e-51.claim: Shakil Mia (28) of Kishoreganj went to Saudi Arabia in 2019 on borrowed money through Altab Recruiting Agency of Banani, Dhaka, left his workplace because of complications with his employer over his iqama (work permit), and was arrested by Saudi police while working illegally and jailed, his uncle said.
SA3e-51.target_section: If you or a relative is arrested

SA3e-52.claim: From jail Shakil told his family he needed about Tk 2 lakh for bail to come home, and his father said they borrowed and sent about Tk 1.8 lakh to a lawyer in Saudi Arabia; Shakil died in custody on 15 May 2026 after, his family said, an air conditioner exploded and the smoke left him unable to breathe.
SA3e-52.target_section: If you or a relative is arrested
SA3e-52.why_new: What families actually pay for bail and a lawyer; guide has a Need to know on legal help.

SA3e-53.claim: Shakil's father said bringing the body home needed about SR 8,000, which the family did not have; after Shariful Alam, MP for Kishoreganj-6 and state minister for textiles and jute, intervened, the body came back with government help on a Biman flight that reached Dhaka around midnight on 12 June 2026 and reached his home on 13 June, 28 days after the death.
SA3e-53.target_section: If a worker dies in Saudi Arabia
SA3e-53.why_new: Cost quoted to a family of a worker who died in custody; guide has no figure.
SA3e-53.h2: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job

SA3e-54.claim: The assistant director of the Faridpur Probashi Kallyan (expatriate welfare) Centre said in June 2026 that in such cases the company usually sends the body home and gives other help, that the Bangladesh government gives Tk 3 lakh after the body arrives, and that if the company won't, the government brings the body home on the family's application.
SA3e-54.target_section: If a worker dies in Saudi Arabia
SA3e-54.why_new: Partly answers the Need to know 'When does the Board or the ministry pay instead of the employer?'; also names district welfare centres as a contact. Case: Gias Uddin Shikder (60), farm worker in Al-Jouf, killed crossing a road.
SA3e-54.h2: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job

SA3e-55.claim: Civil aviation minister Afroza Khanam told parliament on 18 June 2026 that Biman had set a Tk 20,000 fare for migrant workers on empty Hajj-season return flights from Jeddah and Madinah, against Tk 50,000-55,000 before on the same routes.
SA3e-55.target_section: Going home on leave and coming back
SA3e-55.why_new: Confirms the scheme in A0 and gives the usual fare.

SA3e-56.claim: The minister also said Biman's discounted 'T-class' fares cut Dhaka-Jeddah from Tk 62,000 to Tk 48,000 and Dhaka-Riyadh or Dammam from Tk 53,000 to Tk 48,000.
SA3e-56.why_new: Guide quotes fares of about Tk 48,000-50,000 in May 2025 (G0021); this names the Biman T-class fare.

SA3e-57.claim: Biman's T-class fares announced in parliament on 18 June 2026 also cut Dhaka-Doha from Tk 53,000 to Tk 46,000, Dhaka-Muscat from Tk 39,000 to Tk 30,000 and Dhaka-Kuala Lumpur from Tk 28,000 to Tk 21,000.
SA3e-57.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Who pays for the air ticket?

SA3e-58.claim: The expatriates' welfare minister told parliament on 23 June 2026 that of USD 30.32 billion remittances in fiscal 2024-25, the most, USD 4.26 billion, came from Saudi Arabia.
SA3e-58.why_new: Guide has no yearly remittance figure for Saudi Arabia.

SA3e-59.claim: On 30 June 2026 the Bangladesh embassy in Riyadh relayed on its verified Facebook page the Saudi Ministry of Human Resources and Social Development's call for every work permit (rukhsa amal) expired over 12 months, or not issued over six months after entry or transfer, to be issued or renewed within 2026, warning of legal action otherwise.
SA3e-59.why_new: Guide already has this (G0014-16); adds the Arabic term workers use (rukhsa amal) and the embassy Facebook page as where it was announced.

MY3e-1.claim: On 13 August 2025 Chief Adviser Muhammad Yunus raised a Graduate Plus visa for Bangladeshi students with Malaysia's Higher Education Minister Zambry Abdul Kadir in Kuala Lumpur, and expatriates' welfare adviser Asif Nazrul said afterwards that the minister had agreed in principle but that both sides had formalities to complete before it could take effect.
MY3e-1.placement: Student visa (Student Pass) > Can you work?: other: history of the Graduate Pass claim
MY3e-1.why_new: Origin of the claim the guide calls false [N0034]; CONFLICT with the Malaysian minister's denial of 23 August 2025 (draft from article eba0bf40) and with the guide's line that Bangladesh is not among the Graduate Pass nationalities [S0044].

MY3e-2.claim: Prothom Alo reported in August 2025 that about 10,000 Bangladeshi students were studying at Malaysian universities and that, unlike students of other countries, they had no access to Malaysia's labour market.
MY3e-2.placement: Student visa (Student Pass) > Can you work?
MY3e-2.why_new: Number of Bangladeshi students in Malaysia, not in the guide.

MY3e-3.claim: In a statement on 23 August 2025, Malaysia's Higher Education Minister Zambry Abd Kadir said reports that a 'Graduate Pass' would be given to 10,000 Bangladeshi students in Malaysia to let them work were untrue and baseless, that no such agreement was made during Chief Adviser Muhammad Yunus's visit, and that Malaysia had given no consent.
MY3e-3.target_section: What people believe, and the facts
MY3e-3.placement: other: new bullet or added to "A student visa lets you work."
MY3e-3.why_new: Dated, attributed denial; supports guide's 'claims are false' [N0034] with the source and date. Conflicts with the Bangladeshi adviser's account of 13 August (article 541ee832).

MY3e-4.claim: The claim that 10,000 Bangladeshi students would get jobs in Malaysia had been spread in a 2-minute-19-second TikTok video by Haim Hilman Abdullah, chairman of Kedah state's committee on industry, investment, higher education, science, technology and innovation, whom the minister called irresponsible.
MY3e-4.target_section: What people believe, and the facts
MY3e-4.placement: other: detail for the Graduate Pass belief
MY3e-4.why_new: Where the rumour circulated (TikTok), useful for recognising it.

MY3e-5.claim: Prothom Alo reported in August 2025 that 15,000 workers who had completed every procedure could not go when Malaysia's labour market closed in 2024, and the Ministry's first-year report said an agreement had been signed with Malaysia to send 8,000 workers in an initial phase, which BOESL had taken on at nominal cost.
MY3e-5.placement: What happened to the stranded workers of 2024
MY3e-5.why_new: Adds a sixth stranded count (15,000) to the guide's list (16,970 / 17,777 / 31,304 / 40,000 / 11,000). CONFLICT: 'nominal cost' against the guide's Tk 1,62,500 BOESL charge [YI0011, A0056].

MY3e-6.claim: The same August 2025 Ministry report said that after top-level bilateral talks a process had been started to open Malaysia's market to new workers.
MY3e-6.why_new: Guide's Status timeline jumps from 31 May 2024 to June 2026; adds the August 2025 position.

MY3e-7.claim: The Ministry's first-year report of August 2025 said a multiple-entry visa had been introduced for Bangladeshi workers in Malaysia for the first time.
MY3e-7.target_section: Going home on leave and coming back
MY3e-7.placement: other: date the multiple-entry visa began
MY3e-7.why_new: Guide says the yearly renewal includes a multiple-entry visa [H0027]; this dates it as new in 2025 by the Ministry's account.

MY3e-8.claim: Tasneem Siddiqui, acting executive director of RMMRU, told Prothom Alo in August 2025 that despite various pressures the interim government had not let a syndicate form for sending workers to Malaysia.
MY3e-8.why_new: Researcher's assessment as of August 2025, before the later list of 25.

MY3e-9.claim: Prothom Alo reported in August 2025 that the interim government had shut the private mobile app the previous government had allowed for worker registration and built an integrated online platform for overseas employment, on which emigration clearance is now issued directly.
MY3e-9.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: How do I get BMET clearance?
MY3e-9.why_new: Cross-country doc still describes the Ami Probashi app route for clearance [F0365].

MY3e-10.claim: The Ministry's August 2025 report said a 'Probashi Lounge and Waiting Lounge' had been set up at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, with healthy food at a 30% discount.
MY3e-10.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: Who helps me at the airport?
MY3e-10.why_new: Airport service for all migrants; not in the cross-country doc as far as checked.

MY3e-11.claim: Expatriates' welfare adviser Asif Nazrul wrote in Prothom Alo on 20 August 2025 that after bilateral talks sending workers to Malaysia would start within about a month.
MY3e-11.why_new: A dated promise that did not happen (the guide records no restart until October 2026); shows the pattern of announced restarts.

MY3e-12.claim: On 20 August 2025 the CID said the Dhaka Metropolitan Sessions Judge's Court had, on its Financial Crime division's application, ordered the attachment of about Tk 500 crore of property of Ruhul Amin (Swapan), whom it called the chief of the Malaysia manpower syndicate, and of linked people and firms.
MY3e-12.why_new: Asset seizure not in the guide.

MY3e-13.claim: The CID's statement of 20 August 2025 alleged that Ruhul Amin embezzled Tk 8,000 crore through the syndicate for sending workers to Malaysia and bought houses and land with it, and said the attached property included 231 katha of land in seven deeds in Bashundhara, Banani and Uttara in the name of Catharsis International, deed value Tk 15 crore 55 lakh 33 thousand.
MY3e-13.why_new: CID's Tk 8,000 crore figure differs from the guide's other totals (Tk 24,000 crore, USD 200 crore); it is attributed to Swapan alone.

MY3e-14.claim: The CID said in August 2025 that inquiries were continuing against the other members of the Malaysia syndicate and that action under the money-laundering law would be taken against them too.
MY3e-14.why_new: Precedes the 28 August 2025 CID case already in the guide.

MY3e-15.claim: Expatriates' welfare adviser Asif Nazrul said on 20 August 2025 that the agreement the previous government signed with Malaysia itself says Malaysia will select the agencies, that it cannot be changed by force, and that Bangladesh had told Malaysia in every meeting that all recruiting agencies should get the chance, as in other countries.
MY3e-15.placement: other: the 2021 MoU and agency choice
MY3e-15.why_new: Government's own statement that the MoU gives Malaysia the choice; guide has only BAIRA members saying so [MA0007].

MY3e-16.claim: Asked on 20 August 2025 about Amin Nur, whom Prothom Alo called the main figure of the Malaysia recruitment ring, adviser Asif Nazrul said he works with the Malaysian government, that Bangladesh has nothing to discuss with him, and that talks are held directly with Malaysia's government.
MY3e-16.why_new: Government's position on Amin, not in the guide.

MY3e-17.claim: Asif Nazrul said on 20 August 2025 that when recruitment is given to particular agencies workers are cheated, migration cost rises and many kinds of corruption occur.
MY3e-17.why_new: Official view linking the restricted list to cost; supports the Background mechanism.

MY3e-18.claim: At the same 20 August 2025 press conference, the adviser said an agreement had been signed with Malaysia to send 8,000 workers who could not go in 2024 because the market closed, and that BOESL had taken on sending them at nominal cost.
MY3e-18.placement: What happened to the stranded workers of 2024
MY3e-18.why_new: CONFLICT: 'nominal cost' vs the Tk 1,62,500 BOESL charged in the guide [YI0011]; the guide cites only a column for the 8,000 figure [MA0102].

MY3e-19.claim: The adviser said on 20 August 2025 that the interim government had shut the private app 'Ami Probashi' and that BMET now issues emigration clearance 100% online on the government's own digital platform.
MY3e-19.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: How do I get BMET clearance?
MY3e-19.why_new: Cross-country doc still describes clearance through the Ami Probashi app.

MY3e-20.claim: Malaysia's Home Ministry told parliament, as reported by The Star on 26 August 2025, that 803,332 Bangladeshis held valid work permits at the end of June 2025, 37% of all foreign workers, making Bangladesh the largest source of unskilled foreign workers.
MY3e-20.why_new: Exact official figure and date; guide has 'about 8 lakh at the end of 2025' [U0057].

MY3e-21.claim: By the same Home Ministry figures, 49,353 Bangladeshi workers entered Malaysia in 2022 and 397,548 in 2023.
MY3e-21.why_new: Malaysian entry counts; CONFLICT with BMET's departures cited in the guide (50,000 in 2022, more than 3.5 lakh in 2023 [MA0013]) and with 351,683 for 2023 (article c0f5665e).

MY3e-22.claim: Malaysia's Home Ministry said employers sent 20,331 Bangladeshi workers back home in 2022 and 23,065 in 2023.
MY3e-22.target_section: What goes wrong most, and what people wrongly believe
MY3e-22.placement: other: numbers sent home by employers
MY3e-22.why_new: Official count of workers repatriated by employers; not in the guide.

MY3e-23.claim: Malaysia's Home Ministry said in August 2025 that 790 Bangladeshis who had overstayed their visas or whose work permits had expired had been detained.
MY3e-23.why_new: Official detention figure; the article gives no period.

MY3e-24.claim: A Prothom Alo editorial of 7 September 2025 said Cox's Bazar has become a regular sea route for human trafficking, used from 21 points in Teknaf, Ukhia, Moheshkhali, Cox's Bazar Sadar and other upazilas, and that, besides Rohingya from the camps, traffickers are luring a section of young Bangladeshis onto this unsafe route.
MY3e-24.target_section: Irregular routes, and where an irregular stay ends
MY3e-24.placement: new bullet: by sea from Cox's Bazar
MY3e-24.why_new: The guide has no sea route at all.

MY3e-25.claim: The editorial said trafficking gangs become active after the monsoon and before winter, when the sea is calm.
MY3e-25.target_section: Irregular routes, and where an irregular stay ends

MY3e-26.claim: The editorial said deaths in the Thai jungle on the way to Malaysia, torture by traffickers and deaths when food and water ran out on trawlers have been reported, and that more than 657 Rohingya died on dangerous sea voyages in 2024.
MY3e-26.target_section: Irregular routes, and where an irregular stay ends

MY3e-27.claim: On 14 September 2025 the ACC filed a case against 31 chairmen, managing directors and directors of 13 overseas companies, alleging that, while holding posts in BAIRA, they formed a syndicate, took five times the government-fixed Tk 78,990 from Malaysia-bound workers and embezzled Tk 1,159 crore, its director general Akhtar Hossain said.
MY3e-27.why_new: Guide has only a one-line entry [MA0130]; adds number accused (31), the BAIRA-post allegation and the agencies.

MY3e-28.claim: The 13 companies named in the ACC's 14 September 2025 case are Akash Bhraman, Winner Overseas Limited, Shahin Travels, Navira Limited, Adib Air Travels and Tours, United Manpower Consultancy Limited, Greenland Overseas, PR Overseas Limited, Jaharat Associates Limited, Apurba Recruiting Agency, Jannat Overseas, Midway Overseas Limited and South Point Overseas Limited.
MY3e-28.why_new: Agency names for the 14 September 2025 case, missing from the guide. Note: the quotes cover 9 of 13 names; Apurba, Jannat, Midway and South Point are in the next draft.

MY3e-29.claim: The accused in that case also include A K M Mosharraf Hossain and Mohiuddin Ahmed, directors of Apurba Recruiting Agency; Mohammad Rafiqul Haldar Bhuiyan, chairman of Jannat Overseas; and Manzur Kader, chairman of Midway Overseas Limited and South Point Overseas Limited.
MY3e-29.why_new: PR Overseas (Golam Rakib) and Ananya Apurba's Mohiuddin Ahmed already appear in the guide's 2022-24 senders; this ties them to an ACC case.

MY3e-30.claim: Prothom Alo reported that, with the 14 September 2025 case, the ACC had so far taken legal action in 25 cases against 64 accused over about Tk 2,288 crore of alleged embezzlement, counting earlier cases on similar allegations against 12 companies over about Tk 1,128 crore.
MY3e-30.why_new: Running total not in the guide.

MY3e-31.claim: The BGB's Ramu sector commander, Colonel Md Mohiuddin Ahmed, said on 15 September 2025 that 47 human traffickers had been arrested during trafficking to Malaysia by sea and efforts were under way to catch 21 more who had fled.
MY3e-31.target_section: Irregular routes, and where an irregular stay ends
MY3e-31.why_new: Enforcement numbers on the sea route.

MY3e-32.claim: On 18 September 2025 a Coast Guard and Navy operation rescued 66 people, 44 of them women and children, from a traffickers' den deep in the hills of Kachchhapia, Baharchhara union, Teknaf, where they had been gathered to be trafficked to Malaysia; the Coast Guard said most were Rohingya, some had been lured with promises of a better life in Malaysia and others kidnapped and held while traffickers tried to extract ransom.
MY3e-32.target_section: Irregular routes, and where an irregular stay ends
MY3e-32.why_new: Mechanism: the hill den in Baharchhara, lure or kidnap, ransom.

MY3e-33.claim: Prothom Alo reported in September 2025 that Malaysia has more than 21 lakh foreign workers, over 38% of them (more than 8 lakh) Bangladeshi.
MY3e-33.why_new: Bangladeshi share of the foreign workforce; slightly differs from the Home Ministry's 37% (article 04298691).

MY3e-34.claim: Two young men from Munshiganj Sadar, Amit Hasan and Manik Mia, told Prothom Alo in September 2025 that a Cox's Bazar resident, Md Nur, invited them to visit, took them to his house in Marichya, Ukhia, on 2 September, then put them in an auto-rickshaw on the pretext of a trip to Teknaf and handed them to traffickers, who held them in a hill den to be taken to Thailand by sea and beat them if they tried to phone their families; they were rescued 20 days later.
MY3e-34.target_section: Irregular routes, and where an irregular stay ends
MY3e-34.why_new: A case showing Bangladeshis from outside Cox's Bazar being lured into the sea-route dens.

MY3e-35.claim: In a roughly 12-hour RAB and BGB operation on 21 September 2025 in the hills of Kachchhapia, Baharchhara, Teknaf, 84 people were rescued, 66 of them residents of the Rohingya camps; officials said two had been taken there by force and the rest brought by various lures, many with promises of a better life and jobs in Malaysia and Thailand and some women with promises of marriage, and the Teknaf-2 BGB commander said the traffickers fired at the forces and tried to use some victims as shields.
MY3e-35.target_section: Irregular routes, and where an irregular stay ends

MY3e-36.claim: A young woman rescued in that operation said she was married by mobile phone on 15 September 2025 to a Rohingya man in Malaysia, who told her to meet some people to go to Malaysia by sea; she left the shelter camp on 19 September to meet them, no money was demanded from her, and her 'husband' was to pay something once she reached Malaysia.
MY3e-36.target_section: Irregular routes, and where an irregular stay ends
MY3e-36.placement: same sea-route bullet: how the marriage lure works
MY3e-36.why_new: Payment-on-arrival mechanism of the phone-marriage lure.

MY3e-37.claim: Law-enforcement sources said that by 22 September 2025, 65 human traffickers had been arrested and 161 people rescued in Teknaf that year.
MY3e-37.target_section: Irregular routes, and where an irregular stay ends
MY3e-37.why_new: Running count (superseded by later counts; see the 3 October 2025 draft).

MY3e-38.claim: On 25 September 2025 the BGB rescued three men from Khuniapalong Marichya, Ramu (Robiul Alam, 18, Md Tazim, 18, and Md Ismail, 30) from a hill in Baraitali, Teknaf; the BGB said they had been lured with the promise of being taken to Malaysia by sea via Thailand, that ransom was being sought from their families, and that they were threatened with being sold to a trafficking group in Malaysia if it was not paid.
MY3e-38.target_section: Irregular routes, and where an irregular stay ends
MY3e-38.why_new: Ransom and threat of sale to a Malaysia-based gang.

MY3e-39.claim: Prothom Alo listed recent operations in Teknaf: the BGB detained 12 traffickers and rescued 11 people on 16 September 2025, the Coast Guard rescued 66 on 18 September, RAB and BGB arrested three armed traffickers and rescued 84 on 22 September, five kidnapped people were rescued from the Kachchhapia hills on 23 September, the Coast Guard rescued eight women and children near Jummapara hill in Baharchhara on 1 October, and at midnight on Wednesday 1 October a Coast Guard and Navy team rescued 21 people, including women and children and mostly Rohingya, held for trafficking to Malaysia by sea, near Karachipara ghat in Baharchhara.
MY3e-39.target_section: Irregular routes, and where an irregular stay ends
MY3e-39.why_new: Frequency of the sea-route operations in autumn 2025.

MY3e-40.claim: Law-enforcement agencies had arrested 70 members of trafficking gangs and rescued 239 people, including women and children, in Teknaf in 2025 by 3 October, the day the Coast Guard and Navy rescued 38 more (18 women, 12 men, 8 children, mostly Rohingya) from the hills next to Kachchhapia government primary school; such incidents rise in winter.
MY3e-40.target_section: Irregular routes, and where an irregular stay ends
MY3e-40.why_new: Latest 2025 Teknaf count in the batch.

MY3e-41.claim: A Prothom Alo column of 10 October 2025 by Subail Bin Alam and Shafiqur Rahman put the number of Bangladeshis in Malaysia at about 12 lakh.
MY3e-41.placement: other: estimates of all Bangladeshis in Malaysia
MY3e-41.why_new: Higher than the 8 lakh work-pass holders the guide gives; an estimate of all Bangladeshis, not only pass holders.

MY3e-42.claim: The column said the Election Commission planned to start expatriate voting on a trial basis in Saudi Arabia, Malaysia, the UAE and the UK, first at booths in the missions, with voters registering online in advance and voting on the set day after their passport and NID are checked.
MY3e-42.why_new: Only a plan as of October 2025; low priority for the guide.

MY3e-43.claim: Prothom Alo reported on 29 October 2025 that, after the third Bangladesh-Malaysia Joint Working Group meeting in Dhaka on 21 and 22 May, Malaysia sent Bangladesh its 'recruiting agent selection criteria' on 28 October 2025, and the Ministry's press release said the same criteria would apply in future to Bangladesh, India, Nepal, Pakistan and Myanmar.
MY3e-43.placement: The 2026 list of 25: how it was made
MY3e-43.why_new: Guide says only 'Malaysia set 10 conditions' [MB0044]; adds when and how they came.

MY3e-44.claim: Malaysia's ten conditions for a private agency, as published by the Ministry in October 2025, are at least five years of satisfactory operation since licensing; proof of sending at least 3,000 workers abroad in the last five years; experience in at least three destination countries in that time; valid licences from all relevant Bangladeshi authorities; a good-conduct certificate from the sending country's authority; no record of forced labour, trafficking, labour-law breaches, extortion, money laundering or other financial crime; its own training and assessment centre with accommodation; testimonials from five different foreign employers; a permanent office of at least 10,000 square feet run for at least three years; and proof of lawfully following destination countries' (including Malaysia's) recruitment conditions.
MY3e-44.why_new: The conditions themselves are not in the guide; they explain why few agencies qualify.

MY3e-45.claim: The Ministry asked licensed agencies able to meet the criteria to apply to it with supporting papers by 7 November 2025, and said Bangladesh would ask Malaysia to list every agency meeting them without exception.
MY3e-45.placement: The 2026 list of 25: how it was made
MY3e-45.why_new: Application step leading to the guide's 163/423 counts.

MY3e-46.claim: Malaysia's Home Minister Saifuddin Nasution Ismail said in Kuala Lumpur, as reported by the Malay Mail citing Bernama on 31 October 2025, that the police of the two countries were working on Bangladesh's request to bring back Bestinet's founder Aminul Islam Abdul Nor and his associate Ruhul Amin over money-laundering allegations, through government-to-government and police-to-police coordination agreed with Chief Adviser Yunus during his visit.
MY3e-46.why_new: Guide stops at police seeking extradition in 2024; adds Malaysia's October 2025 position. NOTE: places Swapan in Malaysia, while the guide says he is 'in hiding abroad' [MB0037].

MY3e-47.claim: The arrest request Bangladesh sent, which Malaysia's Home Ministry confirmed receiving in November 2024, accused Aminul Islam and Ruhul Amin of money laundering, extortion and trafficking foreign workers; the minister said then that Malaysia wanted Dhaka to clarify whether the purpose was extradition or further investigation.
MY3e-47.why_new: Charges in the request and Malaysia's hesitation.

MY3e-48.claim: Prothom Alo reported in October 2025 that Aminul Islam, founder and chairman of Bestinet, the company that runs FWCMS, has stepped down as chairman but still holds a stake in it; that it is alleged at least Tk 8,750 crore was laundered out of Bangladesh by a ring in the Malaysia labour market under the Awami League government; and that manpower exporters claim Aminul and his Bangladeshi agent Ruhul Amin led that ring.
MY3e-48.why_new: Amin's current role in Bestinet; another total (Tk 8,750 crore) alongside the guide's Tk 24,000 crore and USD 200 crore.

MY3e-49.claim: Over 100 migrants went missing when a boat sank near the Thailand-Malaysia sea border around 6 November 2025; Malaysia's maritime enforcement agency (MMEA) had rescued 12 alive, one of them Bangladeshi, and recovered one body by 9 November near Langkawi, and Kedah police said the boat had left Buthidaung in Myanmar with about 300 aboard, who split into three smaller boats of about 100 each near the coast, as the organisers had taught them, to evade Malaysian authorities.
MY3e-49.target_section: Irregular routes, and where an irregular stay ends
MY3e-49.placement: same sea-route bullet: how it ends
MY3e-49.why_new: A sea-route disaster with a Bangladeshi aboard.

MY3e-50.claim: AFP, citing Malaysian media, reported in November 2025 that Rohingya trying to reach Malaysia or other Southeast Asian countries by sea through syndicates pay Tk 3,52,000 to 3,85,000 (USD 3,200 to 3,500) each, and Prothom Alo added that the boats are often weak and have no life jackets, or that many passengers do not wear them.
MY3e-50.target_section: Irregular routes, and where an irregular stay ends
MY3e-50.why_new: Sea-route price; compare overland Tk 7 lakh in the guide.

MY3e-51.claim: On 13 November 2025 the ACC filed a case against five recruiting agencies and their chairmen, directors and managing directors, alleging they took about Tk 314 crore 34 lakh 72 thousand 500 extra from about 18,767 Malaysia-bound people, on average five times the government-fixed Tk 78,990, its director general (prevention) Akhtar Hossain said.

MY3e-52.claim: The five agencies in the ACC's 13 November 2025 case are GMG Trading Private Limited, The GMG Associate Limited, QK Quick Express Limited, MEF Global Bangladesh Limited and Dhamasi Corporation Limited.

MY3e-53.claim: OEP (Overseas Employment Platform), built under the Ministry with the ILO and the Swiss government, has run since 19 April 2025 after the interim government scrapped the 'Ami Probashi' app, through which workers had paid the private operating company a fee on top of BMET's; it was formally launched on 19 November 2025, and its data stay with BMET.
MY3e-53.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: How do I register on OEP?
MY3e-53.placement: other: what OEP is and its history
MY3e-53.why_new: History of OEP and the Ami Probashi fee.

MY3e-54.claim: On OEP a worker registers with a mobile number, fills in a profile, pays the Tk 200 BMET registration fee online, applies for BMET clearance and downloads the clearance smart card, can contact recruiting agencies directly about jobs and can enrol at a TTC; foreign employers can register and, once the mission attests them, post demand letters that go to agencies.
MY3e-54.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: How do I register on OEP?
MY3e-54.placement: other: what you can do on it
MY3e-54.why_new: Full chain on OEP; the Malaysia guide has the registration steps (Step 1, item 1) but not the employer/demand side.

MY3e-55.claim: By 19 November 2025, 2,647 recruiting agencies had joined OEP; 10,91,161 workers had applied to BMET for clearance through it and 10,24,468 had got it, and 8,37,042 had registered for TTC training, by the figures shown on the OEP site.
MY3e-55.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: How do I register on OEP?

MY3e-56.claim: Adviser Asif Nazrul said on 19 November 2025 that Bangladesh had objected to several of Malaysia's 10 conditions and asked for the deadline to be extended, telling Malaysia that if the conditions were kept there would again be a syndicate with only a few agencies able to send workers, and that Malaysia had promised to relax them.
MY3e-56.placement: The 2026 list of 25: how it was made
MY3e-56.why_new: Dated government objection; consistent with guide's 'Malaysia relaxed three conditions and then one more' [MB0044].

MY3e-57.claim: On 20 November 2025 Immigration raided commercial areas, construction sites and vegetable farms in four areas of Cameron Highlands, Pahang, checked 1,886 foreigners and arrested 468, 174 of them Bangladeshi, for offences such as expired passports and no travel documents; some showed temporary work permits that appeared fake, Immigration's Director General Zakaria Shaaban said.

MY3e-58.claim: Those aged 20 to 54 among the people arrested in the Cameron Highlands raid were to be sent to detention depots in Kelantan, Perak and Selangor, and Immigration figures showed 83,994 foreigners had been detained across Malaysia from the start of 2025 to 18 November.
MY3e-58.why_new: Depot locations and the 2025 national detention count.

MY3e-59.claim: Zakaria Shaaban said intelligence showed Cameron Highlands had become an attractive work centre for foreigners, drawn by its hills and distance from towns, and that local businesses often prefer to hire them; the raids followed complaints from local people.
MY3e-59.why_new: Where undocumented work concentrates; may fit Irregular routes instead.

MY3e-60.claim: Bangladesh Krishi Bank, the second-largest collector of remittances in January to November 2025 (USD 277 crore), receives the most from Malaysia's Merchantrade, and also from CBL Money and NBL Money in Malaysia; its general manager said families can now receive the money directly into their own account, 24 hours a day through Bangladesh Bank, instead of collecting it with a secret PIN.
MY3e-60.placement: other: which remitters reach which bank
MY3e-60.why_new: Guide lists Merchantrade, CBL and NBL as remitters to bKash; adds the Krishi Bank payout route with its 1,038 rural branches.

MY3e-61.claim: Krishi Bank has 1,038 branches and 5 sub-branches across Bangladesh, more than any other bank in remote areas, and has run several savings schemes for migrants that held about Tk 220 crore by December 2025.

MY3e-62.claim: On the night of 7 December 2025 the Coast Guard rescued seven men and women from Jaliapalong, Ukhia, from a traffickers' den in the Baharchhara hills, Teknaf, and detained three men with a homemade firearm; a Coast Guard officer said they had been brought there to be trafficked to Malaysia by sea with promises of jobs for the men and marriage for the women, and were held while the traffickers tried to extract money.
MY3e-62.target_section: Irregular routes, and where an irregular stay ends
MY3e-62.why_new: Bangladeshi victims (Ukhia residents), not only Rohingya.

MY3e-63.claim: Citing Malaysian media, Prothom Alo reported in December 2025 that 182 Bangladeshis were detained in November alone and 377 in one raid in September, and added that Bangladeshis are detained in almost every Malaysian Immigration raid and are later sent home.

MY3e-64.claim: In the last week of November 2025 a group of Bangladeshi workers from Cumilla met near Sultan Abdul Samad Jamek Mosque, Kuala Lumpur, told Prothom Alo they had still found no work, that each had spent Tk 5 lakh through a broker, and that they were trying for factory jobs outside the capital.
MY3e-64.why_new: A late-2025 no-job case; the article does not say how or when they entered.

MY3e-65.claim: Bangladeshis in Malaysia told Prothom Alo in December 2025 that about twice the number of work-permit holders actually work there, many having gone on student visas and not returned, and an IOM report said 25 lakh people who entered Malaysia to travel had not left by 2024, 38% of them Bangladeshi.
MY3e-65.why_new: Size of the undocumented population; guide has an activists' 100,000-200,000 jobless estimate only.

MY3e-66.claim: Prothom Alo reported in December 2025 that, because Malaysia sets a minimum wage, many businesses hire undocumented workers to save costs, with Bangladeshis the largest group among them, and that documented and undocumented Bangladeshis work mostly in construction, services and manufacturing.
MY3e-66.target_section: What people believe, and the facts
MY3e-66.placement: other: why undocumented workers find work

MY3e-67.claim: By the figures Prothom Alo gave in December 2025, 50,090 Bangladeshis went to Malaysia in 2022, a record 3,51,683 in 2023, 93,632 in 2024 before the ban, and 2,486 in 2025 up to May.
MY3e-67.why_new: Exact yearly departures (guide: 50,000 and 'more than 3.5 lakh'); adds 2024 and 2025. Conflicts with Malaysia's own entry counts (49,353 and 397,548).

MY3e-68.claim: The first 23 Bangladeshi workers went to Malaysia in 1978, and the formal manpower agreement between the two countries was signed in 1992, Prothom Alo reported.

MY3e-69.claim: Prothom Alo's report of 14 December 2025 said the market that closed on 31 May 2024 had later reopened on various conditions.
MY3e-69.why_new: CONFLICT: guide says closed to new workers through agencies since 31 May 2024; Prothom Alo of 14 March 2026 also says it had been closed for nearly two years (article 63cad1bc). Likely refers to the BOESL/CLAB sending of stranded workers.

MY3e-70.claim: Remittances from Malaysia were USD 102 crore in 2021-22, 112 crore in 2022-23, 160 crore in 2023-24 and 280 crore in 2024-25, and USD 26 crore in July 2025 and 27 crore each in August and September 2025, Prothom Alo reported.
MY3e-70.why_new: Corridor remittance numbers not in the guide.

MY3e-71.claim: Mominul Islam of Chuadanga, a shop worker at Times Square, Kuala Lumpur, told Prothom Alo in December 2025 that he borrowed Tk 5 lakh to go, now earns RM2,200 (Tk 66,000) a month, and has already repaid the loan.
MY3e-71.why_new: A positive repayment case at a stated wage; the article does not give his start date.

MY3e-72.claim: Prothom Alo reported in December 2025 that 3,604 Bangladeshis had joined MM2H by 2024, fourth among nationalities, and that a 5-year visa comes with an investment of Tk 3 crore 60 lakh and a 20-year visa with more, on condition of investing in property.
MY3e-72.why_new: Bangladeshi MM2H count; guide notes Bangladesh Bank had not approved sending money abroad for MM2H [N0051], which this number sits uneasily with.

MY3e-73.claim: Tasneem Siddiqui, founding chair of RMMRU, said in December 2025 that instead of showcase manpower export the government should push to regularise undocumented Bangladeshis, as Malaysia has done before, and that if the market is again handed to a syndicate, workers will not in practice be able to join jobs.
MY3e-73.target_section: What goes wrong most, and what people wrongly believe
MY3e-73.why_new: Expert view; may be fluff under the guide's rules.

MY3e-74.claim: On 18 December 2025 a High Court bench of Justice Fatema Najib and Justice Fatema Anwar issued a rule, on a writ by M/s Afia Overseas and two other agencies, asking why the Ministry's 18 November 2025 notice setting 10 criteria for choosing private agencies for Malaysia should not be declared without lawful authority, and gave the Ministry and the BMET director general 10 days to reply.
MY3e-74.placement: The 2026 list of 25: Objections and allegations
MY3e-74.why_new: Court challenge to the criteria, not in the guide. Afia Overseas's owner Altab Khan filed the 3 September 2025 Paltan case already in the guide.

MY3e-75.claim: The writ petitioners' lawyer, Md Atikur Rahman, said the criteria would get a particular group selected, create a monopoly and exclude ordinary agencies, against an Appellate Division judgment and the Competition Act.
MY3e-75.why_new: Grounds of the challenge. NOTE: this article dates the Ministry's criteria notice 18 November 2025; article 18f13968 reported them on 29 October 2025.

MY3e-76.claim: On the night of 3 January 2026 the Navy ship BNS Swadhinata chased and stopped a wooden boat about 30 miles south-west of St Martin's Island carrying people illegally to Malaysia, rescued 263 including women and children and detained 10 gang members; the boat had no basic life-saving equipment and not enough food or water.
MY3e-76.target_section: Irregular routes, and where an irregular stay ends

MY3e-77.claim: RMMRU's report 'Trends in labour migration from Bangladesh 2025', presented on 7 January 2026, said that with work to reopen Malaysia under way, trying to reopen it again through the old syndicate's leaders without bringing them to justice was unacceptable.
MY3e-77.placement: The 2026 list of 25: Objections and allegations
MY3e-77.why_new: Researcher's position at the start of 2026.

MY3e-78.claim: RMMRU reported that 11,30,757 Bangladeshis went abroad for work in 2025, 67% of them to Saudi Arabia, then Qatar (10%), Singapore (6%), Kuwait (4%) and the Maldives (4%).
MY3e-78.why_new: Corridor comparison the format asks for: the five top destinations of 2025 listed do not include Malaysia (the article does not mention Malaysia in this list).

MY3e-79.claim: RMMRU's report said India has 192 recruiting agencies, Pakistan 464, Nepal 416 and Sri Lanka 248, while Bangladesh's, once limited to 850 to 900, were raised to 2,300 by the previous government, with 252 new licences approved in 2025; RMMRU's Tasneem Siddiqui added that 300 more were in process.
MY3e-79.why_new: Context for Malaysia's limited-list approach; guide says 'more than two thousand' via Jamaat [MB0023]. Could be CROSS-COUNTRY instead.

MY3e-80.claim: On 16 January 2026 an 18-year-old woman, Sumaiya Akter, was shot dead in Noakhaliapara, Baharchhara, Teknaf, when armed men from the hills attacked a den where a trafficking gang had gathered people to send to Malaysia by sea, a local union member said; the district police spokesman said the coastal Baharchhara area has become the main base of trafficking gangs.
MY3e-80.target_section: Irregular routes, and where an irregular stay ends
MY3e-80.why_new: Names Baharchhara as the hub; violence around the dens.

MY3e-81.claim: Md Jahangir Alam, 40, of Satkhira, who went to Malaysia through a broker at great cost in 2018, fell seriously ill there with a severe stomach problem, lost everything to brokers in the name of treatment in Malaysia without getting proper care, came home on 17 February 2026 and died on 19 February at Dhaka Medical College Hospital, where no ICU bed could be found for him.
MY3e-81.target_section: If you are injured or fall ill
MY3e-81.placement: other: Cases (the section under If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job)
MY3e-81.why_new: Case of brokers exploiting sick workers for 'treatment' in Malaysia; the article does not say whether he was documented.

MY3e-82.claim: His son Afzal Hossain, 18, said the family had to mortgage land and sell cattle to pay for his treatment in Malaysia and his hospital costs after he came home, and that he had been unable to send money home regularly.
MY3e-82.target_section: If you are injured or fall ill
MY3e-82.why_new: Cost of illness falling on the family.

MY3e-83.claim: Prothom Alo reported on 14 March 2026 that Malaysia's labour market had been closed since June 2024 over allegations of syndicate trading and could not be reopened under the interim government despite its efforts.
MY3e-83.why_new: Confirms closure as of March 2026; conflicts with the 14 December 2025 'reopened on various conditions' report.

MY3e-84.claim: Fakhrul Islam, a former BAIRA joint secretary general, told Prothom Alo in March 2026 that the Malaysia market cannot be opened through a ring.

SA3f-1.claim: In a July 2026 column, a North South University migration researcher cited an ILO 2026 forecast that if the US-Iran war drags on, total working hours in the Arab region could fall by up to 3.7%, or 10.2% if things get worse, and that the ILO warned migrant workers would bear the biggest burden as there were early signs of reduced new hiring and weaker remittances in these countries.
SA3f-1.why_new: The guide describes the 2026 war disruption to flights but not its forecast effect on hiring in the Gulf.

SA3f-2.claim: The same July 2026 column says demand across the Arab world is rising for industrial automation technicians, advanced welders, electrical and mechanical technicians, health workers, renewable energy specialists, logistics operators, IT-skilled workers and digital maintenance specialists, that repetitive and easily replaced jobs will come under pressure from automation, robotics, AI and digital management, and separately that demand for large numbers of construction workers has fallen as big infrastructure projects mature.
SA3f-2.why_new: Growth-opportunity and outlook information (one of the corridor-info aims) that the guide lacks; it is a columnist's view citing the ILO, not Saudi-specific data.

SA3f-3.claim: After the 9 August 2026 sofa-factory fire in Riyadh, Expatriates' Welfare Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury said the embassy was in constant contact with the site and local authorities and that officials had been told to bring the bodies home quickly and secure all government help and compensation for the families; the first night's reports put the toll at 10, all from Atrai, Naogaon, by the Naogaon deputy commissioner's count.
SA3f-3.target_section: If a worker dies in Saudi Arabia
SA3f-3.why_new: The guide has no case of a mass workplace death in Saudi Arabia; the initial toll of 10 was later revised to 16 (see the 10 August reports).
SA3f-3.h2: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job

SA3f-4.claim: A fire at midday on Sunday 9 August 2026 at a sofa-making factory in Riyadh killed 16 Bangladeshis: 13 from Atrai upazila, Naogaon, 2 from Naldanga, Natore, and 1 from Bagmara, Rajshahi, by the Expatriates' Welfare Ministry's preliminary identification.
SA3f-4.target_section: What goes wrong most, and what people wrongly believe
SA3f-4.why_new: No workplace-fire case in the guide. A later article (6c96dbb7) says 12 were from Atrai and 1 from Naogaon Sadar.

SA3f-5.claim: After the August 2026 Riyadh factory fire, the Foreign Ministry said Bangladesh Embassy officials went to the site straight away and worked with the Saudi authorities on identifying the dead and the formalities for the bodies, and that once identification was complete the bodies would be brought home in line with the families' consent.
SA3f-5.target_section: If a worker dies in Saudi Arabia
SA3f-5.why_new: Shows identification comes before repatriation in a mass-casualty case; the guide's death steps don't mention identification.
SA3f-5.h2: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job

SA3f-6.claim: According to the uncle of one victim, the workers killed in the 9 August 2026 Riyadh sofa-factory fire were asleep in the factory and its main gate was locked from outside, so they could not get out.
SA3f-6.why_new: The guide has nothing on workers sleeping at the workplace or locked-in housing; a relative's account, not an official finding.

SA3f-7.claim: Guffar Pramanik of Gondogohali, Atrai, Naogaon, said sending his elder son Mohan to Saudi Arabia cost Tk 5 lakh and his younger son Sumon Tk 7 lakh; according to their uncle, Mohan went about seven years before August 2026 after mortgaging the family land, brought Sumon over two years before, and both worked at the same Riyadh factory where they died in the fire.
SA3f-7.target_section: What you pay, and what you earn and keep
SA3f-7.why_new: A Tk 7 lakh price around 2024 for a visa through a brother already working at the factory is above the guide's usual Tk 4-5 lakh range.

SA3f-8.claim: The Naogaon deputy commissioner said on 10 August 2026 that the Bangladesh Embassy's labour welfare wing was identifying the fire victims and arranging to bring the bodies home, and that completing the process might take some days.
SA3f-8.target_section: If a worker dies in Saudi Arabia
SA3f-8.why_new: Who handles identification and repatriation in practice.
SA3f-8.h2: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job

SA3f-9.claim: Moyen Sheikh of Ujanpoi, Atrai, said in August 2026 that he was deep in debt from sending his son Farid, the family's only earner, to Saudi Arabia about a year and a half earlier, and did not know how he would repay it after Farid died in the Riyadh fire.
SA3f-9.target_section: What reaches home, and how long the debt takes
SA3f-9.why_new: Case of migration debt outliving the worker; the guide gives repayment time but no such case.

SA3f-10.claim: Prime Minister Tarique Rahman directed the Foreign Ministry, the Expatriates' Welfare Ministry and the Bangladesh Embassy in Riyadh to bring the bodies of the 16 fire victims home in the shortest possible time, with the Prime Minister's Office giving all cooperation, his press secretary said in August 2026.
SA3f-10.target_section: If a worker dies in Saudi Arabia
SA3f-10.why_new: Context for how long the high-profile case took despite top-level orders (bodies arrived 27 August, see SA3f drafts from bc861f5d). This article dates the fire to Monday, the others to Sunday 9 August.
SA3f-10.h2: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job

SA3f-11.claim: Moyna Begum of Gondogoali, Atrai, Naogaon, said her elder son Mohon went to Saudi Arabia seven years before August 2026 by mortgaging land and borrowing Tk 4 lakh from a samity (savings association), a debt that had grown with interest to Tk 8 lakh, still unpaid when he and his brother died in the Riyadh factory fire.
SA3f-11.why_new: Shows a samity loan doubling over seven years; the guide's borrowing section has no such case. The article gives Mohon's age as 22 while 684eb2b4 gives 42.

SA3f-12.claim: Shahinur Rahman of Par-Naogaon, Naogaon, borrowed Tk 5.7 lakh from a samity against his homestead land at Par-Boalia to go to Saudi Arabia about five months before he died in the August 2026 Riyadh fire, and his widow said the samity could take the land if the loan is not repaid.
SA3f-12.why_new: A 2026 migration cost (Tk 5.7 lakh) and the risk to mortgaged homestead land when a worker dies; not in the guide.

SA3f-13.claim: Rubel Pramanik of Atrai, Naogaon, was sent to Saudi Arabia on borrowed money about three months before he died in the August 2026 Riyadh fire, in the hope that he would repay the debt and ease the family's hardship, the article reports.
SA3f-13.target_section: What reaches home, and how long the debt takes
SA3f-13.why_new: Case of a worker dying within months of arrival with the whole debt outstanding.

SA3f-14.claim: Of the 16 Bangladeshis killed in the 9 August 2026 Riyadh fire, 9 were identified by fingerprint checks and their bodies were due to arrive on Biman flight BG-340 at Hazrat Shahjalal airport on Thursday 27 August, while the other 7 were still being identified by DNA test.
SA3f-14.target_section: If a worker dies in Saudi Arabia
SA3f-14.why_new: Gives a real timeline (18 days for fingerprint-identified bodies; longer for DNA) that the guide's 'How long does the Board take' Need to know lacks.
SA3f-14.h2: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job

SA3f-15.claim: In August 2026 the embassy's Counsellor (Labour) in Riyadh sent a signed letter to the Atrai upazila administration giving the arrival date of the bodies, and the upazila told the families to receive them at Shahjalal airport.
SA3f-15.target_section: If a worker dies in Saudi Arabia
SA3f-15.why_new: How families learn when a body will arrive (via the upazila administration); the guide says only that the Board's desk calls the family.
SA3f-15.h2: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job

SA3f-16.claim: When the nine identified bodies from the Riyadh fire were received at Dhaka airport at about 4:30 pm on 27 August 2026, one relative from each family was present, and the bodies were then taken home by vehicle, according to the Atrai upazila executive officer.
SA3f-16.target_section: If a worker dies in Saudi Arabia
SA3f-16.why_new: Practical detail on airport hand-over; also notes the welfare minister and foreign state minister received the bodies.
SA3f-16.h2: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job

SA3f-17.claim: Rabiul Islam (28) of Naldanga, Natore, was sent to Saudi Arabia about five years before his death in the August 2026 Riyadh fire on a Tk 5 lakh loan, went through a broker ring and did not get an iqama for his first three years, so he could not work regularly or earn much, his father said.
SA3f-17.target_section: Irregular routes and how they end
SA3f-17.why_new: A named case of the no-iqama route the guide describes in general terms.

SA3f-18.claim: As of 28 August 2026, seven of the 16 Riyadh fire victims were still unidentified and their families demanded that the bodies be identified and returned quickly; the Naldanga acting UNO said two Naldanga victims' bodies had not yet been identified and so could not be brought home, and the Naogaon deputy commissioner said DNA tests were being used to identify the remaining Naogaon victims.
SA3f-18.target_section: If a worker dies in Saudi Arabia
SA3f-18.why_new: Bodies that need DNA identification wait longer; not in the guide.
SA3f-18.h2: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job

SA3f-19.claim: Shyamal Uddin Majhi (46) of Bagmara, Rajshahi, who went to Saudi Arabia on borrowed money eight years earlier, died in the Riyadh fire; his coffin was opened at home in the presence of police on 28 August 2026, his elder sister was worried about how his debt would be repaid, and a former union chairman asked the government for financial help for the family.
SA3f-19.target_section: If a worker dies in Saudi Arabia
SA3f-19.why_new: Shows a coffin opened under police presence at home; a detail families may meet.
SA3f-19.h2: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job

SA3f-20.claim: Md Kamrul Zaman (37) of Begumganj, Noakhali, who worked at a shopping mall in Taif, was shot dead at dawn on Sunday 30 August 2026 while phoning his wife after his shift; according to his cousin the gunman was a young Saudi who he heard then shot himself, and the motive was not known.
SA3f-20.target_section: If a worker dies in Saudi Arabia
SA3f-20.why_new: A violent-death case; the guide has no homicide case. Family account only; the Begumganj UNO had no details.
SA3f-20.h2: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job

SA3f-21.claim: According to the CID, a ring took Tk 6 lakh from a man for a fast-food shop job in Saudi Arabia, sent him there on 7 June 2025 with no job, held him in a house, beat him and demanded more money from his family for an iqama; he escaped, was detained by Saudi police and sent back on 22 July 2026, and his wife filed a human trafficking case at Savar police station.
SA3f-21.target_section: If an agency, broker or relative takes your money
SA3f-21.why_new: A case of the 'pay more for the iqama' extortion with confinement in Saudi Arabia and a trafficking case filed from home; the guide's section lacks this pattern.

SA3f-22.claim: The CID's human trafficking unit arrested ring member Md Salman Hossain (33) at Dhaka's Shahjalal airport on 31 August 2026; the CID said the victim had been held in Salman's own house in Saudi Arabia.
SA3f-22.target_section: If an agency, broker or relative takes your money
SA3f-22.why_new: Shows a trafficking case leading to an arrest when the accused flew home.

SA3f-23.claim: A September 2026 column, citing BMET via the BSS news agency, says about 11.17 lakh Bangladeshis went abroad for work in 2025, more than 7.52 lakh of them to Saudi Arabia.
SA3f-23.why_new: Conflict: the guide gives 755,194 to Saudi Arabia in 2025 [SB0017]; 8cd6aabe gives 11.32 lakh total abroad in 2025 vs 11.17 lakh here.

SA3f-24.claim: International media reported that on 9 August 2026 Yemen's Houthis attacked an Aramco facility in the Jazan area of Saudi Arabia, two days after Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan signed a joint defence pact in Makkah.
SA3f-24.why_new: The guide mentions Houthi attacks on airports only; attacks also hit oil facilities where Bangladeshis work (see 74b2212a).

SA3f-25.claim: Md Sohag of Companiganj, Noakhali, died of a reported heart attack at home in Abha on Monday 31 August 2026; according to his sister, his iqama had expired some months earlier and his passport had also expired and he had been unable to renew them; his body was in a hospital cold store and his sister asked the government to bring it home.
SA3f-25.target_section: If a worker dies in Saudi Arabia
SA3f-25.why_new: Case of a death with expired iqama and passport, where the guide says repatriation takes much longer [E0090].
SA3f-25.h2: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job

SA3f-26.claim: Md Sohag's sister said their father Rafiq Uddin also died in Saudi Arabia, in 2003, and the family could not bring his body home, so he was buried there.
SA3f-26.target_section: If a worker dies in Saudi Arabia
SA3f-26.why_new: Older case of burial abroad because repatriation failed; one sentence in the article garbles this, the quoted words are the sister's.
SA3f-26.h2: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job

SA3f-27.claim: On 7 September 2026, Abdul Karim of Kanaighat, Sylhet, who had a ticket home after about three years in Saudi Arabia, and his neighbour Khalid Ahmad were killed when their car crashed at Al-Khurma on the way from Taif to Jeddah airport; Karim's son, also working there, broke an arm.
SA3f-27.target_section: If a worker dies in Saudi Arabia
SA3f-27.why_new: Road deaths are the largest accident category (see b9d4992b); the guide has no Saudi road-death case.
SA3f-27.h2: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job

SA3f-28.claim: Another migrant from Kanaighat, Sylhet, died in a road accident in Saudi Arabia in July 2026, after five Kanaighat migrants died in a road accident in Qatar in June 2026.
SA3f-28.target_section: If a worker dies in Saudi Arabia
SA3f-28.why_new: Pattern of road deaths among workers from one upazila.
SA3f-28.h2: If a worker dies, is injured or loses the job

SA3f-29.claim: By BMET data, 105,466 Bangladeshi women went abroad for work in 2022 and 62,317 in 2025, a fall of about 41%, while in the first eight months of 2026 more than 42,000 women went to 48 countries, about 14% (5,214) more than a year before, over 90% of them to Saudi Arabia and Jordan.
SA3f-29.target_section: CROSS-COUNTRY: How many women work abroad?
SA3f-29.why_new: Annual and 2026 women's departure numbers; the cross-country doc has only the stock and long-run totals.

SA3f-30.claim: Anjana of Manikganj, who had worked in Lebanon, Jordan, the UAE and Saudi Arabia since 2012, returned from Saudi Arabia on 20 March 2026 after 1 month 3 days in which she worked 5 days and spent the rest being beaten at the Saudi recruiting agency's office, then paid for her own ticket home with money from Bangladesh; she said the agency is paid for each woman it sends, so it sends women without a job.
SA3f-30.why_new: The guide's domestic-worker section says the Saudi recruitment office must house and support a worker; this case shows abuse at that office and the worker paying her own fare (Section 'Scams' under Work visa: domestic worker).

SA3f-31.claim: Sanjida Akhter of Narsingdi, back from Saudi Arabia in 2025 after 2 months 25 days, said her employer made her work in his own house, his mother's and his in-laws', fed her only bread, and returned her to the Saudi recruiting agency's office when she fell ill, where the abuse began; she paid for her own ticket home and came back empty-handed.
SA3f-31.why_new: Case of work in several houses (barred by Saudi rules the guide cites, D0012) and abuse at the recruitment office; target is the If something goes wrong section under Work visa: domestic worker.

SA3f-32.claim: An OKUP study in 2025 found that 94% of women workers forced to return had suffered regular physical and mental abuse abroad, 47% sexual harassment, and 82% had worked from dawn to midnight.
SA3f-32.why_new: Not Saudi-only (all destinations); target is Work visa: domestic worker, If something goes wrong, or CROSS-COUNTRY: What are a domestic worker's rights?

SA3f-33.claim: State Minister for Expatriates' Welfare Md Nurul Haque said in September 2026 that legal aid had been started in 13 countries and a safe home runs in Saudi Arabia, and that abuse had fallen as a result.
SA3f-33.why_new: Confirms safe homes still run (guide: Riyadh, Jeddah, Madinah [E0038]); the 13-country legal aid is new but the article gives no how-to.

SA3f-34.claim: People in the migration sector said in September 2026 that women workers going abroad don't know the language and have no cooking or housework training, that employers (kafils) make them work in several homes and abuse them, and that Saudi Arabia is turning to alternative markets, taking workers from African countries.
SA3f-34.target_section: Women domestic workers: the money should run the other way
SA3f-34.why_new: Competition from African workers is new; training gaps contrast with the compulsory one-month course in the guide.

SA3f-35.claim: More than 28 lakh Bangladeshi workers were working in Saudi Arabia in September 2026, making it Bangladesh's largest labour market, according to Prothom Alo.
SA3f-35.why_new: The guide gives yearly departures but no figure for Bangladeshis working in Saudi Arabia now.
